title: For speech, this microphone is a stalwart classic for a reason.
text:
This microphone is meant for speech, it has a mid-forward, smooth response.

The omni pattern means there is nearly no proximity effect so you don't get the muddy loading of the low mid frequencies if you are not disciplined about positioning. This is excellent for husky, bass or baritone voices. It has a very natural room sound due to the pattern as well.

The pop filter on this mic is one of the very best there is. Of over a dozen mics I own, this is the only one where I can use it bare without any wind screen over it. The damping for handling noise is also incredibly done.

Even with the omni pattern, it still rejects background noise quite well.

The runner up for me for speech is the Shure SM-57 but it requires a wind screen for sure and the speaker needs to stay in a disciplined position to maintain a steady sound quality. For ENG/interview use, the RE50b is far and away the right option as the 57 isn't meant for that level of rough and tumble handling.

I never owned or used one of these until now and I'm surprised I'd never run across one earlier.

For people doing podcasting or recording of speech who are new and don't have command of EQ and advanced processing equipment, this mic will give you a giant advantage as its default sound quality is far cleaner than most other mics. It has a high enough output that most USB interfaces or budget mic pre-amps will handle it well.

title: It's a classic for a reason
text:
This is a classic microphone for a reason. Smooth frequency response, nice detail and decent output level. I've used these for years on stage and now I use one for speech use stand mounted. For speech you definitely want to add the Shure windscreen for it.

For speech I prefer this due to the narrower profile and the black windscreen vs the silver ball on the SM-58. The foam screen for this mic actually works better than the ball does as well. It looks less obnoxious on camera.

I have a very bass heavy voice and many mics have far too much low-mid and bass emphasis that I have to spend a lot of time fiddling with to mitigate. This mic has a great sound profile for those with heavy bass/baritone voice profiles. It has a smooth and natural top-end as well that doesn't exaggerate the gravely overtones in my voice.

I have a pile of mics here and it's almost funny that I landed on this one as my favorite. "There is a mic for every voice." I've always said.

title: If you use an SM-57 for speech, this is a must have and works perfectly.
text: Simply, I use an SM-57 stand mounted for speech use and this windscreen is perfectly suited for it. I set it about 1/2" off the grille of the mic underneath.  I prefer this combo as it's narrower and black vs the round silver ball of the SM-58 and frankly, this wind screen works better than a 58 anyway...it just isn't as durable for knocking around.

title: Solid noise isolation, aggressive sound profile, coiled cord is not great more than 3' from device
text:
These have very good noise isolation, almost like hearing protection. If you want to block out ambient sounds these will work great. They are so sealed up however that they will not be the best if you are monitoring yourself speaking or singing as you will hear the rumbling head harmonic resonances with these.

The sound profile on these is very aggressive, very bright upper mid and highs. It's great for clarity when listening at low volumes but I find it a bit fatiguing over time. They kind of remind me of what I remember of Sony 7506s but I don't currently have a pair to A/B.

These would be good board/live mixing headphones due to the isolation and bright character in high noise environments.

The cord is very annoying, it's a decent quality cord but tightly coiled and if you sit more than 3' from anything it will pull heavily on you. If I'm going to keep using these, I'm going to need to take a heat gun to this cord to let it out several feet.

The cord would be nice for walking around with a player but my headphone distribution amp at my desk is about 3' from me and the cord is hanging in the air horizontally putting drag on my chin right now, very annoying.

If you don't need the noise isolation, Beyerdynamic DT-880 or AKG 240 Studio with open backs have much more smooth and neutral sound profiles. The DT-880 are still my go to for all day listening.

title: I was curious...and I'm not sure this is even worth $25
text:
So obviously at $25 my expectations were low, but occasionally I find things from China that are very high value for the money. This is not one of them.

This is poor quality, even compared to tearing apart a cheap desk lamp to mount something to. Very flimsy build, extremely poor hinge/joint design, terribly poor quality springs.

If you want the appearance of having a studio boom or want to support something super light weight like a plastic housed CCD cam, it will work for a while.

If you want to mount a basic studio mic like a Shure SM58, this will barely do the job and forget about any true studio condenser or a broadcast, large element mic, it's just not up to doing that.

If money is tight, a plain old telescoping mic stand will be a FAR more stable platform for the dollar.

This is not a bargain from China, it's basically going in the trash here.

title: Pricey but you get what you pay for
text:
This is a very solidly made shock mount, all metal with nicely machined threads and pivot points. This is pro quality, not a look alike.

My only nit to pick is that the mount point is probably 1mm "off center" with the weld so it's not perfectly optically square when I look at it. Most probably wouldn't even notice.

title: A classic and a staple to have in your gear pile
text:
This mic has been around forever for a reason. It is an extremely versatile microphone that can be applied in many roles. A big part of the versatility is a relatively high output level, large diaphragm and the really well engineered variable high pass filter ring.

The high pass filter selector takes this from a very powerful bottom end response for capturing bass cabinets and toms to being able to thin it out to use for things like an overhead mic for drums or communications grade speech recording.

For voicover or singing work you will need to manage plosives with pop filters or application of compressors. It has a great articulate quality for voice with the emphasis on the upper mid-range frequency response. Once managed it performs very well across many types of voices. I have a lot of low frequency energy in my voice and run these at the mid-point selection of the high pass filter selector. Works great.

The cardioid pattern has a nice forgiving sweet spot to it allowing for some freedom of movement with a predictable and manageable proximity effect. With practice you can get some great dynamic speech results as well as vocal effects while singing.

If you are strictly doing voiceover work and don't have appropriate outboard processing gear or experience with processing, other mic designs like the EV RE series, the Rode or the Heil PR40 may make it easier for you, but this microphone has broader applications.

title: Good value for the price, very effective dead-cat in wind.
text:
The Rode VideoMicro really improved audio vs the internal mic of my FZ300, the shotgun pattern works well and the dead-cat wind screen is very effective. Good value for the price.

Oddly, I also have the VideoMic Me and the front to back rejection of the Me is a lot higher than this mic, which surprised me. It has some front to back and side rejection, but it isn't as pronounced as the Me.

Weirdly Amazon seems to have linked the VideoMicro and the VideoMicMe as one product for this review submission, they are not or at least my two examples perform pretty differently.

text: Capture the internal attack sound of the kick and the thump from the outside. Works great in a combo setup. Recommended for recording acoustic drums.

title: Best value in an expression pedal
text: Great value, especially if you can find it on sale. We have a few of these in use in our rehearsal space, for our keys and bass player. Our keyboard player uses it for a volume pedal. Our bass player uses it with his Zoom B3 bass pedal for volume or wah effects. Does the job well.

title: Awesome pedal
text: The standard Blues Driver pedal is a well-known workhorse in the blues world. The Waza craft customization adds an extra layer of options to the sounds you can create. I bought this pedal for use in my studio and rehearsal space, and our guitar player immediately loved it and wanted to know if I would part with it. Of course I said no. I think I'll hang onto this one as long as I'm making music. It may say Blues Driver on it, but you can use it for other genres as well. It's a great sounding pedal.

title: OK for the price, but required repair
text: The pedal has had infrequent use on a practice pedalboard I keep at my house for visiting players. The toothed gear slipped off the internal potentiometer. I took the pedal apart, slipped the gear back on, and it is working again - for now. There is no retention mechanism for this gear, it slips onto the shaft of the potentiometer and is expected to just stay there. Seems like a flaw in the design. For the price it is an OK pedal, the wah and volume functions work as advertised, it is small and doesn't take up much space on the pedalboard. The quality of construction is the weak spot and I expect it to stop working again.

title: Good quality
text: Better than others. No rust like I saw with a different brand. Added this to the top of a chrome mic stand that our guitar player uses, so he can get his mouth on the mic better. He had an aversion to boom stands. He had an aversion to any music gear that didn't exist in 1972. This helps give him a little more clearance between the mic and his guitar.

title: Rusty Chrome
text: I bought this to use on a chrome mic stand. Unfortunately, the first one I ordered was fairly rusty on the inside threads, as well as the spring inside the core. I returned it and asked for a replacement, which was also a little rusty. I'll probably send it back as well and look for a different brand. I ordered a black version of this as well and it is not rusty.

title: Right shape, wrong size
text: These look exactly like the bushings that came with my '90s MIM Precision bass, but are slightly bigger. Tried tapping in with dead-blow hammer. Got it in but it made a hairline crack in the maple. Whoops. Ended up sanding the holes to get them to fit.

title: It seems to work for SM94
text: It is a tight fit, but it will take my older SM94 soon condenser mics. They are 24mm, not 20 like most pencil mics. They work and don't seem like they will snap right away, so that's good. Had a little trouble finding clips that work for this mic.

title: Fit a '95 MIM P Basd
text: I was worried that it wouldn't fit. It was a wee bit tight around the pickups, but all in all, guys great and the screw holes line up perfectly. I works definitely purchase again, if I had another Mexican Precision Bass that need a facelift. Even can with screws, and a pick.

title: Zero wiggle
text: The install went smooth. I used a spare nut from the old mono jack, as others have pointed out, you may need a second nut to get the placement height right on your pickguard or metal boat. I recommend this jack, it's well built and the connection is solid.

title: I have several of these and recommend them
text: I've added tablet holders to all the mic stands (4) in the band room, I added another to my stationary bike so I can watch videos there, too. I recommend the Hola mic stands as well, good features at a great price 👍

title: Good, not great
text: The cables are sturdy and perhaps just a little too long. I prefer this type of cable for pedalboards, but other brands I have are a little shorter so there is less extra cable between the pedals. That said, they seem well made and do the jobb and the price is right.

title: Overrated board with design issues
text:
Disappointed after reading all of the great reviews. The two tabs and strap they supply to attach your power supply don't work. I ended up using hook and loop. The holes for your power cables to come out of your power supply are too small and far apart. I'm using right-angle cables just to get the cables into the power supply, due to lack of clearance near the two holes, which should not be necessary.

The top of the board is OK, but not great. The pedals attach fine, but the large spaces are overkill for routing cables and because of the poor power supply attachment and location, almost worthless.

At this point, disappointed with this purchase but unfortunately didn't figure out all of this until after sticking on the hook and loop and starting to build my board.

Look elsewhere for a better, more practical design.

title: Low cost, basic fit
text: These covers don't taper very well. I have purchased other covers that taper around the head of the mic better. I would give them three stars, but they were inexpensive.

title: Great for electronic drums
text: These Zildjian anti-vibes are the only sticks I use on my electronic drums. I wish they came in more sizes, like 8D, the slightly longer cousin of the 7A. But I've been using these sticks for the last 5 years with either Promark or Vater grip tape, and the combo helps alleviate the shock of hitting the bouncier mesh drum heads and rubber cymbals. Highly recommended!

title: Fuzzy beater
text: So far I really like this beater. Using it on my Ludwig Classic kit, and it gives you a really nice feel. I think it is just a word beater with some fuzz on it, but it works great

title: Bargain Double-Kick is Still Kicking
text: I've had this pedal for a few years now, and it still works great. Nothing has broken on it. My adjustments have held firm with no issues. I also like that it doesn't weigh as much as some of the other double-chain drive pedals out there. For this price point, I believe this is the best double-kick out there. Gibraltar came out with the new GTC6-DB kick at NAMM 2020, and and today's pricing shows it is $80 more than this pedal, but if you closely look at them both you can see they are pretty similar. Let's face it, double-kick pedal prices are insane. I suppose some of them are worth it, however many are not. Anyways, if you want to spend less than $200, this is a good option while it lasts. Hopefully they don't discontinue them too soon.

title: Roland durability in a handy form factor
text: Clamps onto the side of my 14" snare drum, and allows me to trigger percussion or accent sounds very easily. This is my second one, I've had the first one for several years with no issues. That one is mounted on my edrum kit.

title: Solid, but not quick release
text: Sturdy tablet holder, that attaches to a mic stand and is very solid. If you need a quick-release model, keep shopping. If you want one for the band practice room that holds your lyrics and set list, and you're not going to move it around a bunch (or maybe you are, and you're the patient sort) then buy it.

title: Great kit for repair or upgrade of P Bass
text: I used this wiring kit on a Squier P Bass that is about 8 years old. The pots on the import bass were very small and cheap, the soldering had failed, so I opted to rip and replace. I had to drill out the holes in the pick guard to make the larger pots fit. The only thing I didn't like about this kit is the cloth- braided wire. It's hard to work with. I understand they are going for that vintage vibe with this kit, but plastic-coated wire is a little easier to strip. All in all, this is a fair deal, and more convenient than buying the parts separately. I ended up replacing the pickups, too, and used the Seymour Duncan wiring diagram. The bass now sounds better than ever.

title: Great for gigging, just works!
text: I played a show with this pedal last Saturday. My number one favorite feature, it packs up easy and is super light-weight. I have a couple other pedals that are bigger, fancier, and a lot more trouble to transport. I'm going to keep this one just for gigging. It works fine, really, so if you were going to own only one pedal, this would be a fine choice.

title: Thin
text: These are quite thin, hopefully they do the job and protect my wood rim.

title: Best bang for the buck in mic stands
text: For the money, these are probably the best deal on Amazon. They are sturdy and easy to setup. They are not cheap and hard to adjust like other stands in this price range. The telescoping arm works well, I can reach it behind my drum kit, or you could keep it shorter for vocalists or guitar players. The two pack is a great deal.

title: Good but loud!
text: These are crazy loud. If you were are practicing at home, get something quieter, or prepare to annoy everyone else in the band, and also your neighbors. Other than that, they are great maracas, and cut through on stage very well.

title: Best clutch for the money
text: Great clutch, well designed and easy to use. I might need to replace all my others with this type. The design is simple and sturdy.

title: Feels good, wears quickly
text: The drum tape is OK. It is less expensive than other brands. It feels fine, it just doesn't hold up as well as the other brand I frequently use, which makes it less of a good deal.

title: Expensive, but one of the better drum dampeners
text: These work very well for drum dampening.  I use two smaller ones on my snare, and one bigger on the toms. Taking off one star due to high price for what you get.

title: The best drum key I've owned
text: I love this drum key. The piece that extends at the top allows you to finger tighten the drum heads, which makes evenly tuning the head easier. That one feature is very helpful. The key also fits very well, and is solidly built. If I need more, I'll definitely but another of these.

title: Get a cover like this!
text: Good for your EV speakers. Protects them from damage as you haul them around. These seem to be high quality, we'll see how they hold up to some abuse...

title: Great sticks for edrums!
text: I have the same pair from three years ago, and I use them with my Roland mesh-head drum set. I put ProMark stick rapp on the sticks as well, and between the two, the sticks are much more comfortable than standard sticks on bouncy edrum heads. I highly recommend them.

title: Heavy duty and also just plain heavy
text: This is a well-made boom stand that is best used with heavy cymbals, like a 22" ride or  mounting your upper tom on it. For smaller crash cymbals, it's probably overkill. It is heavy! That's my chief complaint, just a lot of weight to lug around. It has memory locks, and is very adjustable, no issues there. All in all a great stand.

title: Vintage look, light weight, no memory locks
text:
I like this stand a lot. It looks great, and functions well holding up a smaller crash cymbal. I'm using it in straight mode right now, not using the boom, and I really like that you can go either way with this stand. I also really like how light weight the stand is, and the small tubes and single-braced legs. It makes it easier to move these around, and if you have a giant bag full of heavy stands to lug around, you know what I'm talking about. The only reason for the 4 stars instead of 5, is that the stands should have memory locks, especially since these stands cost as much as more middle or heavy-weight versions. Memory locks just make setup and breakdown quicker and easier. If they add those, this is a 5-star stand. This one joins my flat base snare stand, and likely won't be my last flat addition from the Gibraltar series.

Edit Feb 2020: The Ludwig Atlas Classic stand has reversible rubber feet. Then you can have two flat-base stands next to each other and the legs can overlap. That is not the case with this version. If you need two of these stands next to each other, you may want to opt for the Atlas.

title: Roland makes the best cymbal pads
text: These pads are well-made and can take years of playing. I've had the CY-12C pads for years and they still work like new. These aren't inexpensive, but if you can afford them for your kit, you won't be disappointed. Make sure your trigger module supports two-zone cymbals.

title: This is a non-slip yoga, err, drum mat
text: I have a yoga mat that is basically the same material. I tell you what though, my drums do not slide on this mat, they sink-in and stay put. The price is right, too. And in a pinch, you and your partner could do couple's yoga on it. I'm not sure how durable it is, however. I have not moved it around very much or packed it off anywhere yet, so who knows. But in my spare bedroom, it works very well. Just taking off one star, because I don't think it will last very long.

title: The Best Sticks for edrums
text:
If you play electronic drums, you know they can be bouncy, and the rubber cymbal pads can transfer the shock up your arms and into your shoulders. These sticks, combined with Promark Stick Rapp, work great, they are the only ones I use on my Roland kit.

https://smile.amazon.com/ProMark-SRBLA-Black-Stick-Rapp/dp/B0071LLXH0/

title: Decent audio qualty, poor fit
text: I have a bug head. A huge cranium. My hat size is 7-3/4. When I put these headphones on, the bottom half of each earpiece has a gap. No adjustment has fixed it. I suppose if you have a smaller head, these would work OK, but for me, they just don't sit on my large melon correctly. That said, even with a little gap, the audio quality is not bad, especially at the price point. IF you want some low-budget cans to record your basket-weaving podcast, these would work fine.

title: Excellent direct-drive kick pedal, good value too
text: This is my first direct-drive pedal, and I've only been using it over the weekend, but I really like it. Has great feel and doesn't squeak (yet). I'm not sure what I was expecting compared to a chain drive, but the difference is very subtle. Gibraltar is a good value in kick pedals. This one has all the features I need at a very reasonable price compared to the Iron Cobra, Eliminator, and DW 5000 series stuff.

title: Good hardware for a trigger module
text: I have a Roland TD-25 mounted on this arm, and it works great. It's not very long, but it's very adjustable and sturdy. I like to position the module between my hi-hat and rack tom, as shown in the picture. This arm works well for it's intended use. If you have a very large kit and you need to hang the trigger module way off to the side, you might want to use a different bracket. For my 4-piece kit with 20" kick, it is the perfect size.

title: Nice snare stand at an amazing price
text: The stand is well-built and uses metal in all the right spots. This is my first piece of "flat" hardware, and I really like it. Very adjustable, yet stable. Legs don't get in the way behind a small kit. I recommend this stand even if you don't have all flat-leg hardware. It's a solid choice.

title: Most band for the buck mic stand
text: For the money, this is a good mic stand. It doesn't compete with pro gear, and you should not compare it to stands that cost two or three times as much. If you need pro level, spend more money. That said, I have had this stand for three years, and I use it next to my drums frequently. It has a long boom that works great for that mic position. I recommend this stand, and will probably buy another for my practice space.

title: Solid throne
text: Very solid round throne. It's comfortable for me to sit on for an hour or two at a time. I like the memory lock settings that make it easy to break down and set back up. Overall, very pleased with it, and anyone looking for a pro quality throne should consider it.

title: Pig hog makes fine cables
text: Quality cable that I use to connect a keyboard to a mixer. I wish they made them in a wider variety of sizes, currently 10 foot looks like the longest available.

title: Medium Celluloid Picks - What's Not to Like?
text: Fender medium celluloid picks, always great to have on hand for guitar players that like celluloid. These are a decent price and good quality, I recommend them, if medium-weight is your thing.

title: Low-cost instrument patch cables are a great deal
text: This low-cost cable pack works great for small mixer or synth setups, when you just need to patch a few things together. All of the cables seem to work fine with no issues. You can't beat the price, that's for sure. I'll probably end up buying two or three more of these packs, just to keep on hand. I always seem to need one more of these short patch cables than I have laying around.

title: Heavy XLRM to TRS Cable, Good for Speakers, Not Good for Mics
text: These cables appear to be well-built, heavy-duty cables, sporting a thick 16 gauge cable. That makes these better suited for speaker applications than other cables with finer gauges between 20-24 gauge,  which are better suited for microphone or other line-level applications. If you are a singer and looking for a mic cable, I recommend you look for something lighter gauge, and optionally quad-star shielding, as that would be better for that application, and less heavy to pull around in a hand-held mic situation.

title: Solid Boom Stand, Worth Every Penny
text: This K & M is by far the best boom stand I own. I wish I had a few more, they are so much better built than the cheaper knock-off versions. Everything is metal or heavy-duty on this stand. I expect it will last years in my band practice room. Definitely splurge for this version, if you can afford it.

title: Excellent Drum Pad Stand
text: This is a great stand for the Roland SPD-SX drum sample pad, if you buy the accessory that attaches to the pad. Very well built, and cheaper than the Roland branded version. If I could change anything about it, I would want to make the top section a little taller, so that if I played my pad standing up, I'd having the option of raising it a little higher. But as I use it sitting down behind my drum kit now, that's not really a problem, and I think for most people, it's plenty tall as it is.

title: It's a patch cord! So just buy it already!
text: It's a patch cord for effects pedals, or whatever use you may have. It's works fine, I hope it holds up to some abuse. I'd give it 5 stars, but the metal sleeves need to be tightened from time to time, which I guess is to be expected, but annoying none the less.

title: Decent, Low-Cost Cowbell
text: The size and price are right for this cowbell. The welds won't win any awards, but for the price, it seems like a good deal. The tone is a bit ringy, and it does come with some dampening foam on the inside, but one piece fell out almost immediately. I've got more foam weatherstripping laying around, so I'll use some of that.

title: Must-have for guitar and bass
text: If you play guitar or want a gift for a guitar player/bass player. buy one of these, they work well, and are very portable.

title: Great music stand for use with a keyboard
text: I'm using this with an On Stage Z-style keyboard stand, and it works great. If you have a keyboard without a sheet music stand built-in, your options are limited. I combined it with an On-Stage KSA7575+ mic bracket, and together they are a reasonably priced solution to this problem, with the added bonus of easy break-down for travel.

title: Lightweight Hi-Hats Sound Great
text: I have had these hi-hats for a month or so, and I am happy with my purchase. These are thin hats; if you play loud rock music, these are not for you. They are also not for you if you bash your cymbals hard. If you are looking for hats that have a "chick sound that really cuts through", these are also probably not for you. If you are looking for lighter hats that have a drier sound, then these are recommended. Very nice hats, at a great price-point.

title: Low-cost cable doesn't work for me
text: I purchased this cable a while ago to connect a mic to a mixer. The cable doesn't give a noise-free connection, so I basically can't use it for what it was made for. Other cables I have work fine on the same inputs and mics, so I must assume it is this cable that causes the bad connection.

title: A greate tray to attach to a music or microphone stand
text: This works great attached to a laptop stand next to my drumset. I don't travel with this, so I'm not taking it on and off, it stays put. It's great for holding a frosty beverage, phone, and other junk you need to take out of your pocket before you start playing. It was a good investment, as it is very sturdy, and has been holding up well to abuse.

title: Heavy-duty Bass Drum Pedal with interesting design, watch for loose parts
text:
This 9711GS pedal is an interesting piece of equipment. I really like it, and I would give it 5 stars, except for two issues I've had with it.

1.) First, the chrome metal top for the batter came loose the first time I used the pedal. Not a huge deal, a couple drops of Gorilla glue fixed it, but irritating none the less. The cap is metal, and if you're going to use the cylindrical weights that come with it to customize the batter, you'll need it to stay firmly in place.

2.) After using the pedal a couple of weeks, during a longer session last night, the bolt holding the spring in place came loose, and the pedal became less responsive and started bottoming-out on the metal clamp. I had to stop, take the pedal off, adjust it, and tighten everything back down.

Other than these two issues, for the price, this is a great pedal. It is much cheaper than DW, Tama Iron Cobra or Pearl Eliminator pedals. It is very customizable, and comes with the wrench you use to adjust it. It comes with a bag.

I'm currently using it with a Roland drum trigger pad, and I also use it with an acoustic 22" kick drum.

If you do end up buying this pedal, when you first get it, read the manual and adjust it to your liking, and then tighten all the bolts very snugly. Also check the top of the beater for that piece being loose. After that, it should be smooth sailing.

title: Port hole does the job quickly and easily
text: I used this on the stock resonant head on my Gretsch drums. It worked great, was easy to use, and install time, including the hole cutting, took about 5 minutes. Buy one of these if you just need a hole in your head, and you don;t want to spend the money on a new one.

title: Good value in a cymbal bag
text: This bag holds all my cymbals, and seems well made, but I'm knocking off one star for the hi-hat section, it's a hair too small. Otherwise it's a quality bag at a good price. It holds three cymbals and a set of hi-hat.

title: Great for playing edrums
text: These sticks are a good choice when playing and electric kit. I combine them with wraps, and the combination works well. I was getting some numbness and tingling after playing for extended periods, and this combo has solved that problem.

title: Built to Last
text: This is a fantastic hi-hat stand. It is heavy-duty and works great, like most middle to high-end DW hardware. Because it only has two legs, it is easy to use with a double-kick pedal. If you only want to have to buy one stand, and you want it to be very well built and last for a long time, this one is highly recommended.

title: Great price for OK quality cables
text: You will be hard pressed to find a colored TRS to TRS cable anywhere for a price this low. That said, one of my cables was faulty out of the package. It was missing the clear plastic insulating tube that the other cables have on each end. My advice to you, check and make sure the plastic insulator is on each end of each cable before using, and if it is missing, cover the soldered connections with electrical tape. I would give these cables 5 stars if they used a hear shrink stain relief insulator,  but for this price I'm probably asking too much.

title: Not Fit for the Studio or Mixing
text:
These headphones are advertised as professional studio monitor and mixing headphones, and they aren't. They are very muddy in the low end, bass tones are hard to discern, the sound is just not nearly neutral or clear enough for mixing work. They remind me of cheaper earbuds that advertise as having more bass. I suppose these might be OK for listening to MP3s on your phone or something, but for over the ear studio monitors, they are not up to the task. There are better headphones for studio work out there, you may have to spend a bit more than $39 to get them. But if you watch the sales, you could get Sony, Audio Technica, Shure or other brands in the $50-60 dollar range, which is what I should have done, but I wanted to believe that these phones had earned their 4-1/2 star rating. I purchased these as a spare set for recording as a group. The guitar player that wore them for a few hours last weekend was not happy with my choice.

If they advertised these as simply over the ear headphones and not professional studio monitors, I probably would not be so disappointed with them. Bottom line, if you're an audiophile, DJ, producer or musician, stay away from these and get something better.

title: Great practice pad
text: It is similar in size to a real snare, and it is best used with a real snare stand so you get used to playing that way. Works great, easy to mount in a stand, no problems.

title: Excellent item, fast shipping!
text: Excellent item, fast shipping!

title: It's nice that Gibson ships their instruments with 'vintage' plastic jackplates
text: It's nice that Gibson ships their instruments with 'vintage' plastic jackplates, but they crack on stage when stressed.  Get these instead.

title: Shelf fit
text: Shelf fit

title: Great, but be careful of the height screws.
text: I love these saddles and have them on all of my guitars. They seem to improve the sound and do absolutely cut down on string breakage. And they look good too. But be wary of the little allen wrench height adjust screws. These seem to get stuck easily. If you try to force it with the allen wrench, it is really easy to strip it so that the allen wrench no longer works. I've had this problem across several sets of these. Luckily, I've got the string action well set, so don't need to adjust them now.... but still.  Might be worth a dab of WD-40 on the screw threads during initial installation.

title: is ok
text: not a great grade, but good enough

title: Great Beginner Clarinet
text: Bought this for my daughter to march with her freshman year of high school. She has an expensive wooden clarinet for concert band that I played years ago. There is a big difference in the sound and her band director thinks that a better mouthpiece will help with the sound. I'm sure this would be a great buy for a new student until they are sure that they want to continue playing throughout school.

title: Great Cable
text: If you need a quality short cable regardless of the type, I recommend this brand.

title: Must have for any electric guitar - protect your investment!
text: A terribly easy install and good quality straplock.  I am pleased that they match my Telecaster.  Straplocks are a must for any electric guitar and these exceed that need.

title: Poor performance, broke after minimal use
text:
I bought 3 Behringer pedals in Nov 2010 and all were very poor quality. I returned the DOA volume pedal right away and bought an Earnie Ball. I tolerated the Behringer delay pedal's awful tone for 6 months--then the off-on foot switch stuck ON. The chorus still sorta works, but the effect randomly cuts in and out (very annoying).

Don't waste your time and money on Behringer pedals. The price seems too good to be true, and it is.

Based on these three bad experiences, I cannot recommend Behringer products for anything other than service as a paperweight. Meanwhile, the BOSS pedals I've owned for years, and the ones I recently purchased, all are excellent products.

title: Perfect
text: Bought this for my son for online school and gaming. It works great. Would definitely recommend.

title: They play and sound good, but high-E breaks easily.
text: They play and sound good, but high-E breaks easily.

title: Excellent XLR Cable, Far Exceeds Expectations
text:
I’m a gigging musician, so I go through a lot of cables. I normally would not put much faith in one priced (as I’m writing this review) in the $10 range, so I got this two-meter cable to use as a patch cord in the rehearsal studio. It turns out, this thing is far better than I was expecting. The cable itself is more robust and has better shielding than any of other inexpensive cabled I have. The male and female connectors seem to be extremely high quality. The spring “neck” at the ends, where a cable normally gets maximum stress, will provide a lot of protection.

I tested it with my go-to Shure Beta 58A microphone and a Bose sound system. The signal was crystal clear, with no detectable distortion or buzz. The connectors fit precisely and firmly in the mic and the amp. Bottom line, this cable is so good that I may end up using it in the recording set-up, or possibly even in live shows.

title: Son likes it
text: My son is a gamer, he seems to really enjoy this mic.

title: A Good Boost for Humbuckers
text: This is a very simple boost with a small footprint that fits nicely on the pedal board ... I like the simplicity and the ability to set the dip switches to my liking ... I find that with humbucker pickups it adds just the right, very slight tone coloration that both fattens up the sound and gives it just the right sparkle ... I don't use it much with single coils since they don't seem to benefit as much from the coloration or the treble boost ... it is a good pedal to have on board when you need that little something extra to get the right tone ... built solid ... a quality pedal that should hold up well ...

title: Capos and Picks – You Can Never Have Too many
text: The Capo has a nice tight set and holds the strings uniformly.  No vibration or off notes from poor contact.  Also haven’t had to majorly retune the guitar between uses with the capo – some capos press so hard all the strings stretch way out of tune – and have been able to use it when the music calls for changes in the Capo position.  I’ve tested it on acoustic, acoustic electric and a hollow body electric.  The picks are nice, but the Capo is the reason to buy.

title: Great for a classic look
text:
Fit well on my Squier CV Telecaster with Fender replacement bridge. It was a little loose at first, but a small squeeze was just the touch needed to make a perfect fit.

I bought it to complete the buttoned up 50s look but it changed the sound on the bridge pickup a little. Maybe warms up the bridge? Still working through the tone, but it was a pleasant surprise.

I typically play close to the neck, so not a huge change to my technique overall. I will have to change my palm muting style with this on.

title: Satisfactory
text: Satisfactory

title: All you’ll ever use from this day forward
text: Does exactly what it’s supposed to do!  Easy for quick tuning by strumming all strings at the same time to see if a single string is out.

title: Solid upright bass stand
text: So I ordered this at the recommendation of the bass player I bought my 3/4, Kay 4-string double bass from.  While I have not used it out on a gig, I have my bass in it at home and have zero issues.  It set up quickly and easily, and as the title states, it's a solid stand for the application.  I'd definitely recommend this stand.

title: Five Stars
text: Christmas gift for my grandson

title: Love love love this Cool little cajon drum.
text: Certainly it doesn't have the rich tones that a regular conga with a skin head would have,... or even a synth head, but it sounds really good. It has nice resonance and you can easily get several different sounds out of it - more so, I think, than with a regular conga. But then, I'm used to drumming on odd things more than real skin drums (If you can make a deck of cards sound musical....I'm probably better at making music with cards than congas or bongos, haha).  Reviews state that it is more a cajon than a conga. Well, yeah, the head IS made of wood. If you've ever hand drummed on tables, furniture, the window ledge of your car door... or just about anything you can get your hands on, then you are going to love this. The tone/pitch difference in the two drum sides is perfect. It's just a bit larger than I thought it would be ( I didn't really look at the dimensions, not that it would matter anyway, but it is 19.5 x 11.5 x 3"), but this is totally portable and can satisfy that need to drum on everything and is a great little portable drum to practice on. It sounds enough like a conga that you can play it with a band - you'd need to mic it for sure. It is loud enough that it can be heard in different rooms in my house, but certainly not as loud as a regular conga would be. The issues I have with this (and I didn't downgrade because of it, because I've just solved them myself) are 1) Does not come with a bag. 2)There are two screws on the side edge for placement of the strap. But they are only on one "side", the front or the back, depending on how you play. I prefer playing with the low drum on the right, so the strap works well for me. Turn the drum around and the strap is attached to the bottom side of the drum - can't see that working out too well for those that prefer the low drum on the left, which I also do sometimes. 3) The strap itself is useless. It is advertised at being a lap strap or shoulder strap, but even with adjustments, it is too short and useless as a shoulder strap. As a lap strap it is useless for me as the drum isn't sliding off my lap without it. It isn't even useful for carrying the drum on your back. Toss. I bought myself a drum strap and I use that for playing while standing. I would often play bongos like that and used a guitar strap. This drum strap I got is actually very useful with the bongos as well.

title: Works great with no app required
text:
There are so many different wireless lavalier mics to choose from these days that picking the right one is a daunting task. Until you get into the $150 plus range, most are pretty close in features and price.

Most of these wireless systems are made in China and range from a low of $15 to upwards of $100. What I really like about this one is that it simply works. It's truly plug and play. Secondly, at least for me, the sending unit is iPhone case friendly.

In my testing, it worked perfectly in other rooms of the house, a good 30 feet away from the phone and through walls. Both transmitters synch right up and no software or app is required. Whether your shooting video or recording audio, it automatically switches from the iPhone's regular mic, to this and provides okay audio. Not studio quality, but good enough for most podcasts, interviews, etc.

Although not shown in the description here, a small hard sided case is included. A very nice touch to keep everything together and much better than a simple bag included with some units.

Overall, I'm happy with this and keep it in my electronics kit for immediate use whenever and wherever required.

text: After playing the laptop conga for a couple of days I have come to these conclusions. The instrument sounds more like a cajon than a conga and is better for some rhythm patterns than others. For example I really liked playing Guaguanco and other folkloric rhythms such as Bembe on the laptop conga. So you would have to experiment and see which rhythm you like to play on it the most. One complaint I have is since you can't tune it, (well the one I received) the low drum is G# and the high drum is D#, for you congueros out there, I would have preferred the standard tuning of G for the low drum and C for the high drum. Of course the portability is very nice and a strap is included to put around your waist or leg so you don't have to worry about it sliding off your lap when you sit. To sum it up, for gigs, or practice where you don't need a true conga sound yet something close, and/or you don't feel like hauling your congas around, this is a good buy. And the price I feel is reasonable.

text:
I did not purchase the 60’s Classic Vibe Telecaster from Amazon but I think it’s only fair to give an honest review.
Purchased from another vendor/site, out of the box the small E string had a terrible buzz coming from the nut and it sounded dull overall when played unplugged witch is a good a test to predict how the guitar will sound plugged in and electrified, after all the pickups do absorb the resonance of the surrounding wood when played. The setup was good and the intonation was great taking into consideration the traditional 3 roller metal saddles (not brass). I didn’t hear that traditional Tele twang when plugged in to my Boss Katana and Bugera V22 and as predicted by the “unplug test” it sounded dull and lacked articulation. I even tried some expensive brass roller saddles but no change.
Overall I was disappointed and sent back for a refund. It was not worth keeping for the any amount of money.

title: Good Strap Locks
text: A solid strap lock. As others have said in their reviews, it's a good idea to use some blue loctite on the strap fitting threads before tightening down. I have about 4 pairs now, and the ones that hold the best are a slightly thinner strap (Fender unpadded leather ones do well). An overly padded strap will keep it from tightening down. Do not use plyers or vise grips (from 1 pair I tried!), you will distort the female receiver and they will not attach! Also, it pays to do the toothpick and wood glue trick to add some grip in the guitar wood, and if screwed in while the glue is drying, its a natural thread lock. I've never had an issue with a stud backing out of the guitar. If you want a less chunky look, get the black ones, they blend into dark color straps well and add a more discrete touch of F!

text: This is a remarkable piece of gear. In addition to amazingly drum-like conga sounds, the box can produce a variety of other tones and pitches by moving around the surface, and responds excellently to finger rolls. It's also 50 lbs or so lighter than carrying a set of congas, and can be played easily on the lap using the lap strap, although I've also placed the box in a snare stand basket, which allows me to play the cajon at the same time. title: Great Music Stand Light (with some minor flaws)
text:
I bought this light to replace a "Martian Antenna" light with 2 flexible 4-LED bulb heads, which I found to be inadequate. This new light, which I attached to the removable music easel on my Yamaha keyboard, provided great coverage, and it completely lit 2 letter-size pages side-by-side; the spring clip on the light held it in place without movement, and the fully-charged battery lasted through a 3+ hour rehearsal (at the medium brightness setting) with one charging indicator LED showing at the end. The only downside seems to be the slowness of the recharging process - it took several hours, even when I used a 5 volt USB-AC adapter for the provided cable (when I plugged the provided cable directly into a USB outlet, the process was even slower). I also note that the provided cable is very short (only 40", including the plugs), so if you want to keep the light plugged into an AC source (with a 5V
USB-AC adapter) while playing a gig, make sure to have an extension cord available (alternatively, you could substitute a longer charging cord from a cellphone, provided it has a Micro HDMI plug for the light and a 5V USB-AC adapter plug).

title: This pedal is a keeper. It's too good and useful to go away.
text: I'm a professional guitarist with forty years playing experience (ouch). I've used a lot of pedals over the years. Most often, there's a honeymoon period with them. You think it's the Grail, then something better comes along, or you start hearing some unnatural junk that it adds that drives you nuts. The EP Booster actually seems to make your fundamental sound better. It's very warm, musical, and slightly compressed sounding, with nothing artificial added. Even at unity gain it adds something slightly magical.  I can gig my Tweed clone amps to boost for solos. I can use it on a jazz gig with my archtops to give my solos a little more tubey smoothness (through my SS amps), then kick it off for chord work. I love one knob. title: Cello is now safely off the floor, and ready for playing!
text:
So like other items on amazon, the price bounces around quite a bit. I first ordered a stand that sits lower to the floor and does not hold the neck or the bow because A) I was being cheap, and B) I really didn't think it was such a big deal to extend and retract the endpin. The reality is that I just set the cello on the floor on its side with the endpin out, which is not safe for the cello nor the people who walk anywhere near it.

It is possible to put your cello on this stand with the endpin out + / - 15 inches. It's not clear from the photos, but yes. And it is sturdy and stable as others have stated.

Recommended: don't be cheap, buy this first because you will buy it eventually. If the price seems high, check back. It changes.

EDIT / ADDITION: I just bought a second one because I now have two cellos (celli, for you sticklers). Again, I thought it would not be a big deal to keep my spare cello in the low stand that I have, but I found I was reluctant to use that cello with having to put the endpin in and out, plus I had that cello's bow laying on a stand. Now I can grab either cello quickly and easily and both bows have a home of their own.

It is a joy to have the stands right there so neither cello is ever on the floor, even if I just go get a drink. So quick, easy, and safe! Highly recommended.

title: Solid interface, with pretty awesome Studio One software
text:
Update*****

I am pretty sure this is no longer plug and play, windows 7 and above requires a driver that's right on PreSonus's website. Easy to install, and works just fine after the install. I have windows 10, and have no problems with it since I installed the drive, just an FYI. It will come up as a little desktop icon that will say audiobox under it. Plus, you need this driver to adjust the sample rate, because you can't change it inside Studio One, at least I couldn't. Took me a little while to figure out why I couldn't change it in the audio setup window, inside the software,and was working with about 60ms of latency, now it's 4.90ms and it's set at 128 samples. 60ms of latency, is way to much to try and get a drum track going in time with the metronome. So,it's very important when adding something like a MIDI controller, because you need to get the latency down to something like 10ms or below.

So I purchased this back in 2012, and registered the Studio One software, but not the AudioBox interface, with an email account I can no longer access. After failing to figure out the password to the old account, because I couldn't do a password update to the old email address, I called PreSonus. I explained the situation, and because I never registered the Audiobox unit, they registered when I called, basically as if I had just purchased it, and merged my old account with the new. So, this made me eligible for the newest version of Studio One. Which I thought was pretty awesome of them.

So, after 4 years of having the interface, it still works perfectly, which is a testament to build quality. Nothing seems to last very long these days. I have been getting to know the new Studio One software, I had never used the old version much, at the time I was primarily using Guitar Tracks 4 from cakewalk. Now I have been trying to use only the Studio One to see how well it will work for me. So far I really like it. It takes a little time to get used to doing things in their interface, but it's pretty intuitive. The software is a really huge bonus with this USB interface IMO, and while it's not their professional version, that's a $400 upgrade, it's very powerful and useful, and comes with 4gb of loops, instruments, and effects.

I recorded some guitar and vocal parts, and so far i'm very happy. no latency problems, clear audio, even though I need a better mic setup, as I don't have quality mics, but I still got a good sound with little effort.

I still wish the controls weren't so close together, it's very difficult to adjust, as well as see what the levels are. Otherwise I really like this interface, and have grown to love it. I will be using it more and more now, and the software too. Overall, I think this is a great deal, for the interface and software. and recommend it.

*******

I got this interface because I was having latency problems with my old one, after having upgraded my recording computer from a desktop to a laptop (dell w/ a core i3 2.53ghz, 8 gb ram w/ windows 7).

Once I hooked this up, no more latency problems, and once adjusted it does seem like a solid interface, but I do get some noise if I have my laptop cooler running at the same time. It doesn't bleed into the actual recording, but annoying when monitoring, and sounds like a phaser in the headphones or my studio monitors.

It has two channels with 48v phantom power, that gets it's power from the usb, NO POWER SUPPLY needed!!! and that's pretty awesome. A mixer control to control the signal of your input in relation to the playback level. It also has a main control and a headphone control, which basically just adjust the levels of each.

The thing that drives me nuts is the controls, they are tight together, and I have very large hands, so it always seems like I'm squeezing in to try and adjust them, and they are all silver so you can't see the little line on them too well. I would have liked this interface much more, if they had put the controls on the top edge with horizontal buttons. Or maybe if the whole box could sit at a 45 degree angle, so it was easier to get to, I guess I'll have to rig up a little stand to do that.

Overall it is a solid interface, that I had no problems getting to work, unlike some other reviews. It is heavy and solidly built, with overall nice features. I haven't recorded a ton with it, but what I have was nice and clear.

title: Not Ready
text:
I recently bought the Audiobox USB. The salesman at Sam Ash Music said it had served him well, and when comparing similar products by competitors that were around the same price range, he said this is the one.

I think he meant well. I do not think he deliberately deceived me. i think he probably only used it on an OS no newer than Windows 7, or he may have used it on a MAC.

Yes, I had the perennial "unknown device" issue when I tried to install. What is interesting is that I normally just tear open the wrapper, decimate the box, take it out, plug it in and get to work, but not this time. This time for some unknown reason, I took the time to read the installation instructions. I downloaded software and driver updates and then proceeded to install the unit. I got the "unknown device".

After a few uninstall/reinstall attempts over a night, morning and early afternoon, even following the multiphase procedure on the support page, i submitted a service request ticket.

Here is where I decided that Presonus is not my idea of a good product provider. I see a lot of discussion about this problem. So, it is obvious that Presonus is aware of the problem. Yet, there is no one available over the weekend to help customers through the issue. What if it is a procedure to follow or a file to download or even an issue that can be resolved via remote access? All of these would be fine. Then if there is no resolution the customer at least feels like Presonus cares about their customers enough to at least try. I am then not opposed to buying other Presonus product.

I am not unrealistic. I know, sometimes even expect, products to fail prematurely or even to not work at all. However, what i do not expect is the company leaving their niche customer community without help from 5:00 p.m. Friday to 9:00 a.m. Monday morning (Central Time). maybe this is not an issue to some, but this is far below the "fails to meet the standard" grade in customer service for me. Does Presonus realize that there are competitors, very strong competitors, in the market? Does Presonus realize that once a customer has paid for the Presonus product, the $50 or so difference in price between theirs and a competitor's more expensive offering is not so great a chasm anymore?

When I train sales professionals, I always tell them that mishaps and errors are almost inevitable. However, these are not what break business relationships. It is the lack or poor execution of a plan to address them. Presonus has made it into my "what would be your response as a customer, if... ?" lessons.

I think it is obvious what my response was. I uninstalled all of the software, and once the replacement process is complete, I will de-register everything and delete my Presonus account.

I am not angry. I am disappointed.

title: GREAT sound. Watch out for increased buzz.
text:
I bought the "medium scale" for my Mustang Bass (through-body bridge) and I'm thrilled to note that they fit perfectly. Silk on the E string starts about an inch past the nut, just before the tuning peg, so you can wind the E peg with all silk, as you're supposed to. I usually use LaBella Mustang Flats because they fit right, but I was getting tired of the sound, so I thought I'd try D'Addario medium scale since I heard they fit, and they sure do.

They also have, apparently, almost identical tension to the LaBella Mustang Flats; I did not have to adjust the action on my bass after installing these.

I'm also thrilled about the overall sound. I usually play flats so these are comparable, but since they are new have a great crisp fresh tone with lovely harmonics... even on the E string! The E string, to my delight, is one of the best sounding E strings ever, no tuning issues or muddiness -- a "B" played on the E strings sounds remarkably similar to a "B" played on the A string, which is frequently not the case; I expect that to get worse over time of course but right now it sounds awesome.

One interesting thing about nylon wrap: I like to play with Finger-Ease lubricant, and on normal flats you can actually get them TOO slick... but somehow with these black nylon strings, no matter how much lube I put on, the strings always have just a little bit of friction... one could say, just the *right* amount of friction. A welcome surprise!

The only bad thing is electronic buzz. The nylon prevents your fingers from making "grounding contact" with the guitar's electronics, so there is a slight buzz unless I brace the heel of my hand on the bridge. I tried to make my Mustang as electronically quiet as possible, but my practice room is awash in EMF; if I ground myself on the bridge, it's dead quiet, but if I don't ground there is a slight buzz. Disappointing but understandable that touching these string to play does not constitute grounding :(

It is too bad there are so few correctly-fitting string sets for Mustang through-body basses. If Thomastik-Infeld made a set of their Jazz Flats for Mustang, I'd be in heaven, but from now on it's ether D'Addario medium-scale, or LaBella Mustang Flats...

title: Bent piece of metal with some holes and a black finish.
text:
This is a basic item, just stamped, folded metal with a finish applied to it, but, well... For the most part, it's done right.

For anyone that has tried to rack mount SOHO broadband network equipment such as cable / dsl modems, and broadband / WiFi routers, you know the frustration of having to use a shelf in the first place since the MFGs assume everyone buying a cable modem for example, will just place it on a desktop. (WRONG!).

I have two of these that I use for my home network, which is somewhat complex as I am a Linux adminsitrator by trade, and I run my own Linux cluster and iSCSI SAN for training purposes (I maintain a training lab at home). One of these holds my Zoom 5341J cable modem, Buffalo WZR-600DHP N600 router, and a 3TB USB HDD that I am using for a DNLA server. The second I use for a pair of TrendNet TEG-S80G 8 port desktop gigabit switches and my Obi100 VoIP adapter.

Likewise the sound and video guys / gals have equipment they need racked up but that isn't offered in a rackable format. This shelf can help if it is light weight enough.

Pros:
- Sturdy, sufficiently thick gauge metal to hold anything you would want to store on such a shelf.
- Sized perfectly to work with a 12 inch deep wall mounted relay rack.
- Perforated base allows for airflow to any mounted items.
- Perforated base allows velcro strips to be run through to secure items to the shelf to keep the from sliding around. Also useful for mounting transformer blocks up and out of the way.
- Accurate hole placement, with well slotted holes allowing for sloppy racks.
- Reasonably well executed, attractive finish.
- Well protected / packaged.

Cons:
- Weight capacity somewhat limited by design (no rolled lip from side to side). I am not taking a star for that because, well I didn't WANT a heavy duty shelf. That is a different thing. I wanted one to hold light electronics and offered perforations improving breathing, but sacrificing structural rigidity somewhat. So don't go trying to put that big old UPS on this thing unless you want to watch stamped steel get a hernia...
- Likewise, the shelf itself can be a bit bowed right out of the box. Not something you might notice initially, but on the shelf my switches are on, there is a noticeable bow, probably 1/8" overall, which is acceptable for my purposes, but not ideal.
- The Finish on the shelves does NOT like having screws run in and out against it. I did some adjustment, moving things on and off the rack until I found where I wanted things, and by that time, the finish around the screw holes on one of the shelves had started peeling off. VERY disappointing.

Overall I am happy enough with these. I took 2 stars off of my initial review down to 3 after fiddling with them for a while due to the bowing and the flaking finish. I expect these to stand up to many years of use doing what they are meant to do. Just sit there and have stuff lay on them. These could be, and really should be much better. It's such a simple item that the flaws are things that really shouldn't be overlooked by the manufacturer.

title: Excellent upgrade for ANY Strat, but……..
text:
I’ve used Graph Tech saddles on all my Stratocasters & ‘S-type’ guitars. They do tackle a serious issue, which is the string suffering from abrasion from the saddle after utilizing a tremolo bridge - and ultimately breaking. You wouldn’t think it could be causing wear, but that one tiny spot is where the string moves longitudinally against something which causes wear. Graph Tech saddles (& nuts) work because of the material they use. Being graphite infused or based the strings aren’t able to build up friction as they slide over the shoulder of the saddle as the tremolo bridge moves. At the point where the angle of the string ‘breaks’.

It isn’t a perfect solution though. At least not yet. These saddles have had complaints from players who experience issues with the saddle height screws. Often they’re really difficult to adjust, and as people do, as it becomes more difficult they apply more and more force, which can easily strip out the threads. And at that point the saddle is ruined.

I’ve experienced this too, but NOT in every set I’ve used. Only a few times. The best solution I’ve found is to use a good quality gun lube, because the lubricants used with firearms typically don’t evaporate & the better examples don’t collect as much dust, grit, or grime. And typically, the better brands don’t contain anything that will cause an unwanted reaction from the materials it contacts. Corrosion, discoloration, etc. Cheap chemical lubricants can ruin more than you’d suspect. Personally, I’ve had good results using ‘Gun Butter’ and ‘Frog Lube’. Any quality brand will do the job, but these are what I’ve found to work really well. Using them with a syringe style applicator (they are available in several different types of containers & applicators) you can add just a tiny amount of lube on the exact spot you need it. And just the tiniest amount is best. Too much lubricant seems to actually attract debris buildup.

The solution I’ve found is to remove the saddle height adjustment screw completely. Make sure it’s clean & free of any dust or debris. Same for the threaded hole the screw goes in. Canned air is good if you have it to blow through the tiny screw hole. Then apply a bit of the lubricant to both the screw and the hole. Then run the screw all the way through the hole. All the way from one extreme of its travel to the other extreme end, and then all the way back. Wipe away any excess that works itself out. Importantly: if you meet resistance - STOP. Remove the screw, clean everything, and try again. Don’t strip these tiny threads. They’re small because they need to be in order to do their job, and being so small they’re a little delicate.

It’s also useful to add the tiniest amount of lubricant to the string itself if you have string trees or retainers on the headstock. A tiny amount exactly on the point the string meets the string tree. Because this is another area where friction wear can occur.

If you do these two things - chances are you will avoid any issues & maybe even never break a string again. The only good time to change strings on a guitar, is when you WANT to. Not because you’ve snapped your high E in front of an audience right in the middle of a solo.

Sorry to have been a bit wordy here, but I’ve seen friends ruin saddles & end up so frustrated that they tossed their instrument into the closet. It’s not altogether uncommon, but it usually is entirely avoidable.

I really do hope this helps.
