title: Defective out of box
text:
First of all, the item did arrive in the factory box, and there was no apparent damage of any kind to the carton. The person who delivered it, gently placed it on the doorstep, and we were able to get it straight away. Since it was purchased as a gift, we didn't want to really unpack the item, but we did open the top of the box to make sure the keyboard looked new and undamaged. It SEEMED okay. But...after a couple of weeks, I felt a bit uneasy remembering the reviews seem to reflect a lack of quality control, so I tested it (with batteries--I didn't unwrap the cord which I planned to check later). Several keys did not play at all, so I removed the batteries (the batteries were mine--the cord comes with the keyboard), and put it back in the box. I intend to contact Amazon to see what I need to do for a replacement or refund. Hopefully I won't have to pay to ship it back to China.

Update--I sent it back through the usual Amazon return process and opted for a refund rather than a replacement. I felt too uneasy to risk another defective product since the item was meant for a child's upcoming birthday. I bought this as a toy, and especially at this price point, I didn't expect a quality musical instrument. But it should at least work as described. Since there were good reviews, anyone considering buying this item should test it out immediately even if the item arrives in seemingly good and new condition (as ours did).

title: Really pleased with the warm tone of these strings
text:
I decided to do a bit of an "upgrade" on a poor neglected Yamaha guitar I had that was a gift from a non-guitar playing friend (which is why you shouldn't give instruments as gifts to people if you don't know much about instruments or the preferences of the musician to whom you wish to gift the instrument--but I digress). Putting a better grade of strings did improve the sound, especially after I managed to fix the loose tuners that caused the strings to constantly slip out of tune. I also managed to lower the action and do some basic tweaks and cosmetic makeovers ( a bright blue pickguard), and now I am playing the guitar whenever my arthritis and my neighbors will tolerate it.

D'Addario is a good standard brand of guitar strings, and they make various strings for both steel-stringed acoustic guitars and nylon-stringed acoustic (classical) guitars. String choice and response is very subjective, so you might need to try various kinds of strings before you find the strings that make your particular guitar sound the best to you. HOWEVER, make SURE you only put steel strings (and despite the name, "Phosphor Bronze" is considered a type of steel string) on a steel string guitar, and nylon strings on a nylon stringed guitar. While no real harm will come to your guitar if you put nylon strings on a steel stringed acoustic, they may not tune properly because of the difference in tension. No matter how "light" steel strings are, they are too much for a nylon stringed guitar that typically will not have a reinforced neck and the added tension will damage the neck of the guitar--even bending or snapping it. Don't do it.

title: Easy way to add some pizzazz  to your guitar
text:
I ordered the decals to go along with a faux blue abalone pickguard I also ordered. Luckily, the color did match close enough, so it actually looks like they go together (different company made the pickguard). They were fairly easy to apply, but I almost messed up one of the pieces (maybe that's why you get an extra), because I was thinking they were just like stickers and all I had to do was peel off the backing and then stick them on. Not exactly. Decals come with instructions---so if you haven't used this product before, please read the instructions. You will need a couple of tools to get the decals on so they look like the inlays they are supposed to look like. You need a plastic card (like a credit card) or something as a burnishing tool, and a pair of scissors or craft knive/blade (to cut the decals apart for easier handling and to trim them if necessary so they fit your particular sound hole. Other than that, take your time to carefully position the pieces (I overlapped mine VERY slightly so there woudn't be any seams) because while they are easily removed, they aren't exactly something that can be repositioned easily once you peeled away all the plastic.

Overall, I'm very pleased with the product, and my old Yamaha 325 Folk Acoustic really is starting to look pretty sharp. Those having more expensive, or valuable guitars, but not wanting to go to a luthier to install actual inlay or something, might want to consider a more "deluxe" product if one is available. However, for a quick, easy makeover (especially if you might want to change looks from time to time), this is exactly as advertised, and I'm quite pleased.

Make sure you look carefully at the color code when you order. I couldn't tell at first glance why there were two listings for "abalone"--but one was blue (which I needed) and the other green. The listings look very similar otherwise, so make sure you order the color you want.

title: Rigid and thick for protection; incredibly beautiful color and shine for looks
text:
I bought the pickguard to beautify a long-neglected Yamaha 325 Folk Acoustic. The replacement is better than the pickguard it replaced, though the shape did not fully cover the lighter patch of wood revealed when I took off the old pickguard. I could tell by the picture when I ordered the pickguard that the shapes were different, but I hoped for the best. Overall, the uncovered area doesn't bother me SO much, and I may decide later to order some small decal to disguise it. This is no way the fault of the company, and the pickguard itself is GORGEOUS! I am really glad that I broke down and purchased it over several cheaper options I also considered. The pickguard is not just a sticker or lightweight decal, but has some real thickness (it's actually rigid) so that it could actually function to protect the guitar from pick scratches. I bought it mostly for looks, and the color and iridescent shine really looks like abalone shell instead of whatever man-made material (plastic?) this happens to be. The picture makes the color look really flat, but the color IS close to the one I got (the description does say there is some variation between pickguards, much as it would for real shell).

I paired the pickguard with inlay stickers from another company. Luckily the match was close.

title: Super cute and well-fitting padded case
text: I received a new, concert sized ukulele for Christmas, so I had to get a case or bag for it since the ukulele did not come with one.  My daughter offered to buy me a case, as part of her holiday gift to me. The order was placed on Christmas DAY, and I already received it this afternoon on December 28!  I was surprised to see the size of the box, and feared that maybe the wrong item or the wrong sized item was inside. However, when I opened the package, there was the ukulele case basically balled up and crammed into the tiny box about a third of the size of the case. It sounded crunchy when I tried to smooth it out, so I thought maybe there was paper stuffed inside the bag for extra protection (no such luck).  It was still wrinkled when I put my ukulele in to try it out for size. Luckily, not only was the case the perfect size (snug but not tight or difficult to get in or out), but just leaving the uke in the case for awhile this evening pretty much ironed out the wrinkles. (It IS a padded bag, NOT a hard case, but STILL...). The gift tag was also completely blank, so if I hadn't KNOWN my daughter had purchased this for me, I might have wondered who sent it.  Still, I'm giving the CASE five stars because I actually love it (it's pink and has cats, what more could I want)! If you want a cute case that will protect your instrument from normal bumps and falls (like it falls off the couch or off a car seat if you travel with it), or just to keep it safe from dust and light (I'm sure some moisture would be tolerated, but this is canvas so I would not count on it being anywhere near waterproof--and I'm not going to test it). Overall, the case looks well-constructed, and the zipper looks to be nylon toothed even though the pulls are metal.  If you plan to travel with your ukulele either by plane or any public transportation where it might need to go into some luggage compartment or travel hold, I really recommend you get a hard case instead (especially if your ukulele is an expensive or otherwise precious instrument).  I was really so pleased with the case (especially once I got it out of the crumpled up state it was put into), that I wanted to order a guitar bag from the same company, but apparently they don't have them at present (I went straight to the Music First site).Overall, I'm thrilled with my case, and am thinking of an excuse to take my ukulele somewhere so I can show off the bag--ha, ha.  I also would suggest since reviews for this product also include cases for soprano ukuleles as well, that you take care to order the right size case for your ukulele (as well as the right pattern or color).

title: Colorful picks for nylon-stringed instruments
text: Well, what can I say? They're felt picks. I bought them for use with a ukulele, and they work quite well to strum and pluck the strings. Regular plastic picks, even lightweight ones, tended to "click" against nylon strings, and I worried if the harder material might wear out the nylon strings faster.  Instead, the pick makes the sound of my uke surprisingly loud, but clear and warm. The felt material (which is pressed into a rigid, non-bending piece), is easy to grip because it is not slippery like plastic can be.  I suspect that the picks will eventually fray from use, and definitely discolor over time as the felt absorbs oil and dirt  (washing your hands before playing should help).  The picks also work well for classical guitars for those who like using picks (but don't want to scratch a guitar that usually has no pickguard). It works well to get a bright, rich sound when strumming chords on nylon strings.

title: One of my favorite classical guitar strings
text: I've used these strings before on my classical guitar, and loved them. I ordered this new set since I do change strings every few months. The sound of the black trebles is very clear and warm., and I like the way the strings look on my guitar.  The strings have ball ends which actually makes no difference to me, since  I have had no problems with tying on traditional nylon strings either. They settle in very quickly--after a couple of days--but it depends on how often you play your guitar. There is no stated tension for these strings, so when I bought my first set and opened the package I was a little appalled because they looked so thick.  I have some arthritis in my fingers which flares up from time to time, and smallish hands (and classical guitars have wider necks as well), so I was surprised that they were not hard to press down on at all. It would of course depend on the action on your own particular guitar.  The manufacturer website describes the strings as having medium tension, and this seems about right. Despite the label as "folk singer",  I don't thiink these would work that well on a steel stringed acoustic guitar.  Those want a really bright tone to their guitars might not like these strings either. While the tone is very clear and pure, it is also very mellow and warm, which is what I personally prefer.

title: Much better than I expected--very, very pleased
text:
First of all, when you order a cheap ukulele bag, you need to expect a cheap ukulele bag. There are more expensive, better made bags and cases out there, and if you have a really quality instrument, you want to pay the extra money. As it is, I got my soprano Melokia ukulele for free (I cashed in some bonus points from my bank). I also knew how much this uke would cost if I had bought it new off Amazon. I didn't want to pay more for the bag than the instrument, but I did want to keep my uke free from dust, and perhaps have something to carry it in if I took it anywhere. I read the reviews (again--if you get what you pay for), and one reviewer posted some useful photos. I took a chance and ordered the bag, and actually was very pleasantly surprised that it was much better than I expected. There is enough padding so that if, say your uke slid off the car seat when you were taking it some place, it would be protected. If you took your instrument on a plane, or somewhere it had to go into a baggage compartment, you would either need to slip into into a suitcase, or get a hard case. The bag has padded outside pockets for accessories, including a place where you could put a strap. It has very comfortable backpack straps and these are sewn on well, and the rest of the bag is stitched
together neatly and professionally. The zipper does not look very sturdy, so caution there. The brand name is stenciled on and the paint was already rubbing off in spots--this is the only thing that was really wrong with the bag. But again--for the price, I'm really, really pleased with it.

title: Beautiful jewel-toned colors-Set of 10
text: They're guitar picks--what can  more can I say? You get two of each color, and the colors are deep, and jewel-toned. I ordered the .70mm picks which are probably a bit much for the ukulele I ordered them for (though when you pick individual strings, the sound is really bright and clean). I should have ordered  felt picks  for the uke instead, but I'm not much on using picks anyway even on guitars. You could even slip the package into a birthday card.

title: Little goes a LONG way.
text:
Well, it's a bottle of lemon oil, isn't it? I ordered it because I wanted to take advantage of free shipping so I needed to top off my order. I have two guitars and two ukuleles so it's not like I couldn't use it. A little does go a long way, and I used it to clean and refresh the rosewood fretboard and bridge of an acoustic guitar that I had largely left neglected in the corner of the room. I used a soft cloth to rub in the oil and remove the excess and used the cloth (with the oil on it) to polish and clean the rest of the guitar. It looks so beautiful, I plan to start playing it again once I can take it in for some needed set-up. I also used it to touch up my classical guitar, but didn't really dab it on since I didn't want to have to take the strings off. This guitar will be getting a nice rubdown the next time I change my strings.
Note: There is a warning on the bottle not to use this oil on maple fretboards. If you aren't sure what is on your guitar, check first.
One other thing to think about--while the lid screws on very tightly, I'm not sure how safe it is to throw a bottle of oil into my guitar case (I have compartments), so I kept it on a shelf or in a drawer.
Update: That bottle is still nearly full, and the oil (stored in a desk drawer in a plastic bag on case of leaks) still smells fresh . A little goes a LONG way. I have two ukes now. :)

title: Wonderful tone and functionality for a bargain price...comparison to a few other amps below
text:
I’ve had the Boss Katana for a while now. I have several different amps, tube and modeling. The Katana is a great amp at a great price. The tone is really exceptional compared to the other amps I own in this price range...the fender mustang GT100, the katana air, or the Orange 20 watt. Functionally, it has 5 voices that cover pretty much any tone. The effects and reverb options are extensive. It also has variable output power, which is very useful at home. You can hook it up to your phone for backing tracks or to access tone central with hundreds of different presets. I don’t use these features, which brings me to the downside of this amp...it does not have Bluetooth connectivity, requiring a wire connection, which is inconvenient. Additionally the effects selection is displayed by various colored lights which you cannot remember.

If this amp had Bluetooth and a small LCD screen it would blow away the competition. Compared to the Fender Mustang GT100, the katana sounds a LOT better, but the mustang has a very intuitive interface and WiFi and Bluetooth connectivity that works great. The Mustang is a modeling amp that has dozens of different amps modeled, but in truth this functionality is pretty worthless. All the different amp models fall into more or less the same categories as the Katana. I thought the modeling functionality would be really worthwhile, but it really isn’t as useful as it sounds. The Orange 20 watt has its own voice, but the amp is very primitive in terms of functionality. The Katana Air is a portable amp that sounds nowhere are good as the katana 50, but does have Bluetooth functionality. Final comparison...to a hand wired ‘57 tweed deluxe tube amp. While a tube amp always makes you feel good, I really have to put the Boss Katana 50 clean tone right up there with it.

Overall a great amp at a great price. Hopefully, Boss will include Bluetooth and an LCD interface in future models.

title: Pretty good, but there's a better one out there
text:

I know it seems like a silly complaint, but I'm a bass player, and reaching all the way to the top of the headstock and having to hold down the button isn't as easy as you'd think. Let me just tap the button to turn it off. Why hold it?

I've tested at least 8 clip-on tuners, and this one so far is 2nd best with the Snark ST-8 Super Tight Clip On Tuner making it to #1. Even being 2nd best for me, I can only give it 3 stars because of that darn hold-button-to-turn-off design

title: The best of the best - 5 stars!
text:
I've purchased at least 8 different types of clip-on tuners and this one is easily the best so far. I use it mainly to tune by basses (which can be a challenge for some tuners). Here are the simple reasons why I like this one over some of the others:

- The clip is the perfect tightness. I've tried some that are not tight enough so it doesn't pickup the vibration very well. And I've also had one that was too tight, to the point where it was difficult to clip it on with one hand (the Fender clip-on was way too tight).

- It starts up and shuts down fast. I know this seems like a simple feature, but I've tried others, and some take a while to boot. Also, others I've tried require holding a button down for a few seconds to turn off. Both are quite annoying. With this one, you just tap the button and it's on in under a second, tap the button again and it instantly shuts off. So simple, but other manufactures don't seem to get it.

- The accuracy is impeccable! And trust me when I say this, because I use it to tune bass guitars! Others that I've tried struggle on the lower strings like the E and A. I also have a 5 string with a low B and most can't even do it. This one has no problem with all strings. It struggles just a little bit with the B, but nowhere near the problems I've had with others.

- You can position the face in any angle, so it doesn't matter where you clip it! I've used other tuners where they limit the angle of where you can position the face. This can be really annoying! I have no idea why other manufacturers don't simply give you all angles. If you look at the design of this one, it's quite simple the way they've designed it. Other manufacturers should take heed.

- The display is nice and bright. My Jazz bass has a really long neck, and with some of the other tuners, it was hard to see the display when clipped to the furthest point of the headstock (my eyesight isn't that great, and if on stage, the bright lights can also make it difficult to read). This display is large, bright, and easy to read.

This is easily a 5 star product

title: You get what you pay for
text: I see a lot of good reviews, and maybe I got unlucky, but this is a very cheap cable. When I plug it in, my tone gets a bit duller (and loses a bit of volume) and just after a few weeks, I'm already hearing static like there's a connection problem. I changed it out with an older cable just to make sure, and lo and behold, the cable is already broken. I wouldn't recommend this cable. I'd pay a bit more for something maybe a step up in quality just to be safe.

title: This is the worst tuner I've tried yet (FCT-2)
text:
I'm not sure why this is getting so many good reviews. I have a feeling that it's because the product page is merged with other models. The FCT-2 is by far the worst clip on tuner I've ever used (and I've used many manufacturers and models). I'm really surprised that a company like Fender would think this gadget is acceptable quality, because I'm definitely a Fender fan when it comes to guitar, bass, and amplifiers.

Anyhow, there are so many things wrong which basically makes this tuner unusable:

- The display is way too dim. I mean, you can barely tell if it's on or off (and there's no way to adjust it that I've found).
- When you pluck a string, you can barely see the meter change, and you absolutely can't see the note (i.e. G, A, C, etc). You can see where the letter should go more than the displayed letter itself. Duh
- The clip is way too tight. I can understand that they'd want it tight enough so that it detects the vibration better, but I have other tuners that aren't nearly as tight and they do a great job (I'm thankful to still have a few Intellitouch PT10's lying around). It's so bad that it's close to the point where I need to position my hand correctly just to put the device onto the headstock.

So there you go. They failed on almost everything a clip on tuner needs to be.

title: You might not like this if a little latency bothers you
text:
Not to be too negative (because I know some people don't mind a little latency), but I had to return this product because I just couldn't tolerate the latency, especially when playing bass. I own a mid-range wireless setup for live gigs and there's very low latency. But this one is just a bit too much. The output is always dragging behind the beat. And it's not good for recording either because now you're summing the latency of the wireless as well as the latency of your audio interface going into your computer. Also, the audio quality is not all that great either. I didn't try it with guitar, only bass, and it made my bass output sound a bit weak with a little unpleasant saturation (not the good kind of saturation). I could probably live with it if the latency was better.

But I have to say, the packaging is great, the transmitter and receiver devices are very well designed, and is very easy to operate. But in end, I just see no point and keeping this product because it just isn't "tight" enough for me. But maybe if I had an electric acoustic guitar, it might be tolerable.

Well now I know the difference between a low cost unit and a mid-range/high-end unit. ;)

title: Simply the best vibration tuner!
text:
I've purchased at least 6 different types of vibration tuners and the Intellitouch PT10 is the best of all (I use it for bass). What it does better than all the rest:

- Can position the viewer to any angle you want with ease.
- You can view the screen pretty well on an angle.
- Clips onto a thick headstock pretty well and stays.
- Easy to use (interface).
- Stays on the headstock when the bass is put back into its case.

With other vibration tuners, I had problems with all the bullet items above.

Until something better comes along, this is my go-to tuner. And if people are interested why I use this over a pedal based tuner:

- I can tune before I go on stage while my equipment is already on the stage.
- I can take my bass anywhere (even while watching tv on sofa, bed, etc) and still be able to tune it.
- It requires no cables so I can use this with all my basses, guitars, acoustic guitars, banjo, etc.
- Easily fits in my case, so I don't even need to carry around a pedal board or anything else other than case and amp/cab.

title: Works ok, not the best
text:
Most vibration tuners aren't that good. Especially for bass. This one is probably in the top 5. After trying almost all of them, I've found that the Intellitouch PT10 is the best. There's a couple reasons why this one doesn't beat the Intellitouch:

- The viewer doesn't adjust/bend as well as the Intellitouch. I struggle a bit to find a good position.
- It's just a little too big. I like leaving the tuner on my headstock when I put my bass in its case. This one tends to fall off because it hits the bottom of the case.
- The LED doesn't have very good angle view.
- The grip on the end of the clamp fell off and I had to super glue it back on.

If you really want a very reliable vibration tuner, I'd suggest Intellitouch PT10 or PT20.

title: Worth the price…but
text: Before you order this, order a set of normal tension regular nylon strings. I prefer DAddario EJ45. This is a great guitar for the price. I own several nylons that cost 3 to 4 times the price and this hangs on my wall with them however…you must set it up. First, take off those high tension strings it comes with. High tensions aren’t suited for this guitar. Second after tuning up and stretching the normal tension strings tighten the truss rod so the the neck is straight. Third, sparingly oil the fretboard and bridge, mine was dried out. This guitar is worth buying a set of gotoh or Grover tuners for, I expect the cordoba tuners to fail eventually. DO NOT grind down the saddle, there’s not enough there to spare and the break angle over the saddle is sufficient. Lowering the saddle will only cause problems. I’m not overly impressed with the fishman pickup system but it all depends on what you’re plugging into I guess. As much as like this guitar I was shocked to see that Amazon did not double box it for shipping, but it survived. What a great nylon for under $500.

After a good setup the mandolin was amazing in sound fit and finish . Now, here’s where this rating took a dive… after just 2 weeks of playing the frets are already pitting. I guess I’ll be practicing my refret skills.

title: Research before buying
text:
Maybe this is my fault for not researching this pedal before buying, but there was zero mention on all the videos and manuals on how to get the ping pong effect.
If you put this pedal in a chain with other stereo boss pedals and use both stereo inputs and outs you will not achieve a ping pong effect. All you will get is a mono signal out of both sides.
Besides that there’s nothing remarkable about this pedal, it’s a delay pedal and it delays.

title: It does what it’s suppose to do, I just care for the sound.

title: Not terrible, but not great
text: I paired this mini ego compressor with a mini Tumnus so I expected good results. First off the tone switch on the Ego made no difference in either position. The blend control worked great, sustain control functioned as it should as well as the attack and level controls. Using this ego compressor in clean mode sounds pretty typical and provides a decent amount of squish and pop for chicken picking. When I added the Tumnus to the mix the Ego got a bit noisy. I wanted to thicken up my tone because the as great as the Tumnus is, it can be brittle and thin. I play jazz and blues so I need Noise free tones. This combination did not deliver. It’s not a bad compressor I just expected better signal to noise ratio when using the same manufacturer. This is not a review of the Tumnus but the Tumnus is noise free when dimed, so why couldn’t wampler make a simple compressor that doesn’t get noisy with its own pedals?

title: The good and the bad
text:
There’s no way a collection of individual effects pedals could amount to the sound and performance of this preamp/DI. THE GOOD: clean, distortion free, low signal to noise. The eq/comp/volume section is very expressive without being brittle or boomy. Compression is subtle but effective, no pops or over attack sensitivity. I love the trim pot that governs the input jack. It caters to whatever you want to plug into this unit. It’s not just for acoustic guitar. The modulation section is transparent and very useful when using the level control to blend in just enough chorus. The delay is warm and simple to set to the sweet spot. The boost switch come in handy when you need to be heard without changing your eq and volume settings.
THE BAD: needs a bypass switch or an on/off button. Low cut switch makes no difference where it is set. Reverb options are lame, don’t depend on them. Pop switches need to be silent. A unit at this price should include a power adapter, 9v battery lasts about one hour.
Overall I really dig this pedal for jazz guitar. I eliminated several pedals from my rig that were noisey and sounded inferior. I feel a bit disappointed that the reverb is so bad. Even tho there are several bad points, the build quality and clean sound response keeps this unit current and wanted by musicians. I would buy it again.

title: Not bad.
text:
I put this set in my classic vibe telecaster. The pickups take up every bit of space your cavities will allow. Had to drill a lower hole in the bridge cavity to get wires out of the way and Dremel a bit of meat in the neck to do the same, not a lot but just a little. The neck pickup is high so there was no way to lower it, lucky for me the height was just right. With all that being said I still think it was worth while. These Generation 4 pickups sound more like single coil tele pickup than the Vintage noiseless do. Gen4 has better eq and overall tone, however a bit less bass and volume (no squish in the neck position). My only complaint about noiseless single coils size pickups are there’s no “quack” or “throaty” attack. But that’s what happens when you use opposing coils (humbucker), to produce no noise, it’s a trade off.
These are humbuckers made to sound and look like single coils. I would rather have a full size humbucker that I love the sound of, rather than an okay single coils size pickup that never quite sounds like a good single coil or even a good sounding humbucker.

title: Not bad, but not what I expected
text:
Plz don’t take this as a negative or even a positive review, this is just an observation while I was installing these and stringing up my telecaster.
My original intention was to get locking tuners on my vintage 50s tele without reaming the holes in the neck, as far as that goes, mission accomplished. While stringing the new tuners, I noticed the top of the shaft (where the slot is to loosen and remove the string) moved clockwise as I stretched the string. At that point the string should be locked into the shaft pass through hole (right?).
So I would stretch the string until the top of the shaft stopped turning clockwise. No where in the directions did it mention this. I did this on every string, when finished everything seemed okay. I tuned up and stretched a little more and saw some movement again but very little. At this point I was regretting the up grade and figured I’d end buying a new set of fender locking tuners (the strings lock with a thumb wheel on the back of the tuner, but the tuners hole must be reamed larger to fit 😫 something I don’t want to do.

After a time of stretching and tuning, things seemed to stabilize but compared to the other style of locking tuners, this process took entirely too long with way too much fuss. If I knew I’d be going thru this, I would have stuck with the original tuners and saved $80. Well they’re on now, and I’m committed to see how this plays out. The gears are very stiff and the hardware seems average quality, screws are larger, and the bushing look identical to the old ones. I own a dozen guitars and they all have locking tuners, maybe I might end up with a guitar that doesn’t have them. I hope this observation was some help to you.

title: An actual compression pedal not an effect pedal
text:
Before you add this to your cart, ask yourself these questions; do I want a comp pedal to use an effect or to use as a signal compression device? There’s a difference, using as an effect you hear a massive difference when you kick it on. As an effect you probably want “squash, punch, and a bit of extra gain. This pedal does NOT do this.
This pedal is for audio compression on a wave form basis. It offers a ton of compression but with subtle attack and zero gain. I use this for clean jazz guitar and bass where I want attack volume to be calmed down without you knowing it. It does the job, for the money it’s worth it, you won’t find this in an effect pedal. Moving up to the full size might even be nicer having the blend control.
My only complaint would be that I could never get the tone print to work and there is a bit of line distortion but not enough to get upset about, what would you expect for $80?

The medium, standard, whatever you want to call it does not fit a 34 inch scale bass!!!!  On the part of the string that goes into the tuning peg, the winding of the string comes below the nut!!! title: Noisy but was able to work around
text: Win 7 drivers installed easily and worked well right out of the box.  Studio One software also installed easily and worked well, although the interface doesn't make sense to me.  I use a thirteen-year-old version of Cakewalk Guitar Tracks 2.0 that is so intuitive, I don't know why newer DAW's can't have an interface that is as logical as Guitar Tracks. Newer Cakewalk software also has a similar interface to Studio One, hence my choice to continue to use Guitar Tracks.  My main problem with the device is that I needed to run the gain controls about 80% or more to get any reasonable output from the device no matter what DAW I was using, and running it that hot introduced a ton of noise into the system.  After numerous emails back and forth with PreSonus tech support (yes, I did get a response from a helpful real person, although it usually took 2-3 days each time to get a reply) I finally came to the conclusion that USB power from my computer (a rather robust PC desktop) is just not enough to run the preamps, phantom power, etc. plus my external hard drive, printer and wireless mouse.  I have an old Behringer mixer and have now put it in line in front of the AudioBox.  Output is now very satisfactory and I can keep the gain down way below the noise threshold.  This is not the way I intended to use it, but it is now very quiet and I am very happy with the quality of the recordings.  So - if you plan to use the AudioBox on its own, be certain to try it immediately and check the gain and noise levels.  You may not have enough power to make it work effectively.

I have been modding a Waterstone jazz bass that I really like and wanted to upgrade the wiring along with the new DiMarzio Dp123 Model J Bass Pickup set I was installing. The kit gave me what I need to do the job and do it well. All very good quality parts. Highly recommend.

text: Most people know the reputation of the SM7B. It does what it is known to do. A quality, legendary studio microphone.

title: A good buy
text: I have lived with this for a few weeks now. The boom stand is well built. I actually attached (screwed) the mounting plate into a table to hold the boom, and in doing so, it is very stable. The range of motion is very good and the provided XLR cable - while some Chinese off-brand (Yongsheng) - seems adequate. You do have to really crank down on the knobs to get it to lock, but it is not what I would call difficult. All in all, a recommended buy.

title: Not bad until you factor in the kick stand
text: I would have easily given 5 stars but for one thing - the kick stand in the back is terrible. There is a small, flimsy, thin piece of plastic in the back that swings out to hold this unit up on a table surface. It is not a question as to IF this thing will snap off, rather WHEN. I have owned Korg stuff in the past. This is the first Korg product I am disappointed in. Seriously, another 10 cents per unit would have solved this problem. Other than that, it is fine. Korg, get your act together.

title: Surprisingly good value
text: I have not used this brand before, but I tested a mic using three different shock mounts. I do not have a Rycote to compare it to, but of the three shock mounts, this one - in general - did the best job of minimizing unwanted transmissions. Each shock mount had its ability to limit the transmission of specific frequencies to the mic, however, overall this one performed best.

title: Good  value
text: I do audio production on a regular basis and have more expensive headphones for recording. I wanted something lighter to use around my home office for meetings. This fits the bill. Good audio for the buck. Reasonably comfortable. Semi-portable. Recommend.

title: Solid accessory
text: I needed to extend the reach of my desktop mic stand. This does a great job. I have to weight down the base now that it is top heavy, but the boom arm is great.

title: Build quality could be better
text:
In general, this shock mount does the trick. There are two aspects of its build that could be better.

When you squeeze the two pieces together that open the 'tube' where the mic is held, it makes this annoying clicking sound. I have two of these units and they both make this click every time, which does not provide a great sense of confidence in in how it is built.

Also, the 'tube' consists of the outer metal band and an inner piece of foam. The foam is glued into the inside surface of the tube. On both units, the foam is not completely glued to the metal. Not a big confidence builder for me, as I wonder if down the line the glue will completely fail.

Other than the these two issues, the shock mount seems fine. There is definitely room for improvement but it is serviceable.

title: Not a great microphone and you're better of looking for something else
text:
-This is a review for the Blue Yeti USB Microphone

My Experience: To say my experience was not great would be an understatement. I would get constant complaints about my audio being terrible and at first I thought it was just them until I got more and more complaints about my audio. Even with the lowest sensitivity people would tell me they could hear themselves more than they could hear me. The included wire was very long however if there is anything touching it, it would have a lot of interference, even touching it with my fingers would have some kind of static noise going on in the background, that and the connector used was so bad. I would have taken either micro-b or the usual usb type B connector that you find on other mics like my old Snowball which honestly I prefer over this thing. The only cool thing imo would be the fact that you can hear yourself while talking which is something the snowball did not have as well as a dedicated mute button for yourself

Positive:
+ Dedicated Mute button
+ Passthrough for headphones
+ Able to hear yourself
+ Able to change sensitivity

Neutral:
| No included pop filter

Negative:
- Sound quality is not that great
- a lot of interference if anything is touching the wire
- usb-mini b connector

Recommended: I would not bother going for this product

title: More comfortable than stamped saddles. Easily installed and adjusted. No meaningful tone change.
text:
String saddles are not difficult to install if you know how to set intonation and string height.
These are no exception. They installed easily and are easily adjusted.

These fit my 2013 Fender American Standard stratocaster, as expected. If your Stratocaster, Telecaster or guitar with a similar style bridge has a bridge spacing of 2 1/16", these will fit just fine.

I bought these to replace my stock stamped saddles, which were very uncomfortable to palm mute with. These are a big improvement. I can't comment as to whether they prevent string breakage, as I haven't broken a string on any guitar in many years. My guess is reduced friction at the saddle (thanks to the lubricating agent) will in fact prevent the string from getting caught on the saddle and breaking when tuning or using your trem, but I haven't done any testing on that front.

I noticed no meaningful difference in tone after install. Some people will claim they can hear a difference, but I don't think they could tell the difference between these and any other steel saddle in a blind hearing test.

title: everyone who buys this is already planning on buying it
text:
I bought this to go over the corresponding "Fender Pat. Pend." ashtray bridge to make a knockoff Esquire out of a Squier Affinity. It performs the task admirably. When received, it was a little deformed and didn't fit correctly. Just a slight squeeze with the hand was all it took to reshape it to snap on to the bridge as intended.

I'm not actually sure how much this actually works to reduce feedback, hum, or microphonics, and it definitely doesn't suit modern playing styles where people pick or strum really close to the saddles, but the way I play I find I have a nice place to put my palm down while fingerpicking closer to the neck. Plus it looks super cool. I've always liked the early Fender basses with the pickup covers, and I definitely like the look of this pickup cover as well.

Since my retrofit of the guitar left behind some ugly holes, it performs the added function of covering up the obviously Squier-y elements of the guitar, like the old bridge holes left behind by the longer and wider Squier bridge. I'm convinced that Fender made everything on Squiers just a little bit bigger than their Fender equivalents so you couldn't ever retrofit their guitars with Fender parts and pass it off as a Fender. I'd recommend if someone else was making an "eSquire" that they shouldn't pass this up either.

text: Put on a modulus 5 string flea bass. I’ve set it up to be my bass for thick and fat basslines and other basses for the fancy slappy trebly stuff. They are thicker gauge than I usually use but the lower tension makes them feel like normal. The wrap around the low B on the bridge side (the purple silk) was pretty fat and thick which made getting it through the bridge hole tough. Luckily it got in there but it was really close to not working for me. They sound great and they feel great. I’ve tried flatwounds a few times and always hated them but these have more high end content and feel better than Chromes. I hope they last a long time because a $50 pack of strings sucks to buy haha. If you’re looking for a flat wound alternative and want to setup a bass for a unique sound these are the way to go. title: High Quality Speaker Amp. High Value w/ a Software Bug?
text:

I am using an Ibanez As73 with it.

It gets great metal, rock and blues sounds. The clean channel doesn't want to work with my guitar. But I put it on the acoustic channel, and it works fine.

The tough part is remembering the settings you had before you switched them to make a different sound! Really I've only had mine for seven days.

Prepare to have tons of fun if you have the patience to configure and re-configure. They say it is programmable with their free software on their website.

My amp starts with different settings than what I was using when I turned it off, which is weird but is probably a software bug. 4 stars overall.

title: Believe the hype
text:
I know these amps are basically their own meme in the guitar world now, but wow. Believe in the hype. Excellent volume, easy control, ability to set multiple saved profiles for easy settings, and wonderful tone. I play everything from jazz and blues to death and black metal through mine. Very happy with it right out of the box. Handles high gain distortion really well too.

My *only* complaint is that balancing the volume can be tricky when using a noise gate. I like to have the gate turned up high for all my gain, but then the volume bottoms out so you have to nudge it up more, and it seems to jump right to ear-melt level which isn't where I want to be. Solved the problem by lowering the volume on my distortion (Wampler Dracarys) and then cranking the noise gate back a little bit.

title: Forget Kyser, Buy This
text:
This $7.99 capo does what Kyser styled capos can't: it clamps on the guitar neck with a minimum of pressure, but more importantly has no extra metal protruding to interfere with your fretting hand. And although this model reportedly isn't designed to be used on a 12-string, I do on a Harley Benton and it works great.

As with any capo occasionally you'll have a buzzing string on the first try. So what? Unclamp and take a new bite. At this price buy one to keep with every guitar and rock on. You can get three for the price of one Kyser and get a better designed product. That's a win-win in my book.

title: Great Guitar For The Money
text:
I'm not sure what the reviewers knocking this guitar are talking about. The one I have sounds great, keeps tune for a long time and is easy to play. I used it as a bridge between ukulele and guitar and it's perfect for that purpose. The scale is short, the strings are steel and the chord shapes are the same, albeit for different notes. The brain will quickly retrain if you're an adept uke player.

Best of all it has a guitar sound so even if that's as far as you go, you can get in where you fit in with others or playing solo.

title: Great Entry Level Harmonica Set
text:
As a beginner with nothing to compare it to except my $10 practice harp, I feel the consistent pre-purchase player reviews saying these were the best blend of value and quality was correct. They have a warm tone, great airflow, and are easy to play single notes across all ten holes. I've been able to recreate the harmonica parts on early Beatles, Dylan and Neil Young as well as Old West trail songs and other rock solos. I'm still acquainting myself with the instrument and developing the ability to play by ear, so I haven't put these through the paces of hard blowing and drawing of the blues. All I can go on is the praise of durabilty most owners say these have. The case is fine, although a polishing cloth (not included) would have been a welcome addition.

Update (2/18/18): OK, after having played these for a few months I can attest to the claims of great value for the money. They play clean single notes, chords and bends easily. I don't play blues yet, but in rock, acoustic or country setting they are top notch. The thought that these are a hair on the quiet side is probably true, but it's fair enough trade for the clean, crisp pure tone produced right out of the box by all six in the set. Another feature that bears mentioning is ergonomic design of the cover plates. They're pressed from stainless steel in one piece so there's no bent or cut edges at the corners to painfully grab facial hair.

If you're on the fence with this set or Suzuki's in general, don't be. Quality and value come together here.

title: Really good at absorbing...liquid.
text:
You ever seen those little toy pills that you throw in a cup water and it puffs up, gets bigger, and becomes a foam sponge in the shape of a dinosaur or something? That's what these are. They're flat squares that you soak in water, they puff up, get bigger, and become foam sponges that look like acoustic panels.

Will using these be better than just a bare reflective wall to absorb sound? It is better than nothing I suppose. Is it going to work like the denser, more expensive auralex, etc foam panels? To be fair, even those more expensive panels are still really inefficient when compared to better insulation filled panels. They can help tame some of the higher audio frequencies, but aren't effective otherwise. These foam panels are going to perform even worse. A blanket hanging on the wall would probably provide the same results, if not better.

I already have auralex brand panels and insulation filled panels in my home studio and was hoping these could work for another room. Like anyone looking at these type of "acoustic panels", it's the price that lured me in. When I purchased this 12-pack it was selling for $30, with a discount code that brought it down to $10.50. Now it's listed for $15.99...that price should be a red flag and still too much in my opinion.

I ended up tacking these on the wall behind my hanging guitars to provide some cushion for them. They work well for that at least. And if I ever have an incident that requires me to soak up a bunch of water, they'll be the first thing I run for.

title: much better, easy replacement, great improvement!
text:
I used this to replace the full-tune bridge on my Ibanez artist.
The original bridge on the Ibanez has the wire tightening and very loose adjustment screws. It rattles and buzzes.
The Gotoh bridge is very tight, no loose screws and every part fits perfectly without any space for movement, which causes it to be dead quiet, letting the strings ring perfectly without any buzz or rattling.
Very good product. I loved it so much that I'm replacing all my tune-o-matic bridges for this one. You just need to be careful to order the correct one. There is basically two versions and you need to know which one you need and also be careful to order a matching finish: nickel is not the same as chrome! Make sure you match what ever is the tail piece you have so it doesn't look weird.

ONE small complaint - I REALLY wish they would give you an optional speaker grill/cover of some sort.

title: Absolutely Worth the Investment
text:
I ordinarily use a high end microphone with a professional mixing board for my podcast. However, I had an opportunity to interview a guest on the ride up to a meeting with a DJ at a radio station in NJ. I brought along my portable mobile studio setup, (very expensive, I might add) and it ended up not working. AT ALL.

I decided to try using a USB mic that plugs straight into the computer and almost immediately, came a cross an ad for the Tonor Q-9. Best decision I could possibly have made!

It arrived within 4 days and I immediately booted up my Macbook Pro to try it out. I was quite impressed with this kit. Now, I'm not saying this sounds as good as my more expensive high end mic, but then, my USB interface requires the computer to be plugged in to work. Which renders my expensive studio setup completely useless as a totally mobile solution.

However, the Tonor Q-9 USB mic is exactly what the doctor ordered for taking my show on the road. It's crisp, records effortlessly, and after finding the "sweet spot" - I was able to record with no echo or background noise. What little noise I encounter, I can fix in post production during editing. I do that anyway, no matter which mic i use.

This may not be the greatest mic you can buy at any price, BUT for the money - you can't beat this at all. Besides the mic, you also get the accessories most other brands require you to purchase a la carte. So, yes!... If you're in the market for a decent, inexpensive USB mic for podcasting, gaming, even recording vocals for music - I would not hesitate to recommend the Tonor Q-9 USB microphone. If not as your go-to, then at least as a very good back-up!

title: Before you buy take a closer look at the 100 !!!  I wish i did!
text:
It is a nice amp. Like any amp, takes a while to get the sound settings the way you like, i like keeping things simple. One thing i do not like about this amp is the lack of presence knob, you can set the presence but you need a computer and the Boss Tone Studio (BTS) software (the software is free from the Boss website runs on Microsoft or Mac machine) hooked up to the amp with a USB cable. With the BTS software this amp has great potential in the right hands, for someone that likes keeping it simple, there are just too many adjustments that can be tinkered with on this amp. Not sure if this is a plus or a negative yet, I'm kind of in the middle on this. Overall, it is a nice little amp for the money. I only play the guitar for myself, so I cannot comment on how this amp might be use for gigging or recording, but it is very loud!!! I keep at 5w or 25w almost all the time, the 50w setting is just to loud for my practice room, makes my ears feel like they might start bleeding if I keep it on the 50w setting. Seems to have great potential for recording in the right hands.

close to a year after purchase ... The more time I spend with this amp the more I like it and appreciate what it can do. the biggest to con for this amp is the switch options. There isn't any foot switch options for the effects at all, this is not good. there is basically only one switch option that changes preset channels, so you only have (4) presets you can select with a foot switch. There are so many effects on this amp and this is very limited. this amp would be much better with a foot switch option to control the effects on the amp, currently there is no way to do this.

Before you buy the 50 take a closer look at the 100, I wish I did. #1 look at the foot switch options closely #2 look at the loop chain options. Plus the 100 does sound better than the 50 most of the time, the 100 is either equal in tone or better than the 50. If you are on a tight budget the 50 is a great amp - if you want more than just a very nice practice amp you should take a closer look at the 100 before buying. again, I wish i did.

title: Cheap, does the job
text:
If you want a new clarinet, don't want to spend much money, this is the one. I've been practicing on it for a couple weeks now, no complaints. I'm still getting my chops back, so maybe more comments later. I'm not buying the other comments about a poor instrument, or "bought it for my child". If you really know clarinets, you know ANY instrument will be difficult for children, and ALL new clarinets go together difficulty. You need to know how to handle new cork in the joints. If not, now is a good time for lessons from a pro.
The only con for this instrument would be the tiny case. Not any room for accessories. I bought a brief case, lined it with foam rubber, cut out the joint shapes, and voila! I had plenty of room for an accessory drawer and vertical swab or two. And a plus: Not mentioned in the description was a C barrel. These usually tune poorly, but at least it was included, and I'll be able to play with a piano accompaniment easily when the time comes. My only other gripe has to do with reeds. I'm an old-timer and like to actually LOOK at the grain in several reeds before I choose one. Now, they all come sealed in an opaque wrapper. So back to old style - buy a large quantity, say a dozen, pick out the few really good ones, and toss the others, or sell 'em to beginners. This Hisonic does the job. Thanks for a good ax at a good price.

title: Is it the right amp for you???
text:
This amp has been reviewed countless times. If you’re no stranger to You Tube then you have probably watched a demo or two. The question really comes down to if this is that right amp for you. The tricky thing is, that’s a question only you can answer.

The first thing to point out is the tone. If you are tone chaser and you’re ever searching for that perfect tone, stay clear away from this amp! It’s very unlikely you will buy this and brag to your friends about your incredible tone. The amp is solid state and will typically lose in a tone comparison against any reputable high end tube amp for tone, dynamics, and response.

So when you hear players ramble on and on about how the Boss doesn’t measure up when it comes to tone, there is no need to worry. Some refer to this as a beginner amp. That really is subjective and it’s only fair to point out that there are pros that use this amp. The real question is, “Does the amp sound good enough?” Most will readily agree that the Katana has a “useable” tone. Not necessarily the best tone. If that makes sense.

The features on this amp are simple, straight forward, and incredibly user friendly. You should be able to immediately dial in some useable sounds. When you utilize the Boss editor software you will have numerous effects to choose from. Some of these effects in the editor are unimpressive or not useable. But, there are quite a few that are. I am not going to go into all the features, but I feel the simplicity and quality of the features make this amp very worthwhile. Some people try to use this amp as a modeler. It can be done, but I don’t think that is where this amp shines. There are better modeler amps out there at this price range.

The amp goes up to 50 Watts. Which is very loud. So unless you’re playing to large venues (something other than local night clubs or church events), this amp should more than suit your volume needs. It also has a built in Attenuator 25w/ 0.5w settings for night or quiet playing.

What you get vs. what you for equates to an outstanding value overall. There are effects pedals that cost more than this amp! Additionally, service and maintenance with a solid state amp is virtually nothing. You don’t need to worry about changing tubes, servicing switches, or carrying a heavy 80 pound tube amp around. The Boss isn’t an outstanding value because it does a few things better than the rest. The value in this amp comes from versatility!

title: Amazing sound quality at an incredible price.
text:
I wanted a USB mic for my desk to up my podcasting quality. Up till then I was using my iPad Pro with “studio quality” mics and my iPhone 11. The short of this review is that I was blown away by the massive difference with this mic and the iPad Pro “studio quality” mics.

Let’s start with what you get and the quality and the value. At first I wa skeptical that I could get good sound for $38.99, yes I paid $38.99 for all this, it it had great reviews so I decided to take a chance. I was not disappointed. The description is pretty much accurate with respect to what you get. The mic itself feels very solid and being a USB mic, the volume up and down buttons are essential. Do not get a USB mic without a volume control.

Now let’s talk about the quality of the sound. The noise floor on this mic is amazing. In a quiet room, with the volume set to one press below maximum, there is virtually no distinguishable noise, certainly no electronic noise or susceptibility to interference from other electronic devices.

If you have never used an external mic like I haven’t, using an external mic is a game changer. Since all I used were my iPad Pro and iPhone to record audio, I tended to use iOS based apps. With this mic hooked up to my Windows PC, I discovered Audacity which is a free audio editing software.

Now I record my podcasts directly into audacity. I set the mic volume 1 down from max, then I position the mic about 6-8” from my mouth. That gives me consistent audio in the -12 to -9 range with peaks at -6 to -4 ish.

The raw sound from this mic made me sound like a professional DJ! LOL! I’m not kidding. The audio recorded on my iPad Pro had much more echo and sounded tinny. This Q9 sounded very warm but clear.

Now comes the best part.... I record in 32-bit float, something I could not easily figure out how to do on my iPad, Then apply three “ effects” in audacity to process the audio. First I apply a normalized to bring up the levels to -0.1db. Since I record in 32-bit float, there is no distinguishable negative effect. Next, I apply a compressor to bring up the lower parts. At this point the audio is sounding pretty good, but then I apply a noise reduction to take out any background noise like when the AC in my house kicks in. At this point the audio is ready for a podcast, but I also apply a noise gate to cut anything below -48db to just give it that “professional” touch.

When I compare this audio quality to any professionally done podcast from big radio names like NPR and others, this quality matches theirs in my mind.

title: #1 Beginner Harmonica - Compared
text:
----------Hohner Special 20:
-(****_) overall: My preferred beginner harmonica, recommended to anyone as a first harmonica, and to experienced players who want the best harmonica at this price point. Anything less expensive will lack in quality and be difficult to play, which could turn off an aspiring player. It's good enough that many experienced players will never find a need to spend more on a harmonica. Not rated higher because you get what you pay for, and my preferred harmonicas are in the higher price range.
-(****_) Sound: Excellent. Loved it, and one of its strongest point. It's good enough to make a song truly enjoyable. Even as a beginner you can get a nice sound. It's not as good as top-end harmonicas but I never realized that or cared until I owned a top-end harmonica.
-(*____) Durability: The real achille's heel of the Special 20. This harmonica will not last. The brass reeds are not durable, reason why many top-end manufacturers use different reed materials specifically to improve durability (at a higher price point). Within a few months my harmonica had to be replaced.
-(****_) Playability: The comb is made of plastic and protrudes, which makes it slide nicely. The holes are easy to single out for a beginner. The notes are easy to bend. The biggest disadvantage is some notes tend to get stuck and over time make the harmonica difficult to play. IMPORTANT: 1-2-star reviews often complain their 2-draw was broken from day one. The 2-draw is not broken, it is simply a very difficult note for beginners to play. Admittedly, the 2-draw on the Special 20 is difficult to play (arguably more than usual).
-(***__ Aesthetics): A pretty decent looking harmonica. The case looks fine. Feel perfectly happy with it, but it doesn't have the look and feel of top of the line harmonica like a Suzuki Firebreath or Promaster.

-----------Comparison with other Harmonicas:
--(**___ overall) Hohner Big River: Nothing memorable. It's perfectly fine but there's no reason to buy it over the Special 20 (the $ savings is minimal). Unlike the Special 20 it has a wood comb, but if you want a wood comb buy a Marine Band 1896 Classic.
--(***__ overall) Hohner Marine Band 1896 Classic: Great beginner harmonica at an affordable price. It has a wood comb. I slightly prefer the sound of the Special 20, the plastic comb of the Special 20 slides easily, and its holes are easy for a beginner to single out, so my preference goes to the Special 20.
--(***** Overall) Suzuki Firebreath: Amazing. Not cheap, so I recommend the Special 20 as a first harmonica until you decide you're going to stick with the instrument. Even if you're "sure" you'll stick, I still recommend starting with the Special 20 because beginners are more likely to misuse and break their harmonicas, and so you get the pleasure of looking forward to and appreciating your future upgrade.
--(***** Overall) Suzuki Promaster: Amazing. Same comments are the firebreath.

----------Note on which key to buy first:
--I recommend starting with a key of C.
This is the accepted standard since most beginner songs and lessons will all be in C. One harmonica is fine as a beginner.
--Then in this order: D, A.
A is common in blues and country. D is also common and often considered easier to play than the C (the 2-draw should be easier)
--Then F, G, Bb, E,...
I would argue for the last 4 in this order, but here is gets more debatable. Of course, there are even more keys and variations beyond the ones listed. Feel free to add your opinion, since this tends to vary between players.

title: Does not fit on all Hofner Basses
text:
I bought these strings to try out on my German Hofner basses . I installed the G & D strings with no problem . When I got to the A & E strings they would not fit through the eyelit (hole) in the tuning pegs . The G & D sounded great ,but was unable to install the 2 remaining strings as the E & A strings were too thick to go through the tuning pegs.

I gave these to a friend who had a Hofner Contemporary Bass, and a Hofner Ignition Bass . He had the same problem on his Contemporary Bass. The E & A strings would not go through the tuning pegs on A & E .

So, we tried them on his Hofner Ignition Bass, and they fit with no problem going through the tuning pegs ! The strings sounded & felt really good on the Ignition Bass initially, but the string tension is VERY high (Very Tight ) .He played them for about 4 days ,and said they were really stiff & was afraid the tension might damage his bass. I played on his bass and the strings were very stiff, I noticed a slight forward bow in the neck, which wasn't there previously . Also made the tuners on the Ignition a bit loose.

So, we took these DAddario strings off his Ignition bass .Botton line . These are vary heavy gauge strings,& I would not advise putting these on Hofner basses . Just my personal opinion .

He bought a couple sets of LaBella Black Tape strings for his Hofner Contemporary, & Ignition basses. We installed them with no issues on both Hofners. The Labella Black Tapes sounded,& played great ! The low tension of the LaBella Tapes was awesome . These particular DAddario are a good string,but, not a good idea for a Hofner bass . The tension on the DAddario was at least 5 times greater then the the Labella Tapes . I have DAddario long scale tapes on my Fender P bass with no problem ,however the Fender is a tough, heavy bass . These DAddario would probably be a great string for a Gibson EBO ,or other solid body type basses of this scale ?

title: I have never paid less money for a great tone.
text:
I'm writing this from the perspective of a guitar hobbyist that generally uses this amp to practice at home. I'm not necessarily a "gigging musician", I play for the fun of learning at home. While I can not speak for how this amp sounds in a full band situation, I can definitely speak as to how this amp sounds when playing at home at all volumes.

I purchased this amp after trying both the 50W combo and the 100W combo. You will see a lot of people talking about how the 100W combo has more features, more programmable channels and and effects loop as well as more wattage, a bigger enclosure and a speaker with a bigger magnet. Pure and simple, the 50W sounded better to me. The tone is warmer and smoother than the 100W. My preference of tone is obviously my opinion, and I have read other reviews where the reviewer preferred the 100 to the 50. The warm tone of the 50 just happens to be exactly what I am looking for.

The Features:
As far as the features go, you have your 5 amp voices that you can build your tone on top of. The Acoustic, The Clean, The Crunch, The Lead and the Brown. I view all of these as the base tones on which you can build with built-in pedals and effects. You can add gain to each of these voices with a gain knob, or you can use built in drive pedals to give you different flavors of gain. The cool thing with these voices is that the built in gain keeps the character of the amp model by just adding more gain to that particular voice. The built-in drive pedals give you options to add a different character to that particular amp voice, giving you a wide variety of options. There are plenty of options that can help you dial in just about any type of tone. The pedals are primarily meant to model the pedals that Boss is famous for manufacturing, so you have overdrive, blues driver, as well as metal zone type pedals, there are other non-boss options that model Rat pedals, and even a fuzz pedal. On top of that you can use the built in modulation effects , phasers, flangers, choruses, even octave effects. Finally there is another knob that powers your reverb and delay effects, and you also have a choice as to what type of reverb or delay as well as a tap tempo button. There are eq controls for your treble, mid and bass as well as the gain and volume control for the amp voice. The unexpectedly cool feature on this amp is the wattage selection switch that allows you to use the amp at full power, half power 25W as well as .5W. I had wondered why this feature was necessary on a solid state digital combo, until I tried it. It allows you to give the amp a fully cranked tone at a lower volume, great for practice or recording, and when you switch to the higher wattage, the tone remains the same at a louder volume. On previous modeling amps that I had used, if you find a great tone at a low volume and then crank it, the tone changes quite a bit. And of course on a tube amp, you can get a great tone at a certain volume and then slightly change your volume only to realize that you have just gotten yourself out of the sweet-spot and now need to tweak and adjust to try and get that tone back. The Katana, stays very consistent at different volumes.

The Tone
The 50W Katana is fantastic for a great warm fat tone at all gain levels. You can use the eq to get a bit more clarity and punch, but at noon on the eq dials, you will find that the tone is very smooth. This is without a doubt my preference. I could definitely seeing people that prefer the cleanest amp tones preferring the 100W to the 50W, it did sound somewhat clearer and more articulate. But the tone on the 50W gives some real warmth to the single coils on my strat, and a very smooth fatness to the humbucker on my HSS strat. Each channel has a great character to it, for a clean tone, I like the clean channel with just a little gain mixed in to add some extra sustain and warmth. For a hard rock tone, I love the crunch channel with the blues driver on it, and I also love the lead channel without any extra gain. The smooth full sustain of the brown channel is one of the most fun lead tones that I have ever used, full warm totally saturated.
I find that adding the pedals to the amp voices is great fun and really helps find a different character. But with nothing but the adding gain to the crunch, lead and brown channels I can find some fantastic tones. If there were no pedals to add on top of them at all, I would still say that this amp is a great value. It just sounds amazing with nothing but those voices and the tone knob.

The Tone Editor
On your computer you can download a tone editor and plug the amp into your computer. With this feature, the tonal combinations and possibilities are endless. If you don't like the pedals that are pre-set into the amp, you can find other drive pedals that you can make your new default. Once you set these pedals up, you don't need to keep your computer plugged in, you can just set them up to be used with the drive dial.

Negatives
To be clear. This amp is a great value as it is. There are no glaring omissions at all. I would like to have a few more channels to save pre-set tones and a footswitch to change from one to the other easily and quickly. For $199 though, you get such a great tone from this amp. And you get it EASILY. You don't have to monkey around with computers and apps.

Overall
I have never gotten a better tone from a solid state amp. Period. I have never gotten better saturated higher gain tones with any amp, especially not at low volumes. I have never had an easier time getting a fantastic tone out of an amp. I sold my Fender Bassbreaker 15 after having this amp for a week. I like the sound of this amp far better and the ease of use far better. The fact that I paid $199 for this amp just seems unbelievable to me.

I enjoy the 88 keys, which I have not had in years, I had a very heavy Yamaha 88 key controller in the eighties, and had used the roland A30 with 76 keys for the last eighteen years. I loved the Roland, but it had gone to the shop four times in this last year, and could no longer be maintained. Life is about change, and I believe the M-Audio 88es is a reasonable substitution. No one in the band notices a real difference, let alone the audience.
I'm adding this after six months of use, maybe thirty, thirty five gigs. No problems of any kind, I did purchase a very inexpensive soft coverlet case, which suffices, but doesn't really fit well....this keyboard is very long, and very slender. I've become used to its nuances, and have no complaint. I did buy the extended warranty if it goes wonky on me............meets all my needs, works every time.........so far. title: Fantastic piezo pick up
text:
Fantastic piezo pick up! My luthier made it nice and thin so it really sounds just as nice on my fine violin as the original bridge while playing unamplified. I was worried about that. I play professionally, mostly classical, and needed something that wouldn't feedback during noisy cocktail hours and dinner parties. While not a nice sounding as the microphone set up I use, there is absolutely no feedback, even at unbearable volume levels. Here's the downside to this pick up: it is strange to use it to play solo. There is a very noticeable little punch with each bow stroke that I've never encountered with the many other pick ups I've purchased, no matter how lightly you play. Paired with my Baggs Para Acoustic DI box, I can turn the low register way down on the EQ to virtually eliminate the punch, but it affects the overall tone more than I'd like. When playing chamber music with others, the punch is undetectable even with the low register turned up where I like it. So, it serves its purpose very well. I wouldn't record solo with it, but in a group it's fine. Glad I got it installed, I now have an all purpose gig instrument that's hassle-free. Good job, Baggs...

Edit 7/6/16 - I've finally found the perfect EQ from the PADI. I no longer hear that punch, it seems my bass was way up and disproportionate to the rest of the EQ. Now it sounds amazing, I'm going to try recording with it...

Edit 8/27/2022 - The bridge pickup still works flawlessly. I've been playing through a Bose T1 digital mixer for the last few years, and the violin eq setting on the Tonematch automatically has a low cut/high pass filter at about 80hz, so no ugly bow sounds. So glad I went this route.

Fantastic piezo pick up! My luthier made it nice and thin so it really sounds just as nice on my fine violin as the original bridge while playing unamplified. I was worried about that. I play professionally, mostly classical, and needed something that wouldn't feedback during noisy cocktail hours and dinner parties. While not a nice sounding as the microphone set up I use, there is absolutely no feedback, even at unbearable volume levels. Here's the downside to this pick up: it is strange to use it to play solo. There is a very noticeable little punch with each bow stroke that I've never encountered with the many other pick ups I've purchased, no matter how lightly you play. Paired with my Baggs Para Acoustic DI box, I can turn the low register way down on the EQ to virtually eliminate the punch, but it affects the overall tone more than I'd like. When playing chamber music with others, the punch is undetectable even with the low register turned up where I like it. So, it serves its purpose very well. I wouldn't record solo with it, but in a group it's fine. Glad I got it installed, I now have an all purpose gig instrument that's hassle-free. Good job, Baggs...

Edit 7/6/16 - I've finally found the perfect EQ from the PADI. I no longer hear that punch, it seems my bass was way up and disproportionate to the rest of the EQ. Now it sounds amazing, I'm going to try recording with it...

Edit 8/27/2022 - The bridge pickup still works flawlessly. I've been playing through a Bose T1 digital mixer for the last few years, and the violin eq setting on the Tonematch automatically has a low cut/high pass filter at about 80hz, so no ugly bow sounds. So glad I went this route.

title: Better than expected for <~$200
text:
Despite ordering from Amazon Warehouse with a note that this was repacked and had slight damage (under 5%) it is much nicer than I expected for a budget LP Special ll, which is what the base guitar is despite the Slash AFD branding (Note to Amazon Warehouse personnel: Oversized cheap box full of crumpled brown paper is a crappy way to ship expensive items). All I can find for damage is a tiny speck of missing color near the neck joint, and a tiny, slight indent in the finish near the bottom of the face.. hard to find unless you're really looking flat across the face in bright sunlight.

I love almost everything about this axe, it's lighter than my Epi LP Studio, which itself is considerably lighter than a Standard LP, so that puts this in the "almost too light for the best sustain" category, along with the bolt-on neck, but it surprised me with how good it holds a note, and my back and neck appreciate the lesser load.

The set up was very good overall with low action, no fret buzz, level frets, and a decent intonation right out of the box, but as mine was possibly pre-owned it may have been set up by someone with knowledge of guitars. All I needed to do was a light filing of the fret ends and adjusted the intonation on the high E string.

The neck is a nice glossy finish, which will probably be lightly sanded to my preference. The fingerboard, which is supposed to be rosewood (highly questionable) is dull and dry looking, with bland white plastic dot inlays, soon to be drilled out and replaced with larger perloid ones. I used a rag and some tung oil to bring out the shine and it soaked in kind of patchy, so several coats left overnight may be in order. The tuners are individual with chrome domed covers and they seem adequate for the job. The strings are nice, probably Epiphone stock electric mediums. I stretched them into tune easily and I'll keep playing them until one breaks.
The nut is hard white plastic, and should be replaced with one that better matches with the cream binding. Same goes for the pickup surrounds.
There's a nice glossy mellow yellow face with a 50/50 split flame maple top with cream binding, and see-through cherry finished body without any back binding. A difference between these in comparison with a Studio of Standard LP is the totally flat face without any "arch" whatsoever.
I appreciate where the selector switch is relocated as on other LP's it can get in the way when jamming out hard, causing problems that are easily solved with this setup.. and no noticeable issues between these with two instead of the usual four knobs: just be fairly quick with your fingers if you don't like the way it sounds between the two pickup settings. This is actually my favorite feature of this guitar other than the cool pickup ring tuner, which is a totally awesome invention.

The ceramic pickups are nice and hot, similar to the ones on my American made Ibenez travel guitar. They don't have much in the way of potting, with a quick wrap of black electrical tape around the coils, but they are the spicy pickups used for the LP Standard AFD, so I can't complain. They don't squeal unless I'm almost touching my amp, turned up to a window rattling level, but have a nice open tone with plenty of attitude.
Included are a cheesy gig bag, almost unpadded and not up to the usual Epiphone quality even though it bears the brand, an equally cheap narrow nylon strap, a 7' cable with 45 degree end plug, three thin unbranded tortex picks, a hex wrench for neck truss rod adjustment, and a safety sheet.

This was a birthday gift for myself and I'm quite satisfied with the guitar. The accessories are not worth much and anyone who wants real protection and some storage will invest in a decent guitar case. I have a regular Epiphone soft gig bag and it's not only lined with soft material, but the outside nylon is quite dense plus it has a better handle with plastic tubing and straps for backpack carry.

4 Stars guitar, 2 Stars accessories.
