title: Review of the Logitech G Pro along with 4 other mice
text:
My DeathAdder 3G had been acting up on me for the past couple years and despite my attempts as resuscitating it (tried using compressed air on click switches as well as doing a 'scotch tape trick' on scroll wheel), the unit finally stopped working. My problems with this mouse at the end of its life were that 1) a click would sometimes register an additional click - making me accidentally open files when I wanted to just select them. This made dragging files around really frustating. 2) The scroll wheel would also randomly insert an upward scroll movement in the middle of a down scroll - which would make viewing webpages and documents a chore.

My requirements for a new replacement were that 1) I wanted a mouse with good switches (preferably Omron) to avoid the double click problem. 2) A scroll wheel that would smoothly scroll and was of solid construction to not end up w/ the same scroll problem. 3) A mouse that could entirely turn off its LED lights as I have my desktop in my bedroom and prefer to have no external lights.

I ended up trying several off of YT Rocket Ninja's Top 10 Mouse list. Although I do not game very much anymore, I figured a mouse that could survive the rigors of heavy gaming would be of higher quality than other office mice and would thus last longer and provide better feedback. Here are my thoughts on various mice that I tried and the Logitech G Pro which I finally ended up getting. (I tried each mouse for about a month to give me time to form a proper opinion.)

[[ASIN:B00GU4F4OM Redragon M801 Mammoth]] - This mouse was the first candidate that I tried based off of Amazon's recommendation list. It had a really nicely textured mouse surface and the clicks were really crisp (Omron switches). The mouse was of a comfortable size for my hand and the cord was a nice braided one. It really was a quality piece and the price was by far the cheapest out of any of these other mice ($28). The software was also really light compared to the Razer Synapse software which seemed to want to update every 2 days. My main problem with this mouse was that you could only turn off the LED lighting to the wheel and dpi switches, and not the giant slash and side trim pieces. I did however find a YouTube tutorial that showed how you could unscrew the assembly through the weight compartment to pull the internal connector to disable the lights but did not want to go with the hassle). For people that don't care about the LED lights and/or on a budget, I would actually give this a 4* recommendation.

[[ASIN:B01KUAMCV4 Logitech G403 Prodigy]] - The next mouse I tried was the G403 after discovering Rocket Ninja's YouTube page. This was his #1 selected mouse so it was a good next choice. I learned that having the distinctly separate mouse buttons from the chassis aided in the longevity of the click buttons (The DeathAdder 3G had the buttons integrated in the overall shell of the body). Unfortunately, I found the mouse wheel to be much looser than my original DeathAdder as well as the Red Dragon and decided to return this mouse and look for alternatives. (3.5*)

[[ASIN:B01LXC1QL0 Razer DeathAdder Elite]] - I went with the DeathAdder Elite after my experience with the G403. Being a more expensive version of the original DeathAdder and also scoring high on the Rocket Ninja list, I thought that being done with this process and getting the updated version might be my final answer. The mouse was almost identical to the DeathAdder I had before with better mouse texture and lighter clicks. Unfortunately, it just felt like the old DeathAdder I had in nicer packaging. I strongly believe that in a few years, I would have ended up with the same problems as much current DeathAdder mouse. I also felt that it did not warrant the more expensive price point of $67. For a $40 mouse, it would be okay. For a $67 mouse, it felt cheap. And with mixed reviews and Razer's reputation of having products which do not last, I also ended up returning this. (3*)

[[ASIN:B01HHGHCH8 Nixeus Revel]] - Next was the fairly inexpensive Nixeus Revel. It was the first software-less gaming mouse that I tried and it had several really high points and one serious low point. I found the product to be fairly sturdy, the buttons and mouse wheel were really good. This mouse was the first one thus far to not have an LED built into the wheel assembly itself and I felt this added to the build quality of the assembly (solid block of plastic vs hollowed out wheel w/ a light). The downsides: If you left the mouse alone and let the screensaver turn on, the mouse would also "fall asleep". Clicks would not be responsive, and the scrolling would automatically switch to the lowest DPI setting. I found that if I switched DPIs, all these symptoms would be alleviated - but again, it was a really weird problem to have. Other reviewers noticed the same. Also, LED lights could not be turned off. (3*)

[[ASIN:B01JPOLLTK Logitech G Pro]] - Lastly, I arrived at this mouse. It had good build quality with the Omron switches and even came with a braided cord. It also had the separate buttons from main mouse body and a non lit mouse wheel. LEDs were also programmable to be completely turned off. I feel that this mouse really met all my mousing requirements and should definitely be on your short list as well. (5*)

title: Great optical mouse, feels small and flat compared to others
text:
The TLDR is this is a good mouse with a really good optical sensor that is fairly small and flat, so did not fit my hand comfortably but you might like it.

The only negative I can say about this mouse is that it's very flat and fairly small. This means that when I held it, the surrounding part of my hand rubbed against the mouse pad (ring and pinky finger, and heel of hand) which was different because I don't claw grip the mouse.
It also means that if you use a relaxed grip (instead of bending your fingers or a claw grip) you'll accidentally hit both the left and right mouse button a decent amount, especially if you pick it up to reposition it (aka low sensitivity).

This is a personalpreference and while negative for me it could fit your style perfectly. Everything else I can say about this mouse is positive. The sensore will be a noticeable difference in FPS games compared to a laser. The feet are smooth but not too smooth. The pointer finger has a slight indentation that nestles your finger. The lighting has a bright deep set coloration. The thumb buttons are easily accessible but you wont fat finger them. Picking the mouse up for repositioning is easy and natural (assuming you hook grip).

title: Quite simply the best mouse I've ever used.
text:
I love this mouse! I previously used the Logitech G402, but didn't like how the right mouse button felt.

So I decided to try the Logitech G Pro.
Here are my favorite features of this mouse:
1. I love the super soft and long cable. Its a cloth braided cable, but super flexible and does not retain any bends.. You want it to lay straight?, it will!
2. The size is perfect. I have large hands, and this mouse feels wonderful to me. My wife has very small hands and she says it feels wonderful too, but she is NOT a gamer and just browses the web. This is very subjective.
3. I love the simplicity.. 2 buttons, a scroll wheel, back page and forward page buttons, and a single dpi adjustment button.
4. The customizable LED's... beautiful. You can use the logitech software to pick a variety of colors, speed, options, or set it to a smooth pulse. It really looks great! The "G" and an entire ring of LEDs along the rear of the mouse..
5. Simple software download and install. Plug in the mouse, then go to the logitech website and download the Logitech gaming software. Install, restart and you're ready. You can customize so much, including individual dpi settings, colors of LED's, mouse surface, remap buttons, etc.
6. PRICE! What a great price. Thank you logitech.

If this mouse fits your hands to your liking (personal preference, I know) and has the right button layout for your needs, You will love this mouse.

In my opinion, it is the best mouse I've ever used. I am not a "hardcore" gamer, but I do play games like BF4, TombRaider, Diablo3, GTA5, etc.. I love this darn mouse.

title: One Little Flaw is a Big Problem UPDATE
text:
Ok...This is all subjective. I do not like this mouse, (and will probably not like any other Logitech mouse again) due to the primary and secondary buttons. They don't click. And they actuate much too easily.

Now...The current deal is to convince you that you need ultra-quiet mouse keys so that you do not wake up any babies. This is ludicrous.

And we don't want the buttons to be too hard to activate due to concerns about carpal tunnel syndrome. That one has some validity.

None the less, this mouse is a nuisance. Or more accurately, this marketing trend is a nuisance.

If I send it back and get a different kind, I'll just end up with another one that has the same problems because they all will. This is not a failure of the mouse. It's performing as it was designed to. It's a failure of good common sense. I don't know why they call it "common sense" since it is not common at all.

Left main button has failed after 2 months. Just barely touch it and the mouse goes wild with double ad triple clicks. If you buy this, you roll the dice.

title: A bit disappointing and misleading.
text:
I bought this for the single-player story mode. I didn't know they released a Bomberman for PS4. I was just browsing the game store when I saw it and decided to get it because I love Bomberman and loved Bomberman 64. I was itching for a fresh new Bomberman adventure. Before I bought it I asked two employees if it had a single-player story mode and they said yes! It's "exactly like how Bomberman 64 was and everything. They got different worlds to explore to." Word for word.

So there I was, sitting there at home pumped for a good Bomberman 64! However... there was no story mode... Yes there's a stupid button labeled "story mode" that you can click on but it's nothing even close to resembling a real story mode. There are a few scenes with dialogue, mainly arguing and bickering back and forth and that's all. There is essentially one level and one objective: kill the monsters and enter the portal to go to the next stage. The next stage is kill all the monster and then enter the portal to get to the next stage again rehashed and repeated about ten times each chapter. The boss was okay, at least they seemed to try a little with the boss fights but their character, motivation, and personalty is non-existent.

Passed the first world? The next chapter is simply a rehashed and repeated of the previous world... Blocks are a different color or texture, layouts are shuffled around, a little more enemies. Same level, same objective: kill the monsters and enter the portal. That's essentially all "story mode" is. Nothing like the original bombmerman 64 story mode. You can beat the whole thing in 3 hours.

I give this a few stars because the skins they have are pretty cool and fun. Also because the game still has multiplayer value and because I still like Bomberman. Get ONLY for multiplayer. If not, save your money.

title: Great retro console, not cheap and does not play all emulators, but does the job if you can't afford anything else.
text:
Quite surprised by this litte device. It won't blow your mind, and there are better devices that play any retro games, but this one play quite plenty of games. It has a nice screen, and overall the quality seem pretty solid.

You can slide in a SD card, and play any GB, GBA, and other old console. You either need the original cartridge, or the roms on a SD card.

Sound is loud, the screen respond nicely; and you can plug it to the tv, for a pixel galore retro experence.

you can do the same with a cheaper Raspberry pi; but then you won't have a portable console, unless you use also a LCD screen; but then you have a portable computer, while this is just a simple console to play games.

The price is a bit steep, considering that with a bit more than 130 you can get a Caanoo, which is vastly superior to this unit, but if you just play GBA games, this is the best alternative to the original obsolete GBA.

title: Built like a tank, stays solidly in place, great switch feel
text:
This keyboard is a bit pricey but I have to say that it's built like a tank.

The weight of the metal chassis keeps it stuck to the desk, I love that. It drives me crazy when keyboards keep creeping around as I'm hammering along on them.

I went with the Cherry MX brown key switches. They have a moderate tension, no buckling spring feel (bit noisy but quieter than buckling spring clicks) and they clack positively when they bottom. It reminds me of old commercial electric typewriters which is what I learned to type on. This feels like a commercial data terminal keyboard, very very nice.

A bit expensive but feels like it will last for a good long time. The only other nit to pick is that so many keyboards have short cords now. I like a tower on the floor a few feet away and this one just makes it. I would have liked another two feet on it for easier routing. The good news is that I could just get a USB extension cable if I want to stretch it further.

title: Great sound; awkward wiring
text:
On the plus side, the headset works great once you have it hooked up. The sounds quality is awesome (clear and precise; no hissing; lots of bass). The mic works fine. I have no problem wearing them for hours on end - the headphones are well-padded and are very comfortable over ears. I actually prefer using these over my stereo system + stock headsets, since voice chats now come in to both ears, and I can better discern the finer game sounds that I previously missed (like the enemy's footsteps behind your back!). All and all, this translates to a much better gaming experience.

My only complain is the complicated wires and their layout. Count this: 1 USB cable for power (hooked up to the Xbox), 2 stereo input lines(with split cable; hooked up to the Xbox A/V output), 1 voice input (hooked up to game controller). All are longer than you probably will need. They soon become a tangled mess. You'd expect that a single USB connection would have taken care of all the functions. But you can't blame the headset manufacture for this though - Microsoft will first need to put in support for a USB sound device. Also the microphone mute button is now inconveniently located on the inline volume control rather than on the game controller connector, making it harder to locate when you have to instantly mute your mic to pick up a phone call etc. during the game.

title: Side buttons are too small but that's my only complaint
text:
I've owned it for years and it has held up nicely.

Literally every positive a mouse can have, this one has, except for one MAJOR problem.

The 12 "G Keys" on the side of the mouse are far too small to be reliably used by my thumb, and I don't have super large hands. I bought this mouse thinking I could use the 12 side keys instead of 1-9 and various other keys for keybinding in MMO's but that just doesn't work.

I can only reliably use about 4-6 of the side keys because the ones nearer to the wrist are incredibly awkward to try to press regularly, and theres not enough tactile information to know which row of buttons my thumb is on.

If anyone from Logitech reads this, we need a mouse with 4-6 LARGE side buttons rather than 12 small ones, it would be infinitely more useful.

One of the best selling points for me is the ability to keep it wired, keeping it tethered doesn't add any additional drag that you're not already accustomed to with a wired mouse and it prevents my toddler from thinking he can walk off with it.

I removed the old Logitech Gaming software and installed the "G" software for the G703 and was able to quickly setup the DPI setting similarly to the MX518 to get the same feel.

Can't go wrong with the G703 as a replacement for the MX518.

title: Super Scribblenauts
text:
What can I say that hasn't already been said? I bought this game on a whim thinking it looked interesting but was still skeptical until I played it. Boy was I wrong to worry... I have never laughed so hard and truly enjoyed playing a game so much since I was a little kid playing Super Mario Brothers on the NES.

I was concerned this game might be too easy or juvenile for me, but quickly realized that I wish I still had the mind of a child as I struggle to think of creative ways to solve the puzzles. There are hints for when you get stuck, but if you're an adult player like me then it's a bit of a cop out and takes a lot of the fun away if you use the hints, as they are pretty straightforward. They're great in a pinch if you get stuck and frustrated, though.

I have brought this in to the office to play a few times and my co-workers swarm around me every time they see me with it, wanting to get in on a piece of the action. It's amazing what a group of 20-something nerds can think of.

Here's just one example of a level which we laughed about all day at the office: Maxwell is the tooth fairy and has to put a child to sleep, take his tooth, and leave him money. We tried what we thought was obvious by putting a moon into the room and making it night time. The child, apparently, was not playing along and continued to run around his room. One of my friends then thought it would be a great idea to equip Maxwell with a Tranquilizer Gun and shoot the little boy with it. I concured, but we first had to get him to the bed. How would we do that? By placing a candy bar on his pillow to lure him in (starting to sound a little creepy, I know). Once he was on the bed, POP, we shot him with the Tranquilizer Gun. The little boy passed out and fell off the bed... FAILURE. After another few minutes of pondering, we jokingly decided to give him a bottle full of Morphine, assuming nothing would happen. Much to our dismay, the bottle of morphine appeared before us and once put it in the boy's hand he took it and promptly walked to his bed and fell asleep. Level complete. Hilarity ensued.

Buy it!!!!!!!!!

title: Not too bad
text: This keyboard actually surprised me quite a bit. It uses black switches (not official cherry's but damn good knockoffs) and has nice double shot keys that let the LED light through without being prone to wearing off. The wrist support is magnetic which was very nice feature, and the deck has very little to no flex, probably some of the least I've ever seen in a keyboard at this price point. Now onto the less great..... The bezels on the keys are not only a chrome look (not my style), but they are actually raised slightly on the edges of the keys and the keys themselves are slightly more rounded that a standard keyboard. I found this pretty debilitating while trying to type out long sentences. The next thing I didn't like was the "RGB". Like many cheaper "RGB" keyboards out there, you cant address it in software or do anything crazy custom, but on this keyboard, you can do even less. Your options for RGB are ON, OFF, BRIGHTNESS, STROBE, BREATHING, SWIRLING, and SNAKE..... You can't change the color, it stays on multi color the entire time which really was a huge killer for me. The final complaint I would have is the fact that the cable is not braided..... for a "gaming" keyboard that has "RGB" and everything, you'd think a braided cable is an obvious inclusion but, it wasn't apparently. Overall I will still rate this keyboard at 4 stars because as long as you don't mind the aesthetics of it, it actually is made well, feels nice (if you don't mind slightly rounded keys) and functions fine.

title: Good, but the g303 did it better.
text:
I like this mouse, it just doesn't compare anywhere close to the g303, which is way better. The G Pro just felt like a step backwards compared to the g303, which was actually discontinued for some reason even though it has almost the highest reviews out of any Logitech mouse on Amazon...

1. Design-wise, there is nothing really special about the G-Pro, it just looks like a plain old office mouse with an RGB line in the middle. Much less extravagant than the legendary honeycomb RGB design of the Logitech g303.
2. I like the clicks on the g303 way better since they feel more crisp.
3. the shape is odd but the sides are flat and easy to grip. The g pro has a downward curve on the side and makes my grip a little weird on it. The g303 has a higher back end of the mouse keeps my hand from dragging on the mouse pad. Sides are also easier to grasp. I found that the mouse wheel also has a better click and the feet are much better than on the pro.

Gpro: Uneven clicks, Right click feels really bad for me. Stiff scroll wheel. The scroll wheel is wider than the G303. I think these are both QC issues.
G303: The clicks are better honestly and the overall shape of it is better as well. Literally, the only bad thing that you can say about the g303 is the lens/sensor rattle, which they fixed actually (right before they discontinued it)

I have been using the g303 for just a day now and it already feels much better than the G Pro. The clicks are stiffer and I can rest my fingers on them without worrying about pressing them. The scroll wheel is also so much easier to press than on the G Pro. I was so used to pressing the G Pro stiff scroll wheel that I thought the g303s scroll wheel was broken at first because it was so much lighter.

I use a claw grip and my hand is 19.5cm from base to the tip of my middle finger and 10cm across the palm not including my thumb. I like the shape of the g303 better for my grip because the diamond shape makes it easier for my thumb, ring and pinky finger to rest. My thumb rests right below the rear side button making it easier to reach both side buttons in game while gaming. On the g pro my thumb rests under the top side button making me have to readjust my grip when clicking the rear side button. The diamond shape also lets me keep control of the mouse while lifting my thumb to press the side buttons. When lifting my thumb on the g pro it would start to shift under my hand.

The g303 also glides a lot better and feels smooth compared to the g pro because the g pros feet are really small. The G Pro I used felt like it was scraping against my mouse pad.

Overall the g303 is better in every way to the G Pro I have used for my hand size and grip. The G Pro is now going into my closet to collect dust.

If you can still get your hands on a new or even a used g303 today considering it is discontinued, I would, because it is still hands down the best mouse that Logitech has come out with in my, and most of the other Logitech mouse user's, opinions.

title: Very Nice Replacement Controllers.
text: So far they work well. They synced up without any issues. They seem pretty responsive and the pointer seems accurate (so far). The design and button layout is pretty cool too. Different than an authentic Wii remote but I actually like it a little bit better. People complain about their remote skins not fitting. Yeah, well no kidding. If you actually looked at what you were buying than you would realise that they wouldn't fit right from the start. Open your eyes and look at the picture! My advice, buy the skins that go to this remote if you absolutely need controller skins. The plastic housing of the remote seems a little bit on the lower end of the quality spectrum. The built-in speaker sounds fine. A lot of people complain about the speaker sounding crackly and distorted. It's a tiny single speaker that alerts you when certain things happen in games (most games don't even use the speaker). The game audio isn't playing through the remote. You're not going to get home theater sound out of it. Besides, authentic Wii remotes sounds like crap too. Again, because it's just an added feature that you can turn off through your remote settings if it bothers you so much. The nunchucks seem to function properly and accurately as well. Made from the same cheap plastic though but that's fine. Just don't beat the controllers up and I think you'll be alright. Over all, I think it's a good product thus far and half the price of used, authentic Wii remotes. If I encounter any issues or problems with this remote then i will adjust my rating to reflect them.

title: Great Minimal Gaming Mouse : Edit - button failed prematurely
text:
EDIT: 3-21-2021

I've only had this mouse for one year, and the left button sensor is broken. It double-clicks when I press it once about 30% of the time now. Very bummed out because everything I wrote below just got invalidated. Not sure to take a chance and buy another one, or switch brands.

______________________

The most noted improvement over my old mouse is how much smoother games feel with it. My old mouse must have had pretty bad lag, because all my games feel like they got a 30fps boost. Even in Windows, I can feel a difference.

Very happy with the scrollwheel. It has definitive stops that you can subconsciously count, so once you get used to it in your game, you can intuitively select your items by feel. Middle click resists just enough, and the stops on the mouse keep you from rolling the mouse when middle clicking. I put 30 hours into this mouse so far, and I've not yet rolled while clicking.

Left and right clicks are solid and light. The farther out you click, the easier it is, so being a flat-finger mouser, it's very responsive. Saying that, I just tried with the claw style of play, and I don't feel a difference, actually, so looks like it's good for them as well.

Side buttons are easy to click, and out of the way for normal play.

You get 5 usable button mappings. All buttons register, even in older games. I am single-player only nowadays, so I don't use the mouse for much other than left/right/middle click and scroll. I don't even need the side buttons, as I have everything on the kb. I picked this mouse specifically for its lack of functionality.

I clicked the DPI button until I had a good speed in Windows, and then I adjusted my games accordingly. No problems so far.

The distance to lift the mouse before it stops responding is decent, just a few millimetres. This was the second most noted improvement over my old mouse.

My only gripe is that I do not want the LEDs lit. By default, it scrolls through all its colors, when by default, it should be OFF. I have to install software I don't want on my machine just to get rid of it. However, from what people have said, you just need to save the settings to the mouse EPROM and don't need the software to be running. Compared to the nightmare of Razor's software, this is a reasonable compromise.

title: A Couple of Problems
text:
This would be my favorite mouse if it weren't for a couple of major problems.

First the good stuff, the design and size of this mouse is perfect for my hands. It feels very comfortable, it tracks quickly and perfectly, I like the feel of the buttons, and the back/forward side buttons are perfectly placed and sized under my thumb. There's also a button behind the scroll wheel that is configurable (by default it changes the DPI of the mouse but I use it for double-click).

Now the bad. This is the third G703 I have used, the other two both developed problems with the mouse wheel over time. It works fine out of the box but over time it starts scrolling in the reverse direction that you want it to. It will start off doing it occasionally, then becomes more and more random until the mouse wheel becomes unusable.

The other problem is the battery life: this mouse has the poorest battery life of any I've ever used, I'm lucky if I get two days' use out of it. It uses a rechargeable internal battery so you can't swap it out when it dies, you are stuck plugging it in for however long it takes to recharge enough to get you though the rest of the day, then you have to remember to plug it back in at night. It's a hassle. This mouse is really meant to be used with Logitech's Powerplay wireless charging mouse pad, which I tried out a while ago and didn't like. The Powerplay mouse pad is expensive and way too big for my desk, plus there's another wire you have running around your desk to power the mouse pad. No thanks.

There is useless RGB lighting in a couple of places on the mouse, but if you're not going to use the wireless-charging mouse pad my advice is to turn the lighting off as it needlessly uses up precious battery life.

When I first plugged this G703 in the Logitech Gaming Software that I had used with the previous two did not recognize this one. I needed to uninstall the old software and install its replacement, the Logitech G Hub. I'm wondering if this means the new G703 has some internal differences from the older ones I used. I doubt they improved battery life but perhaps they fixed the mouse wheel scrolling issue. If so I will come back and update my review in six-month's time.

In the end I'm going to continue using this mouse. Despite its drawbacks, it's still the most comfortable mouse for my hands that I've used in recent years.

title: Basically flawless
text: I picked one of these up for $10 at a brick-and-mortar retailer shortly before Nintendo stopped production of the NES Classic Edition (which presumably includes the controller), and I have to say this thing is basically perfect. Feels exactly like playing an original NES controller fresh out of the box. The D-Pad in particular is light years beyond any mediocre, 3rd party option. Great for emulator use on PC along with the 8BitDo GBros. adapter. Honestly if you're specifically looking for a NES pad, this is probably worth it even at over 2x MSRP that Amazon is charging now that it's presumably out of production.

title: Easiest Bluetooth pairing, consistent, long battery life
text: I've used this with the new SSBU Gamecube controller and both the NES and Super NES Classic Edition controllers, and this adapter works without a hitch for all of them. Bluetooth pairing is simple and consistent. On my PC, I get some wonky button mapping when using this with the NES Classic Edition controller, but that probably has more to do with my choice of emulator than the adapter itself (it automaps just fine in Shovel Knight, for example). I would have loved for this to have a rechargeable lithium-ion battery like other 8BitDo products, but the battery life with 2x AA is pretty impressive. I've clocked probably over 20 hours on the initial pair of batteries. FWIW: the Mayflash Wii Classic Controller adapter allegedly does not work with the NES/Super NES Classic Edition controllers, so this is the only option I know of for using those controllers with a PC, so thankfully it's an excellent one.

title: Remarkable for the price
text: This controller does feel slightly cheap in terms of build quality, but it feels pretty much like playing a SNES controller if you're not being super nitpicking (and is probably better than playing a 25+ year old original pad at this point). I highly recommend this pad if you don't want to spend $30+ on a 8bitdo wireless pad or need to buy several for multiplayer use.

title: 4.5/5 - Probably the best-designed controller of all time, but not perfect
text:
Pros:
-A good controller distilled to perfection in design. The ergonomics/button placement make it work better for a wider array of games than any other pad I can think of.
-Most reliable Bluetooth device I've ever used. I use this with Windows 10 via DS4Windows and have never had any connection or compatibility issues.
-Touchpad/Gyro are really useful for Wii/Wii U emulation

Cons:
-The build quality is decent but not great. After a few weeks my unit started to feels creaky in the grips where the plastic seams come together. My L2 button also has a slight wobble to it when fully actuated that the R2 button does not have. YMMV.
-The placement of the Options/Share buttons is the one flaw in an otherwise flawless design. I know there's nowhere else to put them, but they're easy to accidentally press when using core buttons in their vicinities.

title: Excellent Cherry MX board with a nice array of features ...
text: Excellent Cherry MX board with a nice array of features (useful media macros, sturdy/thick keycaps, a very high quality detachable USB cable which I can yank in an instant when I spill Mountain Dew on my keyboard like a manchild) for a competitive price. As someone with heightened aural and tactile sensitivity vis-a-vis Asperger's (which perhaps goes without saying for someone writing a review for a mechanical keyboard) and as someone who enjoys the finer things in life, the simple click of a Cherry MX Blue switch gives me a steady stream of thousands of pure dopamine hits throughout the day. It lacks backlighting but this was actually a feature for me since I don't want my PC setup to look like a neon acid trip piercing into the darkness while I'm trying to watch a movie or sleep. I've done some residual damage to mine through a number of sugary drink spills, but that's my own fault and nothing that rubbing alcohol can't fix. It's just a wonderful, utilitarian keyboard that's a great value alternative to similar, more expensive keyboards from WASD or Das Keyboard.

title: This is not SOCOM!
text:
As with ALL the Tom Clancy video games, once again, I am dissapointed...I have yet to play one of his games that's actually "great". The graphics are cheesy, gameplay is not very smooth, and for all the hype about these Ghost Recon games, they should be WAY better than what they really are.

I mean, I can't help it when I keep comparing games like this to SOCOM Navy Seals, but, I gotta be honest here....These G.R. games are lame in comparison. Simply put: The gameplay & graphics in this game are similar to the very first Syphon Filter game for PS-1. Was OK for it's time, but, this is 10 years later!

Is it a fun game to play? Yes.....And I'm not bashing the game, but, when you have extremely "true to life" looking games like SOCOM, anything else is just an "OK" game....Nothing groundbreaking, nothing too fancy...etc

The PROS:

You can be any member in your squad, at any given moment!

Decent weaponry

Decent environments

Realistic "health" (take 1-2 shots and you're out of commission)

Replay value is kinda fun

Every member's stats can increase with each level

The CONS:

Very difficult controls

VERY LAME headset/voice command system

Fairly "cheesy" graphics for a game in 2004

Poor movement per character

Characters say the SAME exact 2 phrases over & over again!

Anyway, here's my conclusion:

It's really a decent game for the $20.00, it's WORTH the $20.00, it has good replay value, and it has it's moments... But please don't pay anything more than the advertised price of $20.00! It's definetely worth it! If you want a DARN GOOD Military game, save up another $20.00 and get SOCOM! It's 10x's better, in graphics, gameplay, controlability, and voice commands! My opinion, SOCOM I and SOCOM II are simply the 2 BEST military games out there on ANY game-console system!

title: Unleash your destructive desires
text:
Not since Grand Theft Auto as a player been able to unleash Hell on a town's citizens(here's hoping they're not sociopaths). For once, in Destroy All Humans, you play the usually-villain-role of martians, attacking Earth for once instead of some far off fictional world. There's moments where you think the game could've gone farther but does it ever get fun.

Story: The Furon race is starting to dwindle down thanks to the lack of genetalia. Not to mention the nuclear war they fought with the Martians. You play Crypto 137, the 137th clone of the original Crypto. Your goal is to go to Earth and extract human brains which happen to have Furon DNA in them. He also finds out what happened to Crypto 136 and a branch of the military called the Majestic.

Graphics: It's pretty funny that a lot of games lately always look "GTA-esque" but with this game, it's pretty hard not to think of it. The graphics have a more polished look than GTA and destroying buildings actually looks like destroying buildings.

Sound/Music: As that 1950's B-movie feel with saucer sounds having that weird whistling sound, your zap sounds for your guns and some great voice acting, including a Jack Nicholson-like main hero Crypto. The music understandably has that 50's soundtrack feel to it as well.

Gameplay: Your character's actions are separated into 2 camps: Psychokineses and your weapons. Your PK as it's called has 4 options: grab people, cows, and later on tanks and either send them into the air, crash them into the ground or give it a "push" and send them flying, even into other cars. Scan is where you replenish your PK and read their minds. Extract is where you use your mental powers to "explode" the people's head scanner's style(not as gory though) and collect their DNA. And Hypno is when you want to create a Distraction, send them to Sleep or other special actions for certain people like opening gates or starting a truck.

Your weapons for your on-foot missions are your Zap-o-Matic, an electricity shooting gun, your fan favorite Anal Probe where a powered up one will instantly kill a civilian, more for others and collect their DNA your Disintegration Ray which completely burns your victim but lose DNA and your which acts like a grenade. Your spaceship also has 4: a Death Ray, working like a heat laser, an Abduction Ray where you can grab people and vehicles and swing them around, a Sonic Boom acting like a bomb and your Disruptor which makes a very bigger boom.

The missions are basic "follow that guy/destroy those/get here in time" fare although there's some mini-games like destroying the town in a certain time, burning cows or going through checkpoints. Your weapons can be upgraded so you can shoot more people, more damage or more ammo.

For once we're allowed to destroy anything(besides trees oddly) and then go back to our normal lives and hopefully not be deviants. Politicians might go after the game but go ahead and get it and start annihilating some human ass.

title: The Last Remnant Xbox 360 Version
text:
A very decent and worthwhile game from Square Enix, in my opinion, The Last Remnant far surpassed my expectations on the Xbox 360, which I have to say, were extremely low after reading online reviews.

I had no hard drive to load the game on, so I feared even being able to get the game to boot after all the dramatized postings I read about lag and freezing. Truth is, the game never caught on me for more than a single second, perhaps two tops, and these were only on the occasional battle. Even when linking long scale multiple battles, which is actually not something that is recommended for game mechanic reasons, the technical faults of this game are nothing that should shy an RPG fan, or any kind of gamer period, away from this title. I realize the 360 is among the newest tier of gaming machines out there today, but the criticism that this has received in my eyes is completely unfounded. Technology isn't perfect, and shouldn't be expected to be.

The story was a little thin at points, but kept up with itself in most ways and is nicely expanded by the recruit able characters. Which is also what makes the 360 version of this game so annoying, the limit to the amount of "Leader" characters, or the unique interesting ones as I call them, that can be used at any one time meaning you must either juggle characters, increasing the number of characters you have to level, or find a few you like and stick with them, which is what I chose to do. Afterwards though it made replaying the game that much better after my first play. The battle system, once you experiment a little, is actually very intuitive and refreshing. One of the most unique I can ever remember. But I stress that is ONLY when you have properly balanced teams. Perhaps I just got lucky with my natural choices, but I rarely had any problems getting good random commands to pop up for me like I've seen many others complain of. The game takes getting use to, but if your a good enough gamer, The Last Remnant can be one hell of a refreshing RPG compared to many released in the past decade.

title: Generation Y and the JRPG term
text:
Yes,I pretty much agree with what all the other reviewers have already said about this game. It's very cool and alot of fun is to be had with this title...

HOWEVER

There is one thing that really irks me with casual RPG players AKA generation Y and today's generation of gamers. An RPG is,was and forever shall be turned based... that's how RPGs started and what has become the game today that you so love. For different reasons 1.) the youth is plauged with ADHD and can only have their attention held long enough with lots of eye candy and ACTION ACTION ACTION!! and 2.) In America we have a pride to think that we can always do something better than any other country--- thus the "western RPG" was born,which is in fact nothing more than an action/shooter with a few mild RPG elements thrown in (leveling up,customization) Fallout and Borderlands do not constitute as an RPG.

Also for those younger gamers who did not grow up with the 8-bit nintendo and whine about how much they would like "JRPGS" if you didn't have to keep fighting random battles; would you PLEASE take a moment to hear what you sound like? You're pretty much on the same page as saying "I would really like the Madden games if you didn't have to pass the football so much." You are talking about a CORE element of the game. Obviously you DON'T like RPGS, so play one of the MANY other genres out there to suit your taste; action,shooter,platform,sports etc. Rather than forcing all the fans of real TURN BASED RPGS watch their favorite genre die off; at least allow for the so-called "JRPG" genre to exist as well as the "Western RPG." Variety is the spice of life you know.

Today we live in sad times where some truely amazing RPGs only get released on small,crappy hand held systmes IF they get released here at all. What I wouldn't give to have the entire Dragon Quest series available on PS3,360 or even the Wii (so long as motion gaming was not implemented) Or how about remakes of Mother 1,2 and 3? Or at least a Nintendo DSi player on the Wii so as to enjoy all these "unpopular JRPGs" on an HD big screen TV? Anyone? Anyone??

title: Outstanding Wireless Mouse - Great Battery Life
text:
Logitech has consistently been making excellent gaming peripherals, and the G703 is no exception.

With tracking up to 16,000 dpi, twitch gamers will be able to happily fly across a MOBA screen or spin in mid-air to get that important crit shot. I prefer RPB's, so I'm happy with a slower 1600 dpi, which also works great for pixel-by-pixel photo editing.

For me, the ergonomics are virtually perfect. The back button is exactly where I want it to be, without having to shift my thumb back to hit it. This is the only mice I own where that is true. In fact, the G703 fits me better than any of the other (countless) mice on my desk, including my Razer Mamba.

Build quality is generally solid, albeit lightweight. Without the included weight, the mouse is feather-light. With it, I found the heft to be just right. Be careful not to accidentally throw the weight out when you unbox the mouse. Buttons are ample in size, responsive, and give a solid, springy click. The mouse wheel has the right amount of resistance, and doesn't feel awkward when used as a third mouse button.

The older Logitech Gaming software will not work with the G703. I had to uninstall it and update to the new G HUB. On the plus side, the interface is extremely intuitive and user-friendly. Unfortunately, it doesn't support my favorite mouse shortcut (holding down button six and sliding the mouse up or down to raise or lower the volume, respectively). Beyond that, however, it was a pleasure to use.

While all of these features are great, the best thing about the G703 is its battery life. A full charge has held up to several days of heavy use. This is most likely because the lighting is much more understated than most gaming mice, but I rarely see the lighting anyway, since it's under my hand. Battery performance FAR outshines my Mamba. In addition, the including charging cable is not proprietary. You can connect any micro-USB cable to recharge or use it as a corded mouse.

title: Durable with great software
text:
These used to be made in the US. Now they're made in Mexico. This is upsetting, even more so in that the "made in USA" imprint on the bottom is covered up by a "assembled in Mexico" sticker.

But anyway, enough of that. I love this throttle and its cousin, the Pro Throttle. It's got half a million buttons on it and is comfortable, apparently modeled after an F16's control stick. It is certainly not the most sexy looking HOTAS setup out there, but it surely is one of the most durable. Nothing feels cheap on these, the buttons feel solid and the plastic is durable. I've had mine for about 2 years now, playing Star Citizen, Elite Dangerous, and War Thunder (all of them poorly).

The downsides are: the throttle slider on the Fighterstick is pretty basic and its easy to bump the trim of the analog stick out of whack. Unlike other similarly priced competitors (X52), there is no Z-axis twist of the stick that can work as improvised rudder pedals.

So it's ugly and simple, why is it 100 or so bucks?
Because the software is amazing, and it's built to last.

The software allows you to take multiple CH products and tie them together, or to add programming for special functions. One of the simple examples I do, is make it do that in 'mode 1', which is toggled by a button on the throttle, the throttle's analog stick is a makeshift rudder, providing yaw. In 'mode 2', the same analog stick provides up/down/left/right thrusters. The game thinks there are 4 analog axes involved, one (X) used for yaw and 2 (X/Y) used for thrust, but it doesn't know that all three are the same analog thumbstick. The sky's the limit when it comes to the fancy scripting/mapping, and there's a huge community online dedicated to this setup. You can use a special button on the throttle like a "shift" key to enable secondary functions to all your existing buttons and hats, giving you double the functionality as before. It's pretty cool!

title: If you have a Wii U, you should probably have this game.
text:
So much better than Brawl, and very reminiscent of Melee. It's a fantastic game that had my thumb hurting after I spent an entire weekend doing nothing but playing.

The normal game case comes in the box, along with a refreshed Gamecube controller with an extended cable, and an adapter that converts 2 of your Wii U's USB slots to 4 Gamecube controller ports. Buying these parts at retail price would cost 110, rather than 100.

The game manual says you can use 2 gamecube adapters (using all 4 USB ports) for 8 Gamecube controllers for the new 8-person Smash gamemode. You can, alternatively, use Wiimotes alone, Wiimotes with a Nunchuck, Wiimotes with a Classic/Pro Controller, the Wii U Pro Controller, the Wii U Gamepad, or a 3DS (if you have the SSMB for 3DS cartridge in). 8 person smash is amazing, but you can only use certain large maps. There are a good amount, but not as many as I'd like. (Not that I'll be needing 8 person smash all the time). The picture I uploaded should demonstrate. I set up an 8-person Smash with 2 new Gamecube controllers, an original Gamecube controller, 2 Wiimotes + Nunchucks, the Wii U GamePad, a 3DS and a Wii U Pro Controller.

There is a ton of content, and plenty of gamemodes to explore and play with. I didn't even play online my first weekend with the game, surprisingly. My only disappointment with the content is that there are very few characters (in comparison to Melee) to unlock. Many characters are available right out of the box, which takes away some of the fun, in my opinion. But in any case, they made up for it with other unlockables, be it trophies, equipment, or music tracks.

I was wondering if I was making a good purchase because I had gotten Smash Bros for the 3DS and I hadn't played it that much, to be honest. But the Wii U... well, I've already put in enough hours to make my investment worth it. This game is absolutely fantastic.

title: It's a GameCube controller with a gloriously long cable
text:
It's a GameCube controller with a gloriously long cable. It works great, I got a second one along with the bundle pack. I thought they were going to be the same, but it's so nice having a fresh controller after using my poor old abused ones.

The original cable seems to be about 2 meters long, where this one is about 3 meters long (6.5 to 10 feet). It feels durable, as it should, and works fantastically. I want to buy more, when they get in stock. Don't pay more than the Nintendo-set price of $30 like someone else said.

Also, you can use 8 of these in Smash Bros for Wii U. You'll need 2 adapters, but the manual does say it works with 2 sets of adapters plugged in and 8 controllers. Though, with 8 people you may want to bring some Wavebirds or extensions. Even with the far superior longer cable, I can imagine it'd still be crowded.

title: Good idea, missing an ending
text:
As others have noted, this game has some good graphics and some interesting ideas in the beginning of the game -- neat weapons, hypnotized cows doing the chicken dance, etc. The first half of this game is great, as you get new weapons and new skills.

But the last half of this game is just tedious. No new weapons and the upgrades your leader does give you usually come just after they'd be useful to complete yet another mission. The missions get longer, and if you fail one, you have to sit through the whole mission setup again, flying down from the mothership, landing on the planet, listening to the leader ramble on about your objectives AGAIN, etc. Then you have to do the whole mission up to where you died and try again. This would not be so bad except that the game tends to create objects, including bad guy characters, out of nothing just a few feet away (turn back and they start firing on you). Or turn your back on the character you're following, and when you turn back again he may be halfway across the map -- and your mission declared a failure by the leader! Having to follow motorcades is just boring and there is no way to speed them up.

Many times I'd have a mission declared a failure and no reason given as to why, even though I was following all the objectives. The weapon upgrades earned by completing the later missions (no other way to get the upgrades) are not even that great in most cases.

My suggestion: play the first half of the game to get the most enjoyment from it, then move on to the next game. The ending is nothing unexpected and not worth the effort.

title: Comfort precision with PowerPlay cordless!
text:
Logitech’s G703 Lightspeed thankfully comes in a modest box, compared to some of their other top end devices, saving on stuff that gets disposed. You get the mouse, wireless unified USB receiver, a 6 foot USB Micro soft, flexible, braided cord, a USB adapter to turn the cord into a wireless extension, a 10g weight insert, a sticker and some light warranty and first setup papers.

Make no doubt about the G703 Lightspeed: it’s not for lefties, but it feels very light and comfortable in the right hand. The two thumb buttons are generously sized and easy to find. Its hump is slightly more centered then some others, so you may want to consider a more fingertip touch grip or defaulting your thumb closer to the back (left side) button and do a reach for your forward. A back-end claw if you will. The sides are rubber and afford an easy to move grip without getting slick. The scroll wheel also has a very subtle rubber feel that isn’t ‘clicky’ at all.

Having recently swapped from a G900 to a G903 with PowerPlay pad, I was excited to see a new mouse supporting cordless charging. My typical productivity DPI setting is around 4k. I use 8k or higher DPI when sniping (zooming etc.). For me, 16k was just too much precision! And I never need the cord, with the PowerPlay pad I’m in heaven.

This unit does require a new software app, “G Hub”, the directions point you to logitechg.com. Where the Logitech apps do very well with multiple devices connected to the same rig, I only had one disc to charge so I installed that into the G703. In G Hub go to the PowerPlay pad, under the menu you’ll find a ‘disconnect’ option. Immediately power off your original mouse. The pad goes into pair mode. You then power on your G703 and you’ll sync up quickly without having to use the USB receiver or cord.

G Hub gets a macro overhaul and I’ve shared a screen cap of some of the features. I quickly set my DPI settings then reassigned the DPI button (just behind the scroll wheel) with a macro. You can also set profiles up and auto detect games or apps to have different configurations. Quick tip: to avoid some of the app mgmt. features and just build a one to fit them all use the little lock icon for macros, DPI and lighting effects. I’ll play with the new macro and config options more and may add a comment and/or respond to questions you may have below.

Overall a fabulous addition to the cordless charging line up, a proven 16k DPI sensor and a very comfortable feel. I prefer a few more programmable buttons but many prefer a cleaner button experience and if so, this one is the mouse to beat.

title: An unusually small gaming mouse with sensitive short-throw buttons
text:
The Logitech G PRO Hero Gaming Mouse is not typical of gaming mice I've used in the past. It's small, smooth, and symmetrical (aside from the two left-side buttons), unlike the steelseries mice I'm most accustomed to, which are larger, textured, contoured, and distinctly asymmetrical. (The Hero could have been ambidextrous if only it had buttons on both sides.) Also, compared to other $50-plus mice, which often feel designed to advertise their poshness through the use of expensive-seeming materials, the Hero feels kinda cheap (without, it's important to say, feeling poorly made).

The top left and right buttons have low tension and a short throw, meaning that they're very easy to click both on purpose and by accident. Sensitive is good, or it can be good, but it takes some getting used to. When I first started using the mouse, I was frequently clicking by mistake because I'm used to resting my fingers more heavily on the buttons than this mouse will tolerate.

Furthermore, because the small size is a bit awkward for my XL hands, I had difficulties with normal non-gaming mousing; I kept torquing the mouse when pushing the left button, moving it off the menu (or whatever) I was trying to hit. Having grown more used to the mouse over time, the main difficulty I have with it is in a game like Diablo III, where there are often rapid flurries of left-clicking, clicks can seemingly get lost. I say "seemingly" because this is more likely a problem with my mechanics than with the mouse's electronics, but nevertheless I find that what I thought I heard as a click did not register.

Another issue I have with the design of the mouse is the placement of the left-side buttons. They're just below the top surface of the mouse with the forward button positioned just ahead of the back edge of the left top button, and the rear button just behind the back edge of the left top button. The front button is easy for me to reach with my thumb, but the rear button requires me to arch my thumb up and back, which is awkward. This might have been made less awkward by using buttons that were wider vertically, but the buttons are quite thin. Again, this is not really an issue with the front button, especially since it sticks out so far from the body of the mouse, but it is a problem with the rear button.

One nice feature of the Hero is that it doesn't require the big software download that some people complain about in order to work. I haven't had any issues with plugging it into a random computer and getting it to function reasonably. This is a contrast to the steelseries mice I mentioned above, which don't always play well with plug-and-play and have unusual configuration software. That said, the Logitech configuration software is also a bit odd and a bit baroque. It offers a lot of options for polling, scrolling, button functions, and mouse lighting. I was surprised to see it allows the DPI button behind the scroll wheel to select from up to 5 different DPI settings. It's hard for me to imagine needing the mouse to have that many different DPI settings (I chose 4).

Bottom line: What I like about this mouse is its sensitivity. What I don't like about it is the small size, the smooth and non-contoured feel, and some button-related issues, including the hard-to-reach left-rear button and possible missed clicks. This could be a great mouse for someone with small to average hand size who doesn't naturally rest too much weight on their fingertips. For me, it's just OK.

title: In-depth RPG, some controls are wonky though
text:
I like this game. The story is intriguing, the characters are cool, there are PLENTY of NPCs you can talk to - and TRADE with. There are collectibles to find, monsters to hunt, unique miniboss monsters to slay, and a whole world to explore. It's fun. But it does have some problems.

The camera controls STINK. You need to hold C and use the D-pad to move the camera around, it never auto-centers behind your character unless you flick the C button quickly. The graphics are equivalent to PlayStation 2 (think Final Fantasy VIII and you've got a good idea of what it looks like) so during fights it's pretty hard to see if you're facing an enemy's face, side, or back - and this positioning is a MAJOR component of your battle since certain skills only work from certain directions. The way the camera works makes me nauseous. AND I NEVER GET MOTION-SICKNESS.

The game's main map doesn't actually show you anything other than terrain and place names. The minimap shows you enemies as red dots, quests as "!" marks, but only if you get REALLY CLOSE to the target. There is NO WAY to resize the minimap either, and it is TINY - almost hidden - in the top corner of the screen. It shows the terrain for maybe 100 yards around your position, but points of interest will not be indicated until you're within 20 yards or so.

Because the map is kind of garbage, and the camera is so wonky, it can be MORE DIFFICULT THAN IT SHOULD BE to find items and characters in this game. If they're standing at the corner of a wall, or behind a crate, YOU WILL NOT SEE THEM half the time even after moving the camera in that general direction.

So yeah... it's an interesting game, but the useless map and the janky camera make it VERY annoying when you're trying to complete side quests or trying to determine which direction your enemy target is facing. I'm still planning to play it... but if you want a VERY SIMILAR game with BETTER MAP AND CONTROLS, get yourself a Wii-U and play "Xenoblade Chronicles X" instead of this one.

title: The most worthwhile title for the Wii ever!
text: Xenoblade Chronicles is a must have for anyone who's played classic RPGs on previous Nintendo consoles or is a fan of a solid, never let you down, RPG. It's a typical J-RPG where the protagonist youth sets out to stop some evil force out to destroy the world. But it's lengthy and ever moving story that keeps you wanting to play more with pleanty of plot twists and turns. I best described it to a friend of mine where it was like Xenogears meets a MMO like World of Warcraft. The reason I say that is that there are a TON of side quest to do. And while not necessary to complete or even divert from the main storyline, it's still fun and rewarding way to expand on the game's challenges. Especially when it comes to defeating a unique monster. Those pose the biggest threat and challenge since the battle can quickly turn against you. The mini-quests that are littered through the game rewards some decent gear, exp, and money. Most are easy to do and are in the areas in which you will be exploring to complete the storyline. Some will have you hunting around for a while since there is a day-night cycle and certain enemies and NPCs are only out during certain parts of the day. There's also a social building aspect of the game where you build relationships with towns you visit, relationships between main characters, and tying NPCs together in a social network system much like Xenosaga 2 (Ex. Boy A seeks Girl B. Hook them up and get rewarded). The game does a great job at explaining how to do things with a brief tutorial, that you can find more information on once you go through the tutorial in the menu. The graphics is quite limited by Ninteno's hardware. That's a shame too. I would have loved more detailed character models since the design is well done and the equipment you find and wear will change the appearance of your played characters. The enviorment is INSANE! When you get past the starting area and begin roaming around, you really do appreciate the scope and detail put into creating the world this is the Bionis. It's just so great to have free-range landscapes instead of the linear paths that the other RPGs have been feeding us lately. I love the music! The music is catchy and is totally memorable!! I find myself humming the main theme and the boss battle themes while I'm not playing. ;) I have done about 30hrs so far and have only dipped into the 3rd area of the game because I have been attempting to complete all the quests I keep coming across. It's very engrossing when you start trying to remember where it was you saw an enemy that now needs to be harvested so you can get that one quest done. Ahh! But it's the entire package that keeps players glued to their Wii. Especially since there hasn't been an RPG come out for the Wii since... Paper Mario? Yeah, so this one deserves a buy. Definetly if you love Monolith Studios like I do. Definetly if you're tired of linear worlds like FFXIII. Definetly if you want to get lost in an awesome story! Get this game!

title: Impulse buy, but no regrets.
text:
I purchased these headsets yesterday at a Best Buy for $59.99 plus tax which was retail price and cheaper than the prices I saw on Amazon currently. Other retailers also carry them but I wanted them now since I just got Battlefield: Bad Company 2 on Tuesday and had been wanting something to use for late night gaming.

Why was this an impulse buy? Well, because the "new and improved" Turtle Beach X11's come out on 3/15/2010 but I couldn't wait until then and from what I read, there was very little improvement on an already solid product. The headset is very comfortable and fits snug so it won't fall off your head if you bend down. The inline amp makes everything plenty loud and chat is audible even with game sounds on xbox live. They are powered by USB which is great especially if you don't have an extra spot for a wall wart but also this means that they cannot be used as stand alone headphones. Mic is a huge improvement on the standard headsets and the boom easily moves out of the way when not in use. The amp controls are accesible to make quick changes if needed and can easily be unplugged for PC use if you use them to switch back and forth from xbox to pc like I do. The sound quality on these headphone are good but not great. A little plasticy but still sturdy. The 40mm drivers really help get all the low end rumble in the game soundtrack but they do have a boost in the low mid bass frequencies. If these are used soley for gaming, then you probably won't notice but listen to music through these and you'll see what I'm talking about. My remedy was just to use a little eq'ing and they sound awesome now though my PC. Cables are fine for me despite what a lot of reviewers state. I don't have problems with the wires getting tangled and appreciate the long cable so that your not stuck sitting close to your TV when your couch or chair is probably at least 8 feet from your TV.

My final thoughts are "GET THESE" A friend of mine has the Tritton AX pro and they sound good but he also paid 2/3 more than I did and these sound better for music than his cans. To me, surround headphones are still a gimmick as the only way to get true surround is with a good home theater setup and good sound imaging and most gaming headsets only do an ok job and to me not worth there price tag. Most people would be thrilled regardless because headphones give you the perfect stereo image off the bat and games sound way better than using your TV speakers or your home theater that may be in a less than ideal spot and have to compromise stereo imaging because of your furniture, etc. You will be able to hear the footsteps and nuances of the game.

If you can't find them anymore then go for the newer X11's and you'll be happy you did. If you want to spend the extra money to go wireless, be sure rechargeble batteries are in your future but for a gamer on a budget or just someone that wants the best bang for the buck like me, get these.

title: Another Review by Another Gamer
text:
The G Pro is a small form factor ambidextrous mouse for people who have small hands, fingertip grip, or claw grip. It's a high performance mouse made for the competitive niche who desire a simplistic mouse with high quality components/sensor. Does this mouse deliver? Yes, yes it does. Is the shape of the mouse for everyone? No, no it is not. If you have large hands and prefer a palm grip or hybrid palm/claw grip then you may not find full comfort in this mouse. You can still use it of course by slightly changing up your grip style but it may not feel like an 'end-game' shape for you.

Onto my personal opinion on multiple areas of the mouse.

Sensor:
You don't even need to write about 3366 anymore, it's about as perfect as you can imagine a sensor being. I believe it's about 2ms of smoothing across the whole mouse (which is not noticeable). No acceleration, prediction, or whatever. The thing tracks where you aim it end of story.

Mouse skates:
2x1x2 design. Which is two skates on the top/bottom and one skate around the sensor. This time around Logitech used rounded mouse feet which tend to offer a better glide feeling: more in-control is how I'd describe it. The mouse feet do make an audible noise on my mouse pad but it has no problems with glide. There is no grab or tug.

Cable:
It's a durable braided cable. A braided cable this thick means it's very unlikely the cable will break during normal usage. The downside of a cable this thick is it is heavy and will create some drag when moving across your mouse pad. It is highly recommended to use a mouse bungee solution with this kind of cable to negate the drag as much as possible. I personally recommend the Zowie Camade as one of the better mouse bungees: if the mouse bungee is too expensive for your taste then the cheapest solution is scotch tape which does just as good as a job but requires some semiannual maintenance to keep the wire down.

LMB/RMB:
Hair-trigger and low delay main mouse buttons. These are by far the easiest mouse buttons I've ever used for clicking in rapid succession. I find it rare that you would ever need to click this fast but just to explain how fast you can make a single fire weapon with no fire limit basically be automatic if you can click fast enough. These are very sensitive clicks so if you aren't a veteran gamer you may find yourself accidentally clicking them, this can be easily learned so after some usage you should begin to develop some self control and stop accidental clicks. I personally have zero accidental click issues but I've been gaming longer than most and wouldn't consider myself a beginner in the gaming mice market. Some owners have claimed different audible noises between the two clicks or different feeling: it could be very possible they received a defect but I think a lot of it is simply in their head or they care too much for minuscule details if it works it works so I recommend you don't worry too much about it.

Scroll Wheel/M3:
Tactile scroll wheel requires force to move up/down. This is very nice for using it as a jump action in games you play. The mouse 3 button (scroll wheel click inward) is a bit tough but not that bad. I do not recommend using it as an in-game key and rather just use it for general purpose like opening new tabs in a web browser and so fourth. There isn't much to write about here the scroll wheel works like a scroll wheel works.

Side buttons:
Small and to the point. It's your basic M4/M5 button except they are fairly tiny which is necessary for the size of the mouse. They aren't my favorite side buttons but I have no complaints because they do what they do.

Mouse coating/material:
I don't know what material is used or if there's any coating. The mouse feels like a high quality plastic which I assume to be ABS and can feel slippery at times. When you use the mouse for a decent period of time and your fingers begin to heat up or get sweaty then the mouse becomes quite grippy. I don't have any real complaints about coating because once I'm playing I stop noticing I'm using the mouse which is a good thing.

Weight:
83-84g ignoring the cable. Super light and weight distribution feels perfectly even across the whole mouse. You may not experience even weight distribution in some mice because of the shapes especially in larger mice.

Shape:
Purely subjective to the user. I find the shape to be pretty comfortable for an extremely small mouse. I have about 18.5-19.5 cm hands and can use a full claw grip, palm grip, and hybrid palm/claw grip. I find the mouse more comfortable than a g303 but less comfortable than say a zowie EC. My hands are pretty big and I can use multiple grips so that should be a good sign for people with fairly large hands that you can use this mouse if you grip it properly. Gamers with smaller hands should feel right at home with this bad boy. Overall this mouse is better all around versus Logitech's G303 in my opinion so those looking to swap over should feel right at home.. and if not there's always the nice return policies for refunds on Amazon and Logitech's website.

Final Opinion/Rating:
I think this is one of the best gaming mice that has ever been made to date. It's all around a performance beast and I'm putting up consistent amazing results in every online FPS I play. I am a very experience player so I already have strong muscle memory for aim and this mouse just put it to work. Logitech did an outstanding job and sure you can find some tiny things you'd like to be changed but in the end of the day it is one of the best small form factor gaming mice on the market and probably will be for a very long time to come.

Final Score: 9.5/10
Mousepad tested with: Zowie G-SR (Black Stitched Edge Edition)

Notes:
Final score is ignoring the shape, I do not add shape into my rating because that is my own personal preference. I rate strictly on the mouse itself. The shape is not the best shape for me so I will also be looking at the larger Logitech G403 which is a larger ergonomic mouse with similar internals. If that mouse doesn't amaze me immediately then G Pro will be my main driver for a long time.

I also tested this mouse on a Glorious XL heavy and a QCK heavy. After testing all three mousepads I determined this mouse glides the 'fastest/smoothest' with the QCK heavy. So if you want a very frictionless feeling glide then pair it with your QCK heavy. If you want a controlled glide with some feedback pair it with an Artisan Hayate.

title: I've found it- the perfect, lightweight, ambidextrous claw-grip mouse.
text:
I have been hunting for the perfect gaming mouse for YEARS- I've been through the top mice from SteelSeries, Corsair, etc. and none of them really fit the bill. The closest I came for a while was the SteelSeries Sensei RAW- I liked it's symmetrical design and pure white LEDs, and the software seemed to work well enough. After going through three of them over the course of 2 years, though, I figured I might have better luck with a different product. I had previously stayed away from Logitech's G series of products for two reasons: when I was originally looking at them a few years ago, they had this over-the-top and tacky gamer aesthetic that seems to be so inexplicably popular. I also had had bad luck with a few logitech wireless mice previously- they seemed to have much worse wireless latency than competitors that I had used. These two factors had caused me to write off Logitech for quite a while. When searching for a reasonably good looking and suitable replacement for the Sensei RAW that wouldn't break the bank, I came across the G Pro.

This is, honestly, the end-game mouse for people that like an ambidextrous claw-grip mouse- and it looks the part, too. Tracking is incredibly accurate, the switches provide a really light click (my preference, since I don't rest my fingers on the buttons), and the 3 programmable buttons (2 on the side, one that's a DPI switch by default on the top) feel nice and easy to reach.

The software is what sets this mouse apart, though. Aside from incredibly simple to use macro functions and on-board memory which are useful for me as I switch between my MacBook and gaming desktop quite often, the software is laid out very well and lighting control easily allowed me to set to my preference- a pure, muted, understated white. Many people reading this might not understand why that's a big deal, but most mice that have RGB lighting can't get very close to a pure white color- it always ends up looking very pink or blue and doesn't go with any other white backlights in your setup (my keyboard, for example.) The G Pro is able to achieve a very clean, icy white color.

The braided cable is a nice touch, and doesn't seem to add much of a feeling of weight to this already very light mouse. That's really the summary of my thoughts on this thing- I can't guarantee that this will be the right mouse for everyone, but it is the right mouse for me. If you like a heavy mouse with a palm grip, or a million programmable buttons for RPG games, or lights everywhere they could possibly be, look elsewhere. If you want a well built product that can legitimately game, but without the "aesthetic" that so often comes along with it, this is a great buy.

title: Good GBA alternative, but not perfect
text:
If you're looking for an all in one solution for playing GBA games, including real carts and ROMs, this is a decent option. It feels study and comfortable to play. Rechargable battery is nice. Built-in TV out is nice.

The biggest problem is the screen. It's not the right aspect ratio, so you either deal with some scaling and blur, or pixel perfect with a lot of border.

If you're like me and are buying this for its additional GB/GBC/NES/SMS/GG ROM support, don't. It's not native support, it's just using emulators built for the GBA. On a real GBA that's a fun, nice option, but on this, the screen issues become even more exaggerated. Even though the native screen resolution is big enough for all of these systems, instead you get the original game clipped/mushed to the GBA limitations, then stretched out and blurry. You'll spend lots of time just cycling through resolutions and graphical options for each game to end up with something satisfactory, and the next game will require something different.

Not to mention all of the different ways the emulator menus work, on top of the revo menus, you have to remember a lot of different button combos just to navigate in and out of games.

title: This is a fantastic mouse with great performance and build quality in an understated/professional style.
text:
This is a very high-performance mouse in a very understated design. A lot of high-end mice go the direction of having a very aggressive style, with ridges and different surface treatments with various textures or colors, or completely off the wall Iron Man-like adjustable panels like the R.A.T. series.

This mouse doesn't stand out like most do, except for the customizable LED, it's a very simple looking mouse. It doesn't cry for attention or look out of place on my desk at work. It is overall fairly light, but has a sturdy build quality. There's no flexing of the body anywhere, the mouse clicks feel and sound great, with a really predictable click force, which is just enough to prevent accidental clicks if my finger twitches. The cord is one of the best I've ever experienced in a mouse, it's sleeved and comes nice and relaxed out of the box. It looks, feels, and performs like a premium USB cable should.

The software allows for very simple tuning of the lighting options, as well as easy remapping of the buttons (for example, I rarely use the back and forward keys, and switched them to copy and paste in just a few clicks, functions I use way more often at work). You can also customize up to 5 DPI/sensitivity settings to toggle through with the button behind the mouse wheel.

title: So well executed; just transparent with use
text: This just disappears in use; no cord hang ups, no wireless lag; everything just works.  Setup was dirt simple, just plug and play, (download the Logitech software for additional functionality like RGB control).  It won't look any sexier on your mousepad, and it won't impress your friends.  What it will do, though, is make every day use and gaming absolutely pleasurable.  If you were frustrated with the tailed demons, but didn't want to sacrifice the control, this won't let you down.  Add in the powerplay and don't even worry about the charge.  You can absolutely get by for a significantly less price point, but this just does everything right.  Sometimes simplicity is the answer.

title: Top sensor, great button feel, all around quality.
text:
This mouse feels just about as close to perfect as I've found. It is incredibly simple, and with the exception of the thumb forward/backward buttons, it makes the controls transparent; it's so good you almost forget about it in use.

It feels great in use, the sensor, (3366) is absolutely tops; I haven't found anything that tracks better. The button clicks are so good you almost wouldn't feel right clicking it in public, though the thumb forward/backward buttons are too far forward for my grip. For reference, the G900 buttons fit my grip perfectly; with the G-Pro my thumb is solidly on the back button, not mid-way in between. This is really my only quibble with the mouse.

The braided nylon cord is a nice touch for durability, and I have not found its stiffness to be a bother. Also, the RGB lighting/Logitech software both work very well.

Just looking at it, you'd wonder how in the heck it's a $70 mouse, but using is believing.

At this price point, Logitech offers several 'gaming' mice, my recommendation is to check them out and see which one feels right, (assuming you've got a store nearby that stocks them). The specs and operation at the $60-$80 range are not too off, but there are some with customizable weights like the G502, or with a slightly different shape like the G403, so go with the one that fits your hand/grip the best.
