There are two further illustrations, one on each page of the story (yes, it has only 3 pages) and they are equally wonderful although this one has a teeny bit more ... elegance? 
 The story itself is about a princess that doesn't speak. After numerous teachers have tried everything they could think of, she therefore gets put in a room with a man-eating tiger. But, typical Gaiman, nothing is as it first appears. 
 There might be only 3 pages but the story is full of wit and again the author was able to enthrall me. I was really there in Cinnamon's hot country, saw all the wonderful but ultimately pointless things she was surrounded by and could almost feel the tiger's pelt too!

First, I'll admit that I never read The Secret Garden when I was younger. I knew the plot and while The Humming Room is strikingly similar, I can tell that it has its slight differences. Roo is a curious girl who would rather hide in small spaces than be alone in a large empty room. She is, after all, very small for her age, to the point where she looks about 4 years younger. She's normally very quiet, only talking when she has to, and she prefers listening to everything that most people wouldn't pay much attention to. You may not believe it, but hiding from the rest of the world can have a slight upside. 
 I quite liked Roo's quirkiness and adventurous nature. She seemed fearless of most things, even when I felt a little uneasy at the time she first hears the humming behind the walls. Overall, the story was very heavy from the murder of her parents to being brought to live in a building on an island that was once used to isolate children with tuberculosis. While living there she uncovers some secrets she would have never imagined. 
 That being said, the story isn't all that depressing and eerie. The ending came a little too soon for me, but seeing that Roo accomplished the goal she set, it left you on a happy note. The author's writing is beautiful and I felt that it complimented this type of story incredibly well. Everything blossomed in this story and it's one I recommend to anyone who loves a little darkness and adventure.

This is the fourth in the series of original (1930) Nancy Drew books. This book includes four nicely-scanned full-page grayscale images and "The Nancy I Knew", an introduction by Mildred Wirt Benson, who wrote this book (to an outline provided by the publisher) under the Carolyn Keene pseudonym. 
 The introduction is in some ways the best part of this book; Benson notes that the first three books sold well, but when original publisher Edward Stratemeyer died, his inexperienced daughters took over: "Overnight, Nancy become more of a home-type person, in early chapters focusing on household responsibilities." Also, "The syndicate's new owner asked that I make the sleuth less bold and that abrupt sentence endings be avoided. In editing, a simple 'Nancy said' became 'Nancy said sweetly,' 'she said kindly,' and the like, all designed to produce a less abrasive, more caring type of character." 
 I didn't like this as much as the earlier books, partly because I'm less interested in household management, partly because there's some transitional clumsiness. Benson notes a problem with the narration of Chapters Five and Six, but it didn't bother me, and I suspect I wouldn't have noticed it ;-). My biggest problem, though, is that there doesn't seem to be much of figuring out clues in this one; the solution is visible from a mile away, apart from small bits withheld from the reader.

It is very rarely that I ever read a novel more than once, as there are so many interesting books out there that I feel the need to devour as many new ones as I possibly can! Anne of Green Gables, however, is one of the few exceptions for me. This was not just my second time reading this novel, but my third! Ever since I first became acquainted with Anne and her wild imagination I've wanted to be transported to her world of Avonlea (and indeed I was during a trip to PEI when I was 11)! Anne of Green Gables is one of the most heartwarming and amusing books I have ever read, and it only seems to get better the more times I read it! 
 I think one of the main things that has always made Anne of Green Gables so loveable to me is L.M. Montgomery's slew of charming characters. Ever since I first read this novel when I was about 10 years old I have been madly in love with Gilbert Blythe! His competition with Anne in school, and his attempts to befriend her after their first disastrous meeting (which ended with a slate being broken over his head) never fails to make me sigh in adoration. Gilbert is not the only character to win over the hearts of readers, but also that of dear old Mr. Cuthbert. I don't think its possible for any reader to not love shy, sweet Matthew, and I never fail to shed tears at the end of the novel as if he were my own grandfather. The character of Marilla is also one of my absolute favourites, and I especially love the way in which Anne is able to transform the stiff older woman into a soft mother-like figure throughout the novel. From Mrs. Lynde's sharp tongue to Mrs. Allen's gentle heart, the inhabitants of Avonlea form a community that makes readers wish they belonged there as well. 
 I was very hesitant to review this book at all, because I find it extremely difficult to put into words how simply amazing this novel is. As a result, I think the only thing I can really say is that if you have not read Anne of Green Gables before then you must now! It is one of the few books that I think everyone should read before they die! Not only is the original novel incredible, but also the 1985 tv movie version of the story, which is one of the few adaptations that I think is as good as the book itself! The imagination and blunders of Anne have been charming readers since it was first published in 1908, and will certainly continue to do so for generations to come!

I received a copy of this book for free from the author in exchange for an honest review. 
 While I enjoyed the premise of the story, I was confused with the length and pacing of the book. It was very short (only six small chapters which could be read in about ten minutes) but a lot happened in that short span (including several years of Delilah's life). As a consequence, the book felt very rushed. The reader has very few clues about when or where the story takes place. We are given a quick background of Delilah's life and then a few scenes at the Fenchurch-Whittingtons before the timeline is pushed forward several years. It was more like reading the synopsis of a book than the book itself. 
 A. J. York has a wonderfully cute and quirky idea here, and you can tell she knows a lot about her characters. But I feel like there could be a huge improvement by expanding this short story into a novel where the ideas could be better developed, the timeline spread out more smoothly, and the readers could be shown the characters' personalities instead of told. On the other hand, I feel like the story might do equally well cut down and reimagined as a picture book because I feel like the premise is very well suited to a fable-like fairytale for young children. 
 Overall, while the story was intruiging, I was left wanting much more than there was. The book is available for free through Kindle Unlimited, so if you have a young child you might consider it as a story to read-aloud.

I loved The Thickety! It had just enough dark, scary elements to keep me completely enthralled, and a perfect amount of fairytale elements to keep things balanced and age appropriate without taking away any of the dark feeling of the book. I loved Kara's character, and watching her struggle with her own values (empathy for all creatures, kindness, and protecting her family) versus the values of The Path (eradicating magic at all costs), as well as struggling with the pull of the book, made her a fascinating protagonist. 
 The magic was wonderful and creepy, and the characters were memorable. There are multiple antagonists, and I loved all of them. Sordyr, the chillingly terrible forest demon who is made of living branches and smells of decaying leaves. Grace, the beautiful daughter of the cult's leader, who has more darkness within her than anyone sees. And Kara must even fight herself as she begins to be taken over by the grimoire. 
 J.A. White uses my favorite style of writing, spare enough to not be distracting and to let the story shine on its own, but descriptive enough that I could feel and see and smell the story. It never felt overly complicated, or overly simple. The black and white silhouette illustrations by Andrea Offerman are also beautiful and eerily haunting. There are so many more fantastic things that I'd love to rave about but I can't spoil anything! 
 I cannot honestly think of one thing I disliked about the book (although the cliffhanger was pretty devastating...in a good way). I'd been in a reading slump where I had to make myself return to most books, but I was finding myself reading The Thickety at every possible opportunity and thinking about it when I couldn't. This is definitely the best book I've read in its genre for a long time and I've already pre-ordered the next book in the series, The Whispering Trees, which is due out in March. 
 Review originally posted at bookyum.net.

I love Jason Segel. I happened to catch him on The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon on September 8th (the Family Feud bit was fantastic, in case you're wondering). And when I found out he was there to promote his new children's book, I about had an aneurysm. The book looked wonderful, so as soon as I saw it in Barnes and Noble, I knew I had to snatch it up. 
 In Nightmares!, Charlie Laird is not having a very good year. Everyone seems to be over the death of his mother, except him. His father just got remarried to a witch of a woman, so he had to move into her creepy purple mansion and leave the house he grew up in behind. His little brother is scared of him. And to top it all off, every time he goes to sleep, he has horribly vivid nightmares. They're not ordinary nightmares-Charlie has managed to open a portal to the Netherworld, where nightmares are real. And unless he can stop them, they're going to destroy his family and possibly the Waking World, as well. 
 Nightmares! was a very easy read, and the structure of the story was simple. It's definitely a children's book, and it's not as dark or creepy as I would have hoped. Still, it was very cute, original and enjoyable. The nightmares make great characters (we meet several interesting ones, such as Medusa's son) and Charlie's band of friends are all adorable. Although the depth was limited, I really liked what world-building there was and the way the nightmare realm was set up. The morals of this story were very strong (loyalty to friends and family, facing your fears, letting go after a loss) and at some points it felt a little cheesy, but keeping in mind that I am reading from the slightly jaded viewpoint of a 23-year-old, I still thought it was well-done and that it would be perfect for its intended age range. 
 Now, on to the part I am really excited to rave about: the illustrations. The story on it's own would probably have been only 3/5 stars for me, but the illustrations, the cover design and the endpapers are worth a whole star on their own. The cover is iridescent, with a pearly shimmer that shifts as you move the book, making the huge full moon appear to glow. The illustrations are very reminiscent of Tony DiTerlizzi's gorgeous illustrations in The Spiderwick Chronicles. Lots of flourishes, creepy crawlies, and gothic aspects. I loved them. 
 And, oh, the endpapers. I'm not even ashamed to admit that I waved them in the faces of several strangers in the bookstore because I just couldn't contain myself. I have tried to photograph them but I just cannot do them justice. BUGS! They are also shimmery like the cover, and just gorgeous. 
 The illustrator's name is Karl Kwasny, and he's done several other book covers but only one other book's interior illustrations that I can find, The Year of Shadows by Claire LeGrand. I've added it to my TBR without even having any idea what it's about, just because I can't wait to see more of Karl Kwasny's work. 
 Overall, I liked the book, and would recommend it to people who want a simple, cute, creative story, or want something to read to their children (I personally think this would be better for children in the 5-7 age range, but that's just my personal experience knowing I wanted more advanced material as a 10-year-old). It's also almost worth picking up for the design and pictures alone. However, if you're looking for something deep, dark or creepy, this might not be the book for you.

Here goes another attempt at a classic. I read this as part of my goal of reading as much classic literature as I can. The Jungle Book, as a story or an idea, has always been part of my life. I watched the Disney movie and fell in love with it as a child, and can honestly attribute it with my love for Jazz. I was also raised up watching the Japanese anime (Mowgli) dubbed in my native language. For me, Jungle Book was and still is the bomb! 
 Upon reading the book, my entire world and idea of The Jungle Book was thrown into haywire, and I was left confused as to why screenwriters changed the story so much in both the movie and cartoon adaptation. As an avid reader and also an avid movie goer, I always find it difficult to separate my liking of the book against my liking of its movie counterpart, and always hope both versions come as close as possible. 
 With my childhood memories in mind, I kept reading, and although I struggled immensely while characters I grew up loving and forming in my head were being decimated and completely re-woven into new characters I still enjoyed this new fresh (and obviously original) take on this lovely story. Nonetheless the main plot is somehow the same and I still loved the story although there were major differences between it and the many various mainstream adaptations. 
 I believe The Jungle Book is a great book for kids and a nice breeze of change for adults although Kipling does border a depressing tone a few times in the book, I did find that there are many important hidden messages throughout. You will definitely find yourself fond of most of the characters. No matter how I look at it though, it seems Kipling relays a subtle message of human moral decline. All in all, it was a good journey through the jungle, meeting a bunch of loony characters along the way.

 Gordon's drawing is rough around the edges, but each image still feels super tidy. Her magazine / greeting-card style of illustration is well-known in that sphere of publication, and she is totally in control of her skill. I wouldn't mind seeing more picture books drawn by her, and would like to see this same kind of sensitivity from her illustration bleed over into her construction of the story. Maybe she should find a partnership with a really great writer.
