The Tale of a No-Name Squirrel, aimed at middle grade readers, is a fun adventure, to be sure. It took me a few chapters to get into the world, but once I did, I enjoyed the myriad layers to the story. Our hero, Squirrel, is the last slave in the kingdom of Bimmau, a land occupied by animals who talk and wear fancy clothes, but also stick together by species and rarely cross those bounds. At a somewhat scandalous wedding between a cat and a dog (this, I admit was hard for me to wrap my head around at first), Squirrel sips a strange drink and hears his deceased mother's voice whispering a puzzle to him. 
 The plot is a straight up quest. Squirrel must work through a series of clues that will lead him to a special key that has the potential to free him from slavery and to reveal his true name. Squirrel and a rag-tag group of adventurers must stay one step ahead of enemy forces who also want the key, because although it has the power to free slaves, the key may also be used to enslave others. Of great fun for me, and my children who also read the book, was ability to play along with the puzzles. There are riddles to answer and codes to break, making this a good step up for kids who enjoy the Geronimo Stilton books, but are ready for a new challenge. 
 I wish I had done this as a read aloud with my kids, rather than them reading the book independently. My daughter didn't like the occasional swear word ("damn" if you're wondering), and some subtle flirting confused my son, but would have kept an adult's attention while reading. 
 I suspect a lot of the book's nuances were lost on them. Part way through, I had an epiphany - the various animal species functioned like a divided human society. Some of the characters were open-minded enough to see past the physical difference and appreciate what similarities existed even when the differences seemed insurmountable. The themes of home, family, identity, and nourishment recur in different places. 
 I really wish publisher Simon & Schuster had included a reading guide or discussion questions, because as parents, sometimes our brains hurt by bedtime and we need a little help, so here's a few thoughts from me. If reading aloud, the parent (and child if they read aloud too) could stop and ask questions about whether Squirrel and Des are good guests and if bees or mice are better hosts and why. There are a number of places where the adult could ask a child why a character behaves they way they do and raise issues of fairness. The Tale of a No-Name Squirrel is a terrific book for raising issues around empathy but also hierarchical societies. Because the animals bear resemblance to humans - and not just for the fine footwear - sharing this story can be a way to ease into some uncomfortable conversations about privilege, whether economic, social, or racial. 
 But if that's too esoteric, then focus on quest and puzzles. I give this a 5/5 for a read aloud story, and a 4/5 for independent reading. 
 Oh - and the disclaimer - I received a complementary copy of The Tale of a No-Name Squirrel from the author in exchange for an honest review. 
 And another oh - the illustrations by Audrey Benjaminsen are charming and add character to the story.

This was my second time reading this wonderful book and I loved it just as much as the first time, if not more! *-* 
 It was everything you want in a good, happy, but also meaningful childrens book. 
 The writing style was honest, realistic and you could easily empathize with the main character. 
 I really enjoyed moments with Kelly, when she comforts her friend and they laugh together. They were cute - in the best way possible - and made me smile. True friendship is something wonderful and magical. 
 The way pronouns were used was perfect. Using "she" right from the beginning and describing Melissas struggle to not be "wanting to be a girl" but "wanting the world to see that she IS a girl" is a way on addressing this topic that probably fits best, and it's awesome. 
 I think it's very important that this book has such a happy and hopeful ending and that Melissa finds support and love in the people in her life that really matter. It took a while, but with all her courage, Melissa could finally show them who she really is. 
 I give this book 5 well deserved stars! :D

I received this book in exchange for an honest review. This was an amusing review of a day in the life of a three year old. The book was well written with catchy sort of rhymes, catching both the attention of kids and the adults who read the book to them. The drawings were cute and colorful as well, which added to the story. A real fun way for a mom to describe a three year olds day.
Beautiful classic story for children about spreading beauty in the world and making a diference.

Even as a parent reading this over and over to my children while we lived in Vermont, I was so effected by the notion that the seeds we sow are enjoyed by others far beyond our ability to comprehend, that I planted lupine seeds in our garden just to remember that small truth. Lupines don't grow here in Utah like they do back East. I miss the East coast. Sniff.

An enchantinfg fairy tale 
 My heart goes out to the beast. Humble, patient, consistent. And the palace! And the riches and the birds and the magic. Beauty was a beauty by heart, by soul. This book showed me what happens when you keep promises. Miracles do not just happen. You have to work towards them for them to happen. You do not just get a prince. You have to pass through your own exams to gain him. Life is that way. Eagerly waiting for the movie!

An Adventure for All Ages 
 4.5 out of 5 
 A teddy bear must do anything he can to protect and save his boy from monsters. Monsters who were said to have gone away. He will stop at nothing and nowhere to protect his child. 
 Michael Gilliland had a great voice for this, light and playful, but "manly" enough to portray a caring but karate-loving teddy bear. The narration for this was really good. Gilliland was a great choice by Sloan for Teddy Bears in Monsterland. 
 This book was obviously written for children, but it can be enjoyed by anyone of any age. If you had a teddy bear growing up, this story is for you. I know for a fact that I believed that my stuffed animals would protect me in the middle of the night, and that's what this story is about. 
 But, if you have kids, know that this would be a light PG novel for them. There is some violence, but really only on the side of the bear versus the monsters. A heartwarming tale that is sure to have the whole family enjoying it. 
 Teddy Bears in Monsterland was a surprise like for me this year, it was a nice light read after some of the heavier books I've read lately. 
 I was given a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. 
 Did you like this review and want to see more like it? Check out Brian's Book Blog

I always have a soft spot for clumsy characters. I also love the illustrations, and word placement (the words tumble as Geoffrey stumbles). Geoffrey a clumsy giraffe, just wants to say "Hello," but he always has a mishap. He gives up, but then some monkeys ask for some help and want him as a friend. So do the birds. Have to try it in my friendship story time.
Duck has lost his new, blue socks. He asks fox and ox, but the peacocks are the ones to spot his socks. I'll have to try this in my clothing story time.

I didn't like this book. It felt... hokey. Is "hokey" a word? I'm not sure, but it kind of felt like it was trying to be a song, and there was a repeated phrase "Hey, hey, bless-a-my-soul!" that made me want to puke, just a bit. Or roll my eyes. In any case, I was Not. A. Fan. 
 To add insult to injury, the illustrations in this book were paintings done in the Impressionist style, of which I am also Not. A. Fan. 
 So there you go. 
 My Least Objectionable Picture: 
 The baby sleeping in the crib with his two older siblings looking on.

I was hooked from the beginning - this would be such a fun book to booktalk - and loved it. It was a great combination of introspection and action. I don't remember another book that so clearly described the mental states a person might have in a moment or day that are so challenging to understand or explain. But there's also a great plot and story to keep things moving. I imagine some kids and adults might be unhappy with so many unanswered questions at the end, but I didn't mind. There was a typo on page 223 of my library copy - does the Newbery committee care about these things? I hope not. 
 (About five years ago, Laurel Snyder skyped with our library's book club when we discussed "Bigger than a Bread Box" and she couldn't have been nicer.)

I'm reviewing this to share my annoyance. A Simon Read-to-Read Level One is described as "Easy sight words and words to sound out," "Simple plot and dialogue," and "Familiar topics and themes." Publishers usually do a pretty good job of creating early readers with simple text that feature movie and TV characters. 
 Some of the words in here are: adorable, advantage, important, beverages, resist, and congratulations. I don't think these are sight words. I get that the idea of Boss Baby makes writing an early reader a little challenging, but calling this a level one is misleading.

The lives of the four kids in this book intersect in a way that is very satisfying. Each kid is diverse, realistic and unique. We even get to see some perspective on the motivations of a bully. I loved how there were little clues in the chapters that tied in to future chapters. 
 There is a bit of magic realism that might throw a few kids off, plus for those who yearn for justice, it isn't clear if someone gets in trouble for something they do. 
 It's a sweet book with some suspense that would make a great read-aloud for upper elementary kids.

This is really old-school, not only because many of the stories come from folklore, but because even the newer stories feel old, with their landlines ringing in the house. This is a mix of silly, scary, and quite scary. I like how it's literally written with tips about how to read them out loud. Scary just really isn't my thing, but this still is requested and I wanted to finally read it. 
 My daughter recently read this at school, my son started it and stopped, which supports that idea that kids really will stop if they are uncomfortable with something they're reading. I kind of wish my daughter hadn't been introduced to the idea that somebody could be hiding in the backseat of a car though.

I read this out loud at bedtime. I was eventually asked to stop using my robot voice, even though I thought it was pretty good. 
 It's a different story and I appreciate that, but it didn't really capture my attention. I enjoyed the illustrations, though there was one on the right side that gave away an exciting event that didn't happen until the bottom of the left-hand page (p. 254) - kind of ruined the moment. Even though there are some futuristic elements, it's mostly an animal/adventure story, with touching family moments.

I read this out loud to my son, and I can't say I was a fan. There were many aspects of the mystery that didn't make sense. I would say, "But how..." and "But when..." and he'd tell me just to carry on and not worry about it. But they weren't just nitpicky things - they were pretty major plot elements. I think there are better mysteries out there, even though the code aspect was fun.

This is shorter than the other early chapter books I've been comparing. I liked it quite a bit. Posey is realistic, nice, and not particularly spunky. I like how her grandpa is a big part of her life, that she really thinks about things, and that an adult in the story admitted they were having a bad day and made a mistake. Great for younger readers - 1st grade or so.

Lola Levine has a pretty standard real-life early chapter book plot - school, friends, family. They're all starting to feel the same to me. She is a little exceptional in that she has Peruvian ancestry and speaks some Spanish. I also liked that she stood up for herself (with the help of her mom) with another adult. 
 Her character is not sassy, but like so many others, knows her mind and finds herself in trouble sometimes. A good series for kids who like soccer.

Liz and her Critter Club friends are really nice girls who get along great. I liked their diverse backgrounds and families, plus the plot that Liz had to go to summer school for math. I did take issue with one sentence - "Tofu dogs were, by far, Liz's favorite summertime food."

Heidi is pretty sassy - she is definitely not happy about attending school after being home-schooled, she says and writes some kind of mean things, and makes a plan to curse her nemesis, the stereotypical mean, pretty girl. 
 There are a few aspects of the story that aren't really realistic, but that only a parent of an elementary-aged kid would likely notice. Also, the reading level and font size make this for a slightly lower-level reader than others I've looked at like Kylie Jean and Clementine. This has an unfinished, cliffhanger ending.

This was a great audio experience - it felt like being told a cozy story by a roaring fire (even though I was driving). This kind of storytelling really lends itself to an audio experience that's good for all ages, and I will be suggesting this to families who want something for a road trip. Historical and magical. 
 (I did try to read this out loud to my daughter last year, and she got bored. I'm no Juliet Stevenson.)

Further research into the nature of girl characters in different early chapter books. 
 Clementine isn't sassy exactly, but she's spunky and disorganized and sometimes lies in this story about school and family. I thought this was very funny, to a point where I wondered if kids get it, since it was so funny to me. I might have teared up a little near the end. I thought the message was great. I could tell there was some backstory with the character of Margaret that I didn't know from book one, but it didn't matter too much. 
 Sadly, I don't really get asked for this series.

Sometimes I'm asked for early chapter books where the main character is *not* sassy - usually this is a parent who does not want Junie B. Jones. However, the other day I was asked for early chapter books where the character *is* sassy. So I'm going to read a few series to determine how sassy the main character is. 
 The Princess in Black is not sassy in this book. She is very kind to her party guests, trying to leave to fight monsters while keeping them distracted with fun activities. Despite this, I think the fact that (spoiler alert) Princess Magnolia becomes the Princess in Black could still make this series appealing to those looking for sassy main characters. 
 Based on my previous reading, I'd say that Junie B. Jones and Bean of Ivy and Bean qualify as sassy. Violet Mackerel is not sassy.

This is pretty much what I expected - girl and brother end up in a fairy tale world, alter history and help Snow White. The narration is breezy and funny, the time travel aspect makes sense, the kids have realistic reactions to danger and weirdness, and I especially liked how Snow White became a more assertive person. I was not a fan of the line "Who doesn't know what a phone is?...Maybe she's homeschooled." 
 These are popular at my library, and seem to be at about a 2nd - 4th grade level.

This is a heartwarming story of friendship and the impact of a great teacher. Maybe it was because I read this over my lunch breaks and it took more than a month, but I had trouble keeping the three narrators straight. I also found myself impatient with the number of flashbacks, wishing for the immediate action to continue. I wonder if I'm like a kid in these ways? 
 I also struggled a bit with the part where the boys are in the alleyway. They showed incredibly bad and dangerous judgement in a story where most decisions were at least well-intended, though sometimes bad. That scene seemed just scary dumb and unnecessary on their parts. 
 I couldn't get my own fifth-graders at home to pick this up. Not sure why, though, except they don't really like sad books, and there's definitely some sadness in here, as the title and dust jacket already imply.

This was well-written, but it felt like the plot was just a vehicle for the author to share what it's like in Vietnam. There are many interesting and vivid details, but the story itself was slow. I didn't particularly enjoy Mia/Mai as a character - her whining got old. I was also distracted by the use of capital letters for her love interest at home. Every time I saw the word "HIM" I shouted it in my brain. 
 I enjoyed her relationship with her grandmother, and the fact that she did evolve as a person, even though it was just a little bit. 
 Also, I feel like the cover implies it's a story that's more whimsical and for younger readers. 
 I read this for the Read Harder challenge: "Read a book that is by an author from Southeast Asia."

I like that this book exists, and thought the author did a good job of showing different types of families, as well as reflecting the combination of the fun stuff (plays!) and drudgery of elementary school. The writing itself was so-so, but I think that as a read-aloud it would still work well. I liked the ending quite a bit. 
 I read this for the Read Harder Challenge: "Read a book by or about a person that identifies as transgender."

This is cute. It has a Harry Potter feel to it, with kids going to school to practice their type of magic. Because Nory's magic is wonky, she goes to a special class, and the message that everyone has their own talents and worth, even if some people think they might be weird, is not at all subtle. There was some creativity in the creation of the different types of magic, and how they can be wonky, but the world-building was pretty minimal. 
 My son likes this series. I would consider suggesting it to younger middle-grade readers who like fantasy and Harry Potter.

This has a fun premise, and the ending brought it up to 3 stars for me. I can see why this series is popular. But the writing is not so good. There are some serious gaps in logic and a lack of explanation at times, as well as some slightly more mature humor in a few cases (which will go over most middle-graders' heads). If a reader were looking for chapter books with a fairy tale basis, I *might* still suggest this. Sorry Kurt.

While this is a survival and adventure story, because of Mark's situation it doesn't feel exciting in a good way. His bad luck and poor choices are painful to read as an adult. Having Mark repeat the phrase "and that's the truth" felt jarring to me. I think it's good to have books that show a child's experience with cancer, and that this will appeal to certain kid readers. I'd suggest this possibly to kids who liked "Out of My Mind."

I liked this concept, and did enjoy it, but am still trying to figure out why it didn't quite work for me. I think I would have liked for Aunt Gertrudis to be a little less extreme. I loved Ephraim and Micah's relationship, though I didn't feel very emotional about it. Great cover and art, and the last line of the acknowledgements is nice. Good for 4th-6th graders who like fantasy (and circuses, I suppose.)

I loved how Child's illustrations were so whimsical, along with some of the type being set in patterns. Pippi is great. She reminded me of Mary Poppins in her own way. I do kind of wish she had been a normal but independent and silly kid, without the crazy strength. (Now I probably won't be allowed into Sweden again.)

I have been asked for the follow-up to this book by some kids who have read it, and who have asked for more books with multiple narrators. Each of the kids is pretty well-defined, and I think Buyea captures this age really well. I had no idea it would have the drama it did, but I suspect kids like that part too. I love the cover. Best for grades 5 and up.

I read this for an award committee, and hadn't read the previous books in the series. It's not the best as a standalone, but not the worst either. Like Rebellion, it felt like there were some creative details, but that the world overall wasn't clearly understandable. The dream world was cool, but I didn't quite get it. Mostly, it bothered me how often telekinesis conveniently got them out of trouble.

This is a nice school story about a girl with dyslexia struggling with her schoolwork and trying to fit in. Her teacher is amazing, and really illustrates how one person paying attention can make such a huge difference. 
 "Absolutely Almost" has set a high bar for this kind of story, and I didn't think the writing was quite as strong. I also thought there were some turnarounds near the end that weren't quite believable. 
 I've realized that not only can kids who feel like they don't fit in get hope from stories like this, but their parents can too.

I think fans of American Girl books and dancing will enjoy this. Isabelle is realistically insecure about being new at the arts school, and I liked how visualization was used by the sisters. I also liked the sister relationship, some bad but mostly good. I thought the writing was a bit over-descriptive, I guess - sometimes the descriptions seemed unnecessary and uninteresting. The real life stories at the end were nice.

Strengths: This depicts kids living in poverty with parents who are in trouble with the county and the law. I felt a little emotional and inspired at the end. Weaknesses: The idea that Daisy and Graham would attempt this is unrealistic, and they made so, so many stupid choices. Also, I was uncomfortable with the character of Ashley - she was a sympathetic character, but sometimes it felt like she was being mocked a bit. Finally, the target age for this is unclear - the cover and description seem young, but I think the content is more middle-school and up.

3.5 stars. This was enjoyable - not particularly unusual from a plot perspective, except for the addition of the chicken farming and her love of movie-making. I liked how Kate handled her new friendships when things got back to normal, and that she appreciated their strengths and friendship. I felt a little conflicted about how the wig situation resolved.

I read this (a signed copy!) out loud to Ava, and it works great as a read aloud. Lots of action, you can do a fun voice for Ereth, and there's opportunity to explain new vocabulary, because there was plenty of it in here. We were both anxious for there to be justice and for the truth to be known.

At first I was a little bored by this, but when Ava and I started reading it together (silently, simultaneously) and I heard her reacting, I realized I wasn't appreciating that there are a lot of funny bits. The author's note is a nice touch. It's so similar to Flora and Ulysses that it's hard not to compare; even the illustrations are similar. It's fun to imagine the life and conversations of squirrels and other forest animals. This was creative, with a nice environmental message too.

This was suggested as a good read-aloud by a mom at the library, and now that I've read it, I plan to add it to my list of suggestions. Rump is a character you understand and root for, and the imagining of his story is very clever. There's plenty of action, especially during his journey, and I loved the humor as well. I guess it could be a little scary for younger listeners...maybe I'd suggest for 1st grade and up.
A nice early chapter book about friendship and school days, school plays and nature. It reminded me of "The Year of Billy Miller."

I read this out loud to a nine-year-old boy at his request, even though he had already read it to himself. If you're not OK with phrases such as, "Oh, do shut up, you old hag," then this might not be the right read-aloud for you, but otherwise it's pretty fun to read it with feeling. Spoiler alert?: It's fun at any age to see nasty people get what's coming to them.

Excellent in so many ways, but if you have read, "The boy and the airplane" and pay attention to one particular illustration (hint: it's the only one with red instead of green), you will probably cry.

Rose has high-functioning autism and a dog she loves. We see how tough her life is - without much money and with a drinking, impatient father - through her mostly non-judgmental eyes. The moments of kindness in her story, from her uncle, teacher, and classmate, are very tender as a result. 
 I didn't feel much connection with Rose, though I don't think it was due to her diagnosis, but instead due to the writing somehow. I also found the parenthetical homonyms to be distracting. 
 For upper-elementary kids who like dog stories and/or who enjoyed "Wonder" and "Out of my Mind."
Funny and sweet, and you really want the bad guy to get what's coming to him because he's just so mean to his dog. There are some jokes adults will appreciate too. I read this out loud.

I re-read this to myself, and I liked it more than when I read it out loud. I don't really pause to think when I read out loud, though I don't know why that should be so. 
 I appreciated more of the emotion this time around, and how sensitive kids can be to so many things. The gaps in the passage of time still threw me off a bit. I also appreciated that there wasn't some enlightening moment explaining why Emma was so mean (i.e., she's an orphan, her mother is sick, etc.) and that she was just a bratty little girl for no particular reason.

This is getting a lot of love, but less from me because it contains one of my biggest pet peeves that I can't seem to get over, which is: when something completely extraordinary, unbelievable, or frightening happens to characters, they need to freak out. At least a little. Maybe kid readers don't really care, but it annoys me. 
 Otherwise, this covers scientific discovery, family relationships, and changing friendships quite nicely. There's plenty of humor in the family dynamics, which is fun.

Don't let the sunny cover fool you. This book will break your heart a hundred times. I loved it. I might donate a copy to my kids' intermediate school library, an idea that's never occurred to me before. 
 Each character - adult and child - is so real, so imperfect. The experience of being in upper elementary school is vivid and realistic and heartbreaking. I feel like every librarian, teacher, and parent of that age should read this just to remember how hard it is (kids can tell us, of course, but reading it this way made it easier for me to remember and understand). 
 I do wish the cover were different - a little more serious, and the model airplane skews it young to me. It'd be great for a book club. I really, really hope that kids find it and enjoy it.

I listened to half of this on audio, but got annoyed by the narrator's voices for the kids. I finished it in print form, but still didn't enjoy this like the first in the series. I know it isn't meant to be all that realistic, but Dan and Amy were so incredibly lucky all the time, acting on the slightest hint of a clue that turns out to be correct and constantly escaping incredible situations. I like there to still be some sense of reality in action/adventure stories, and this didn't have any. Obviously, kids don't seem to mind, though, since this series is still popular at my library. I might be curious enough to see how other authors have carried the series forward, but it won't be soon.

I reread this out loud to my 8-year-old son for a school book group. The large amounts of new vocabulary were definitely noticeable when reading it to him. Sometimes he asked about a word, sometimes I stopped to explain something (including "electric chair," which I immediately regretted) and sometimes I just went on, because to explain every new word would have taken forever. 
 He liked it more than I expected, and cracked up every time the squirrel thought about being hungry. The sadness of Flora's life was more noticeable to me in this reading too, though it didn't seem to bother him much. 
 Weirdly, I kept saying "Florida" instead of "Flora" for the first third of the book. It was fun to have the different voices for the characters, especially William Spiver's.

It was confusing to read this at home while also reading "Fish in a Tree" at work - they both feature middle-grade girls who don't fit in, influential older siblings and absent fathers. I love this book's cover, and how the title and cover really are a big part of the book. There are a lot of imperfect and believable characters. This is a nice choice for kids looking for real-life stories that are more character-driven than plot-driven.

As a theater-loving adult, I loved listening to this. Tim Federle is a hilarious narrator (but also believable as a kid), and I laughed out loud a lot. Unfortunately, I think this story and character appeal to a small audience, mainly theater kids, and the circulation statistics on our two Nate titles support that. 
 Federle uses a technique where right before you find out about something important in the main storyline, he switches to a flashback or explanation about a relationship. Especially since you can't skim ahead on audio, this made me antsy at times, though I'm sure he was using this technique to create tension. 
 I liked how imperfect Nate's immediate family was, and how much his trip to Manhattan opens his eyes to the world outside of Jankburg. 
 This is a fun, unique story that will hopefully be discovered by theater kids and more.
A very silly, very quick read. I'll keep suggesting this to kids who like Wimpy Kid and Big Nate, even though it isn't diary style.

I started to read #5 of this series, and realized I needed to start at the beginning to understand the relationship between the three main characters and their circumstances. The format is fun and makes for a quick read. 
 2/14 note - I brought this home for my 8-year-old daughter, who has a high reading level. She read about half and said, "I don't get it." I sort of wondered how younger kids might comprehend and respond to the contract, writing life, etc. adult topics.

I read book one to familiarize myself with the situation after starting this - I don't think it stands alone well. I enjoyed the format and illustrations. These don't circulate well at my library, and my 8-year-old daughter said after reading halfway through the first: "I don't get it." Having mostly adult characters in situations like contract negotiations may be a factor in that.
Better than expected! A quick read with fun facts and silly but not-gross humor.
The whimsical art created with cut paper and watercolor is perfect for this imaginative story. Who doesn't love balloons, carousels and polar bears? The ending is perfect.

Such a hilarious, quick, creative book involving a father who gets sidetracked picking up milk for his kids and then relays his fantastic adventure to them. The Tim-Burton-esque illustrations are a great match and it's laugh-out-loud witty (I loved the earth redecorating ideas). Eventually, I'll read this out loud to my kids and post an update with their reactions.

I rarely review picture books (I read plenty of them, but they mess up my total book count). I just can't resist reviewing this, I love it so - the brown landscape before the snow falls, the mom's expression at the bathtub, the agony of waiting for the flakes to come, the warmth of the home, and the perfect depiction of a snowy town at dusk.
Meh. I like the premise and the art, but the story had gaps, the made-up language was more annoying than funny, and what hamster is going to sit at a tea party?

I mainly read this because I couldn't decide how young I should go when suggesting this series. While there's nothing inappropriate, I think the boy/girl dynamics make it better for fourth grade and up. I like how girls play video games before school and boys cry in class - lots of real kids in here, as well as funny commentary on school life. I didn't think the flow of this story worked as well, since it's mostly flashbacks in a case file, but the ending was nice on several levels.

This was a little better than the first - I didn't find Nikki to be quite so annoying (though there are still a lot of exclamations, swinging emotions, and bad decisions). I liked the way she persevered with the dance situation, but found it a pretty unrealistic storyline anyway (are there no adults to help out with the planning of an entire off-site school event?) Mackenzie is so bad, she's more like a caricature of a mean girl. This series' focus on social and romantic situations really makes it best for middle-schoolers, but I know younger girls are reading it too, unfortunately.

I loved how this showed the different ways of being odd, how it's a matter of perception, and how it's OK. I wished a few more pages had been dedicated to their friendship, for the missing each other part to have more impact. Excellent, funny details in the illustrations.

This had a higher vocabulary than I expected, and was pretty entertaining. I liked what Franny learned from her experiment, but didn't think it was too didactic. Yay for her understanding teacher too.

If you liked "Three Times Lucky," you'll be happy to know that this has the same wit, charm, and quirky characters as before. The mystery was not quite as straightforward as the first, and I was kept guessing as to whether there would be a Scooby-Doo ending or not. I didn't think this came together quite as well as "Three Times Lucky" (and found myself getting it mixed up with "True Blue Scouts..." at first), but it was still a lot of fun.

This is a sophisticated kids' fantasy, good for those who like Valente's Fairyland series or Ursu's Breadcrumbs. I liked it better than Breadcrumbs, but still felt a similar disconnect with the characters and story that's hard to explain. It's great storytelling and very imaginative, but I didn't feel close to the characters, even though they're likeable.

I like Arnie the Doughnut as a picture book and a movie, and his character translates to chapter book pretty well. The first few pages fill in those not familiar with Arnie ("Mr. Bing...remember when you tried to EAT me...ha ha ha") and goes from there with a mystery involving Mr. Bing's bowling league. It was funny, though a bit of the humor will go over kids' heads, I think. Apparently, in Arnie's world, most objects like pizza slices and bowling pins can talk as he does. Lots of illustrations and a quick, fun read. I'll add comments of my kids' impressions later.

Game creator Mr. Lemoncello created an inventive, Willy-Wonka-like library for his childhood town; now a bunch of 12-year-olds get to spend the night solving a game within the library before it opens. 
 I liked the creativity, the many children's book references, and the whole concept. I wasn't interested enough in the puzzle to see if I could figure out first, but I'm not even sure that was possible. I didn't like how stereotypical the characters were, and didn't buy Haley's sudden transformation. A library map would've been a useful addition.

This is my first Henkes non-picture book, which I read out loud to my 8-year-old daughter. It was enjoyable, and she laughed out loud at times. Her review will follow. Henkes is good in all of his books at capturing everyday life, usually involving friends, school, and family. To me, this made for a somewhat dull chapter book, without much plot. The back cover is all about his bump on the head which - sort of a spoiler - isn't really a big deal or part of the story exactly. I also felt the passage of time between sections wasn't particularly clear, and that Billy seemed a little older than the second-graders I know (and I know a lot of them right now). But Ava enjoyed it, and I'm glad we read it together. 
 Ava: 4 and a half stars. I liked how Sal was so cute and Papa always calmed Billy when he was frantic. I liked how the words told us how Billy was feeling.

Early on, I thought, "This book reminds me a little of Mercy Watson." And then I remembered that Kate DiCamillo wrote Mercy Watson. The characters are beyond quirky, and the vocabulary is high. This makes it appealing and fun for many adult readers, but I suspect will work for fewer young readers, and probably for nobody under 4th grade. 
 I enjoyed the cartoon panels added throughout - they really helped me visualize certain scenes - and the way that adults were portrayed as all kinds of weirdness, good and bad, thought I remained a little worried about the dad throughout. 
 My favorite line (about marriage): "Such tenderness. To have someone get out of bed and bring you little fishes and sit with you as you eat them in the dark of night. To hum to you. This is love." 
 And this is probably the only time I'll ever tear up at a poem written by a squirrel. Sheesh.

I loved how imaginative these kids were, and how their changing relationships were explored. You could speculate that their quest was a product of their imaginations, but the history they discovered in East Liverpool would confirm Eleanor's story (that Poppy knew her name alone is proof), so I read this as a real ghost story. Creepy, but not too scary. I'd think the guy on the bus would (and should) scare some kids too. 
 As a real ghost story, then, I would've liked more at the end to feel more satisfied that all was well. Also, Zach's casual message about their theft felt like it should have been a more serious event with more explanation and possibly regret. 
 I listened to disc one on audio but couldn't get into it and switched to the print version.

This has 26 holds at our library, and I wanted to see if it was a good suggestion for Wimpy Kid lovers. It sort of is. 
 The art is great, and I suspect the title and cover are a big reason for the high holds. It's definitely the style of Wimpy Kid, with the characters being possibly closer to upper-elementary age. 
 However. Even though I thought it was often funny, I don't think kids are going to find it as funny. For example, will they get title headings like, "Orange juice. Shaken. Not stirred" or "You may find yourself behind the wheel of a large automobile?" But more than that, Timmy uses a lot of business-speak, thanks to his detective business, and I don't think kids will get that either. 
 I do think they'll find Timmy's cluelessness in detective work and life pretty entertaining though. 
 It isn't as true-to-life as Wimpy Kid either, mostly because he has a polar bear as a business partner.

I started this 2 years ago on my ipod touch and it was a good choice for occasional reading. I love the messages of empowerment and appreciation of nature, and the ending is so satisfying. The little section from the robin's pov seemed a little out of place.

This covers a lot of coming-of-age territory: changing friendships, standing up for yourself, understanding your history and contemplating your place in the world. It does it well, with a sympathetic main character and an interesting almost-mystery involving the eight keys. It's a hard book to review as an adult - unlike other kids' books, there's not much going on besides the character growth, which isn't so exciting once you've gone through that part of your life. But for the right kids (probably girls, around 11) this could be an important read at a critical time.

Now this is a ghost story, complete with friendly spirits, evil shades, earthly anchors, and possessions. Those who didn't like the otherworldly evils of Harry Potter won't like this either. I enjoyed the unique setting of a crumbling orchestra hall, and the incorporation of classical music (though it might not mean much to kids yet. Will they ask their parents about Mahler No. 2?). We find Olivia in a bad place in several respects, but I found her unforgiving stubbornness when it comes to those who care about her to be frustrating. The logic behind the ghosts mostly works, but gets a little fuzzy when talking about the future. I think the ghost business was meant to be literal and not just part of Olivia's imagination, so I read it as so, and I suspect kids would too. If they don't think too hard about how it works, they should enjoy this frightening ghost story in an unusual setting. 
 I received an electronic review copy of this book from Simon & Schuster via edelweiss.

Kids should find this ninja detective story entertaining enough, but it felt shallow compared to similar Southern mystery "Three Time Lucky" by Turnage. The characters lacked depth, with Randi's family history making her somewhat of an exception. I felt like the breaking-and-entering and ninja sequences were too unbelievable and not at all explored for the serious events they would be in real life. It's a quick read, though, and the mystery itself was pretty interesting. 
 I received this eARC from the publisher via edelweiss.

This is a nice story about the complexities of friendship and family in an interesting seaside setting, though I think billing this as a ghost story is stretching it. The relationships are very real and there are funny moments, especially involving Binny's 6-year-old brother. It reminded me of Linda Urban's books - great writing but a slower pace. 
 I don't think the story will stick with me though. I was also a little thrown off by the few times the POV changed away from Binny's. 
 I read an e-galley from Simon & Schuster via Edelweiss.

A Newbery contender, I think. True Blue Scouts is a mix of adventure, mystery, tall tale, and animal story. There are many, many points of view, all tied together by a funny narrator who is almost as chummy as in A Tale Dark and Grimm. 
 Each little section, or point of view, immediately starts building anticipation for a final scene that you hope, hope, hope will go a certain way. It's done very well. 
 While I loved it, there will be some kids who won't enjoy this style of narration or who might be turned off by the higher vocabulary. But if they read it, they'll be ready in a few years for the ivory-billed woodpecker in Where Things Come Back. 
 eGalley provided by Atheneum Books for Young Readers via edelweiss.

The first-grader in me related to this storyline of wanting to help small things and adopting a ladybug more than to the first in the series (I haven't read the second). The adult I am thinks this is one of the sweetest, most tender early chapter books I've ever read. The very end is slightly unrealistic, but a nice way to tie the end to the beginning. 
 Art not seen. I received this ARC electronically through Edelweiss and Atheneum Books for Young Readers.

Kylie Jean is a pretty typical second-grader, likes pink, has good friends, etc. Her Texas location means there are some southern turns of phrase, which I enjoyed. This story centers around her class putting on a play, with Kylie Jean struggling to deal with a mean new girl in school. She is admirably (perhaps unrealistically) a kind person in the face of some pretty mean words. 
 I've been reading more early chapter books to become more familiar with what's out there, but also to try to figure out what appeals or doesn't appeal to my daughter. She likes this Kylie Jean series.

This is a cute short chapter book about wishing for things, making mistakes, and coming up with creative solutions. The illustrations are fun and plentiful, and I like the U.S. edition's cover more than Australia's. It's nice that Violet chooses an unselfish (but not very business-savvy) option near the end of the story. 
 A few minor quibbles: While the idea of theories and plots is a big part of the story, and this is a good introduction to those concepts, the first chapter might be a turnoff to some younger readers. The handwriting shown is much too advanced for a 7-year-old. And finally, on page 37, there's a line where seven words are run together with no spaces. Kids will be able to figure it out, but at $14.99 for a hardcover, that kind of error should be have caught before it was printed.

A timeless story, and clever in the way it incorporates the myths and stories into the actual events of the book. There weren't too many surprises for me as an adult reader, but I'm not sure if kids will figure everything out before it's revealed. It's so different from other books available for this age. I will definitely suggest it for multicultural reader's advisory, but for older elementary school kids who can think more abstractly.

I read this out loud to a seven-year-old. It turned out that it required some explaining that probably makes it better for someone a few years older, but it was mostly fine and we enjoyed it. I read this when I was young and its message has always stayed with me.

A cute choice for girls who have read all of the Rainbow Magic books. There's some adventure, character development, and creative world-building. The preliminary art is sweet and whimsical. One complaint: if you suddenly were told you were in Neverland, wouldn't you ask about Peter? 
 ARC received from Random House Childrens and Edelweiss. 
 Ava's review (age 7): 
 It was good. Every time I stopped reading, I wondered what would be next. I thought it would be about a lot of different things, but it was just fairies. It reminded me of Rainbow Magic - it wasn't really easier or harder. 3 stars.

This is an unusual book, and based on the early reviews, apparently one you either love, or really don't. I found it so confusing at the start that I wondered if there was a problem with the digital file of the ARC I had received. There's invented vocabulary in an invented world of Hokey Pokey, where different aspects of childhood are represented by places such as a big screen constantly playing cartoons and a place where you can wait in line to get a snuggle. I enjoyed the creativity of these places, once I got the hang of the language, but never quite understood it all. I think I'm just more of a concrete thinker. The problem is, a lot of kids are too, and I'm afraid only a select few will stick with this book and enjoy it. 
 As an allegory for a child's transition into adulthood, it didn't quite work for me either. It's neat to think of it as a special moment, but in reality doesn't it happen gradually, and usually with your friends along with you going at about the same pace? In other words, not something you dread, with your friends watching you go? I look forward to reading further reviews of this, hoping maybe they'll help me make more sense of things. 
 Thank you to Random House Children's for providing a digital review copy to me via Edelweiss.

Though I've read this once or twice before, it's been a long time and this time I read it out loud to my daughter at bedtime. I was struck by how much new vocabulary we got to talk about, and how unique the writing really is. No tears for her, but when we saw the play the night after we finished reading it, I was crying a little near the end and she just leaned over to me and said, "I hate this part."

This is an odd little book that I wanted to like more than I did. Two Mongolian brothers trying to assimilate into an British classroom has its interesting and teachable moments, and I liked how the reader gets to figure out the truth with the author. I was a little confused by part of the storyline in the end and why the brothers acted the way they did - I think I figured it out but it's a bit unclear. The writing is good and I liked the format, but I'm not sure how many kids will relate to Julie's childhood experiences.

Freddie Ramos is the hero of the Zapato Power early chapter book series. Short chapters, comic-book-like illustrations, a little magic (the shoes) and funny one-liners make this a fun choice. There are a few Spanish words that either have the English also included, or make sense in context.

This early chapter book features a smart, independent third-grader living in New York City. It's one of the few early chapter book series to feature primarily African-American characters. Even though she's new to her neighborhood and school, Dyamonde stands up to a mean new boy and ultimately they become friends. 
 I was a little thrown off when the point of view switches to Free's (the friend's) about halfway through, but from then on we read both of their perspectives and I adjusted. The illustrations were a little harsh-looking for my tastes, but they were interesting.

This story would have been fine, except that some of the details didn't make sense to me and it bugged me. Maybe kids wouldn't have a problem with it. For instance, why would Ty give the love cookies even to girls he found really unattractive? And the backwards effects were inconsistent and sort of impossible. And I don't believe people wouldn't catch on to the magic going on. 
 I liked the family dynamics, and found Rose to be sympathetic and realistic.

My 6-year-old son and I just finished reading through these poems at bedtime. Even though it's a "very first" book, he loved them as a bigger kid too. There were a few funny selections, but mostly they were quiet and sweet poems, with perfectly matched illustrations by Karas. It'd be a great baby gift to last through the years.

This book was so fun and unique. I loved hearing the real Grimm's fairy tales, but the snarky, funny narrator is what really made it work. I don't know how many kids get the humor. Hopefully at least the older ones do, but even if they don't, the goriness of the tales should hook them. I also love that Adam Gidwitz went to Park School in Baltimore and gives thanks to Laura Amy Schlitz.
First-grade drama. Juliet learns about individuality and friendship in this early chapter book set at school and home. The colorful pages in this series are a nice touch.

This was surprisingly good. Lizzie is very altruistic, but has realistic kid qualities like talking too much, being competitive, and having a hard time fessing up to a mistake. I liked the diversity of characters - her best friend's mom, Mrs. Santiago, is blind, and her best friend's uncle is a super nice guy with a bald head and tattoos. I wasn't a fan of one feature of this series, which is having the puppy's thoughts inserted in italics. It was distracting and didn't add much to the story.

I feel conflicted about this one. Partly, the pastel, beach-scene cover suggests this is a lighter read than it is. The events at the beginning of the book just made me feel icky for a long time (and also questioning whether it was realistic). The writing was fine, but since I read this at the same time as "Wonder," in comparing the two I didn't think this one captured childhood as well. I did enjoy the ending, though, and think a certain kind of girl will be able to relate well to Stella's personality. 
 Upper-elementary, real-life.

What I actually liked more than Auggie's unique situation was that the writing was so readable and true. I liked the characters and their various perspectives (it could almost be shelved in the teen section). This isn't exactly a spoiler, but could change someone's expectation...Based on the hype, I sort of expected there to be an event that was more shocking or with a deeper meaning, but the book is perfectly great without it. I was just nervous until the end. 
 This would be great for kids who liked "Out of my mind" and would be a good bookgroup/school read.
A nice story for a kid struggling with shyness and confidence, but not too much happens.

Or maybe 3.5 stars. I did like it - Stead has a readable, funny style that's appealing, and her characters are quirky and real. I liked how she addressed bullying, and the loneliness that comes from feeling different and having parents who are often absent. 
 But it sometimes felt slow to me. While there is the plot of the kids spying in their apartment building, it didn't always feel like the story was moving forward.

I've just finished reading this out loud to my 6-year-old son, who is really into states. I've always liked Yaccarino's illustrations, and it was fun to go through the states like on a road trip. For someone just starting to learn more about the states, it was a bit too quirky and ephemeral - many incredibly weird laws and silly festivals. It's probably a little better for later elementary school kids.

This is a fun, Southern mystery for kids. It reminded me of "Moon over Manifest" but not historical, even though the modern-day references were few and it felt kind of historical/timeless. It's full of quirky characters and funny, small-town events. The mystery itself was a little weak to me. It seems unlikely that Lana could keep that secret from the Colonel all that time, and that Detective Starr could be so easily fooled. But those are probably picky, adult complaints that kids won't care about. A good suggestion for kids looking for a mystery.

While this has a bit of magic in it, it's essentially a real-life, coming-of-age story. I really liked how Rebecca evolved in this story, particularly when it came to her perspectives about her parents and little brother. Her experience and reaction to her parents' separation seemed really true to life. I do wish the cover had a more contemporary feel to it. 
 We'll be reading this for a library book discussion group for 9-12 years-olds in August, and have arranged to skype with Laurel Snyder. She's been super nice to work with so far, and we're very excited.

This is great choice for animal lovers and reluctant readers. I love that it's based on a true story (although it seems a little confusing to be set in a unspecified time period versus clearly historical, since it's unlikely animals would be caged in such a way today in the U.S. I think.). 
 I liked the nuances of Mack, George, and Julia's perspectives. Some of the animals' words and thoughts did seem too sophisticated to me, though. Obviously, it's all speculation, but would a dog really say, "You're being a temperamental artist?" I really did enjoy it, though - a quick and hopeful story that could make an animal activist out of most anyone.

This is a nice story, but pretty slow-paced, especially when listening to it on audio (I listened to discs 1-3 out of 7). I was intrigued by the concept and think some kids might be as well. Topics like racism, twins, and the differences between generations are covered. I didn't get to the actual pageant part, but I suspect some kids will like that too. Narrator Bahni Turpin's voice for Grandma Johnson is hilarious.

A somewhat fluffy read that appeals to both genders, this book focuses on day-to-day interactions at a middle school. There's almost no character development (and thus it's hard to keep them straight, but it probably doesn't matter). Details about their town, families, etc. don't really exist. 
 But, it actually has some depth to it, if you consider how this finger puppet changed how the kids interacted with each other and shifted their perceptions. There was a lot about their conversations and concerns that seemed pretty true to sixth grade. 
 Great cover.

Petra and Calder are smart, Chicago kids who connect circumstances and think in new ways to solve a mystery of a missing Vermeer painting. Some supernatural elements. Illustrations with clues and codes.
Beautiful writing, but not very kid-friendly.

I don't think I get why these are popular. I guess because they're fast-paced with lots of illustrations, and have funny mouse/cheese references. But the main characters are adult mice, with sort of adult problems (nothing inappropriate, of course). The story in this first of the series was so-so, and I thought the changes in font color, size, and style were distracting. Hmmm.
A fun friendship story with illustrations (love Sophie Blackall) for 1st-3rd graders. Ivy and Bean are pretty mischievous.

I had passed this one by at the library based on its cover, but finally took it home because of its good reviews in journals. And now it's my kids' favorite of the year so far. They practically have it memorized, and still crack up at the "squishy in my shoe" part, and more. And I've grown to appreciate the interior illustrations, especially the garden scene.

I just finished reading this out loud to my kids. Since it's the second of this series I've read out loud, I've really gotten the voices down, especially Plastic and Lumphy - it's very fun. It really struck me in this one how Jenkins sneaks some pretty serious life issues into these toys' lives. When the dryer might be nearing the end of her life, there's a look at how two different characters deal with such a situation. Plenty of jealousy too. Reading these aloud provides opportunity for explaining plenty of new vocabulary, as well.

The bizarreness of this story meant that sometimes my mind wandered during the audio. Jim Dale is great; some of his voices reminded me of characters from the audio of Emerald Atlas, but you can hardly expect a man to have distinguishable characters from book to book.

This children's fantasy was especially charming. Most of the book is rather dark (literally and figuratively), with two brave kids whose lives intertwine. Lots of lives intertwine, actually - Oliver explored these moments in "Before I Fall" too - and it's fun to be the only one (as the reader) who realizes it. The illustrations match the book's tone well, and the author's note was very personal and touching. For elementary-age kids.

A girl who feels like she doesn't fit in loses her best friend to a witch, so she must go into a fantasy woods to save him. The writing was really nice, with some great imagery, and I especially liked the first half of the book, set in Minnesota. When she goes into the woods, it gets pretty interesting, with Hazel meeting all kinds of characters who mean to do her harm. However, I do wonder if it's a little too "out there" for kids - it's hard to make sense of what's happening a bit.

I didn't realize that after Groundhog Day but before "Before I Fall," there was "11 Birthdays." Reliving the same day over and over is a fun concept, and the evolution of Amanda is believable for her age, and suitable for upper elementary readers. Funny lines and easily readable, with a few lessons about friendship, paying attention to the world around you, and being true to yourself.

The busy page layout and small handwriting made this a tough read for me, though maybe my age is a factor in that. I liked how the book covered alternative learning styles and the fact that the parents were very human and had fears, but I thought the story lacked continuity (or maybe the format just made me feel that way?). Good for upper elementary/early middle school. 
 Also, if you know the song Doodlebugs by Laurie Berkner, it'll be stuck in your head.

This was an excellent, fast-paced adventure and fantasy story. The pace was so non-stop that I found myself wishing that a break in the action about 3/4ths through was the end (which is also when different characters got their own chapters and the story didn't flow quite as well). I enjoyed the siblings' relationship - their funny bickering and fierce love for each other. The explanation of the time travel was a bit befuddling - easier to just accept how it is and move on (which the author practically advises). 
 This was my first audiobook narrated by Jim Dale, and I understand why he's so popular. His various character voices were great. 
 A longish book, it'd be a good suggestion for those who liked Fablehaven, Percy Jackson, and Inkheart.

I read this out loud to my kids - I had seen it suggested that it was a good one, particularly because it's written/formatted in a way that makes it easy to read aloud, which was true. It's a cozy read, simple and not scary at all. The toys had unique personalities and I especially loved the character of Plastic and her perspective. There were chances to explain some new words in here.

Every time I read this, I love it a little more - the art, Cloudette's expressions, and the subtle message (which I do believe my 5-year-olds get). They love it too. Their favorite part is where they get to join in with the frogs to say "Ribbit" together.
Funny stuff! I think parents should read these to remember what it's like. Thus far, in my survey of books like Wimpy Kid, I haven't found anything I like as much.

Once I read and disliked "Dork Diaries," I decided I had better read the other Wimpy-Kid-ish books out there too. This one was much better. Nate is hardly a role model, but he's a decent kid who seems to get in trouble easily. The book basically covers one day at Nate's elementary school. There's no mom in his family, which is unusual, and there are lots of awful teachers, which are unfortunately pretty common in kids' books. I didn't laugh out loud often, but I smiled a lot. Good for upper-elementary kids.

I think I had realistic expectations for this book, and I definitely don't mind fluffy, real-life stuff. Nikki is just awful. And inconsistent. There are just a few glimpses of what might make her different from the popular girls she hates, but mostly she's as superficial and unkind as they are. I didn't even want the guy to like her. 
 I'm trying to think of something nice to say. The drawing are sort of cute. There are a few funny moments. 
 I know these are really popular. But it's going to be hard for me to suggest them now that I've actually read one.

Loved the Penderwicks. The book has such an old-fashioned feel (including the cover); I think though adults might like it because it reminds them of their own childhoods, kids will still enjoy the adventure, humor, family relationships, and romance. Perfect summer read. 
 I was a tiny bit thrown off by an unclear sense of time. I imagine the author wanted it to be modern but timeless, but there were only a few things that set it in current day, which almost just made it more confusing. There's no reason this story couldn't have happened in present day, but it mostly seemed like it wasn't.

A funny, if unrealistic, quick picture book with cute kindergarteners. My kids like how the cat says different things with its meow. But what gets me each time is this line: 
 "She's furry, she's floppy, 
 Like a raggedy doll, 
 And her paws are all fluffy, 
 Like cotton balls. 
 That doesn't really rhyme. And the rhythm is sometimes off with other rhymes too. I find this annoying.
Really great for slightly older kids that will get the humor. My son (five) laughed so hard at her pet shoe (and its name) that he didn't breathe for almost a minute.
The photography and design of this book are beautiful, and there aren't many (or any?) other good books explaining texture to young kids.

I love David Hyde Pierce and thought there were some witty plays on words in this classic, but the audio just didn't work for me. I think it's because I need more plot and action when I'm listening, so certain books, like this one, are better read. I do wonder how many kids understand the humor in here. I listened to one disc out of four.

I re-read this for a book club and loved it more than I remember loving it the first time. In fact, I re-read it because I couldn't remember the plot, though the setting and mood stayed with me. And the plot is great - I just have a terrible memory. Adventure, mysterious pasts, resilience, trust, destiny - all set in Paris with very cool illustrations. I need to remember this for reader's advisory. I don't know who wouldn't enjoy it, really.

This was just fine - a girl moves from India to Iowa with her immediate family, misses home, adjusts to life in a new country, and deals with a mean girl in her class. I was hoping for a little more depth and originality, and maybe something about Iowa City to set it apart from every town (since I've lived there, and it has lots of great things about it). I liked the sections set in India more than the parts in the U.S. Decent suggestion for upper-elementary multicultural assignments.

A good book to suggest for 4th-6th graders looking for something with adventure and humor. I liked the silliness, but some of the scenarios were unlikely to the point of ridiculousness (a kid throws teachers' cars around the parking lot and there's no mention of it later, like that might have been a problem for a few people?). 
 I didn't finish this, but only because I know enough about it to do a booktalk and I had some books come in on hold.
A nice story - the writing is good and it addresses immigration issues sensitively but realistically. Those who like books about friendship and dogs will like it too.

Funny, very short chapters where Scieszka tells childhood stories. It has sort of a "Christmas Story" reminiscent feel to it, and I suspect adults possibly would like it more than kids, though there's enough to keep boys in particular entertained. I might read the "Car Trip" chapter - a puke domino effect story - at school visits this spring.

It's the summer before third grade, and Eleanor is so sad because her favorite babysitter Bibi moves away. But the summer passes by - making lemonade, waiting for letters, and preparing for the new school year. This is a sweet book with some touching moments, but I'm not sure how excited kids will be about it. I think girls at a similar point in life will think it's a nice read.

I don't normally review little kids' books, but I'd like to start including the ones I truly love. This series of board books is adorable, and I think their simple and sweet approach to concepts like bravery and sharing will be welcomed by parents of toddlers.

Sweet illustrations, reminiscent of Hugo Cabret (I was surprised to learn that Cole also illustrates Katy Duck). But despite exciting events and an intriguing historical context, I thought the story was dull. It's a mouse. I guess I've never really been into animal stories, and I haven't read many.

I've heard that this mystery is popular, though it doesn't seem to go out that well at our library (I don't think the cover on the hardback is very appealing). It seems like it'd be most popular with 5th to 7th-grade girls. Set primarily at a private Catholic school in Manhattan, it has an accessible, fluffy writing style, as if your 7th-grade best friend is talking to you. The main characters are smart, and it introducing some math and literature concepts as part of the mystery. A little romance in there too, pretty standard stuff.

Absolutely, wonderful! This book is the embodiment of a timeless classic in children's literature, a book that you can enjoy, and then enjoy again when reading it to your child. This is the story of a brave young mongoose adopting and then saving a family from the threat of the cobras living in the garden. My son and I read the book and watched the film adaptation together--the only negative is that my son is now convinced we need a mongoose just like Rikki-Tikki-Tavi! 
 -Alexis S.
Gaiman's at it again. I remember this story from years ago but this updated addition with gorgeous illustrations really makes it.

Honestly I think of this as an all ages book. Great more unusual addition for a baby shower library (a few to grow into are a must), good for K and elementary story times, and if you want a picture book for grads, get this instead of oh the places you'll go ;)
It was a good solid 4 stars for me. My 8 year old gave it a resounding 10 out of 10 though, and can't wait to get stuck into the second book.

Dari awal melihat pengarangnya, Saya langsung menyambar buku ini dan bergegas ke kasir. Philip Pullman mungkin lebih terkenal dengan bukunya Golden compass. Tapi saya melihat buku2 cerita anak-anak karangannya yang singkat lebih menarik. Kalau di buku "I was a rat" Ia membuat sisi lain dari cerita dongeng cinderella dan kejutan di akhir ceritanya. Dan di buku firework maker's daughter Ia membuat cerita anak dengan menggabungkan elemen dari berbagai kebudayaan. Di buku ini Pullman membuat gaya bercerita yang lain,menggabungkan tulisan dan komik. Komik disini bukan bersifat sebagai ilustrasi, coba lewatkan beberapa, niscaya anda akan kehilangan jalan cerita. 
 Selain itu humor-humor khas Pullman membuat saya tertawa beberapa kali. Salah satunya adalah kutipan-kutipan "singkat" yang muncul tiap awal bab. Bahkan ia mengkutip buku ini sendiri he..he. 
 Ceritanya sendiri sangat singkat, dan bisa dibaca dengan ringan. Cerita tentang 3 bersaudara yang ingin melarikan diri dari tempat panti asuhan mereka. Sekilas pada awalnya nuansa Oliver Twist dari Dickens mewarnai buku ini (panti asuhan, East end, pengasuh antagonis, penjahat pencopet), tapi dengan gaya bercerita Pullman seolah hal itu menjadi kocak.
We used this in class to have a class debate (Opinion spectrum) on this question: Is Frederick a good citizen? Great conversation was created for the roles and values of contribution.

3.5 stars 
 Hugo's story is a good way to teach kids about having a good self-esteem and to be happy with the way they are. Hugo is a happy star fish who likes making others feel happy, but when he's granted a few wishes he decides he wants to change a few thing he doesn't like about himself. Hugo learns a great lesson and once those changes are made he wishes he could be himself again. 
 With it's cute, brightly colored pages, Hugo will teach kids to be happy just being themselves. The only compliant I have is I felt the Spanish translation were really random through out the story. I would have loved to see the translations on every page and not just in the middle of some of the sentences or on certain pages. This is a great story that will each kids to have a good self-esteem and like Hugo learned, they too will realize they're special just the way they are.
"You must do something to make the world more beautiful."
eh
Cute stories,each with their own message, and activities too!

Un tres bon livre pour donner le gout de la lecture aux enfants !

My son found Truckery Rhymes and the library and insisted that we take it home - I'm glad we did! It's a fantastic little book of alternative lyrics for well-known nursery rhymes, all having to do with trucks. "Ring Around the Rosie" becomes "Swing Around with Rosie" about Rosie the wrecking ball crane, for example. 
 My son really enjoyed the truck-based lyrics, and I loved the little jokes - the places where the rhythm is disrupted for comedic effect, for example. The illustrations are gorgeous and have really captivated my 2.5 year old son. Each image is very lively and interesting. 
 I also appreciate the gender balance in the book. Most truck-based books are marketed towards boys and don't have any female vehicles - or, if they do, the female vehicles aren't very interesting (I'm looking at you, Sally from Cars). But here, there are a few female trucks - only one of which is pink. They are strong (Rosie is a wrecking ball crane!), they are active, and there is nothing to separate them from the male trucks. 
 So far, we've only had the book a few hours, but we've already read it through at least half a dozen times. I definitely recommend it!

I rather enjoyed this book, although at first I wondered how a "children's" book could be so long. Turns out that it's actually two stories. These stories are quite readable and engaging. 
 These two stories are different yet at the same time by the time one reaches the end of the second story, the "ring" becomes very much like the "Samayyad."The four siblings of the first story also become very much like the three siblings and one friend of the second story. (Perhaps I should state that the other way round.) 
 That being said, I enjoyed the idea that there's real magic in the world visible to some but not to others while at the same time having very real consequences. Those consequences are much more realistic and much less sugar-coated than one would find in a similar story written in more recent times. 
 I also think that I liked these two stories because of the many similarities to the Chronicles of Narnia, especially "The Magician's Nephew." 
 I definitely recommend this book.

I really enjoyed this book. A fantastical middle-grade read, The Dreamsnatcher takes the reader deep into an enchanted world. With magic, riddles and a family of quirky gypsies, it was impossible to put this book down. A truly fantastic debut by the amazing Abi Elphinstone! 
 The story follows twelve-year-old Moll Pecksniff and her wildcat, Gryff, as they try stop an evil witch doctor from stealing the old magic of the forest. But as more and more witch doctors appear, the dark forces grow stronger... and thanks to an ancient prophecy that states Moll and Gryff are the only ones capable of stopping this evil, they are now the witch doctors main targets... 
 I was really drawn in by the world building of this book. The atmosphere of the gypsy camp, the creepiness of the witch doctors lair, both really captured my imagination. It was virtually impossible to put this book down. Each chapter was short, action packed and full of intrigue and mayhem. A truly delicious read. 
 Moll is a spunky, tough talking heroine. She hides her doubts behind a witty facade and I couldn't help but like her immediately. In this story we see her bravery, loyalty and determination to protect all that she loves. I can't wait to meet her again in the second book. 
 The other characters are all a motley, mismatched cast of strange and interesting people. Earthworm tamers, fortune tellers, joint-dislocating men... lets just say Moll's gyspy family certainly won't bore you. I also like how you see just enough of each character to develop compassion for them which made the show-down at the end all the more dramatic. 
 But the Evil Doers... wow. Skull made a truly fantastic villain. His description, his personality and the dismal eeriness of his lair, everything was written so well. The creatures he created, the whole idea of the dreamsnatch (manipulating people as they sleep), not to mention the cryptic riddles and prophecies surrounding him... Skull not only kept Moll on her toes, but he kept the plot moving forward too. He and the other witch doctors really added spice to the story. 
 All in all this is a gripping, fast paced read that would be loved by anyone in search of a good adventure, with a bit of fantasy and magic thrown in. 5 stars!

This book made me break the promise I made to myself that I wouldn't be reading any of my treasured and oh-so-loved books until the end of the 20-month period I had given myself to "focus on my studies". But after several weeks of not reading, nothing changed. I was still facing the same problems I had, I was still rushing on every deadline and still sleeping on my every attempt to do anything productive. So when I saw this book I just decided to just screw that "20-month challenge" and read as I pleased. I therefore conclude that I could not last without books and any attempt to hinder myself from reading would be futile so I would never dare try next time. 
 So what does this senseless rambling say about The Little Prince? 
 I had tried to deprive myself of life's little pleasures, and I ended up not happy. It is really tiring to try and live a "grown-up" life. Dear Little Prince, I thank you for your wisdom. Plenty of things are missed in life because we are focusing on the wrong things. I am not saying this as an excuse to not do well in school, this is not about that. I just think that we'd do better if we keep doing what makes us happy, and it is not right to blame these little things because we can't see the direct benefit it could give us. Indeed, as what the fox once said, "It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye."
