My children (ages 10 & 11) and I started reading Ghost Dog Secrets as a bedtime story. Everyone in our family is a dog-lover so when the kids found out Ghost Dog Secrets was on both Division lists for the Lovelace Award it was the first one they chose for our family storytime. After finishing Chapter 7 both kids asked if we could stop reading because they were both completely bored. Honestly, I was also bored but I finished the book in order to give it a fair review. 
 It has a great title and a decent premise: boy loves dogs, boy wants a dog but can't have one, boy sees ghost dog which leads him to abused dog, boy rescues dog. The story, however, has several problems beginning with the fact that Rusty and his friend trespass on someone else's property in order to steal/rescue abused dog. This NEVER ends well in stories or in real life. I will also qualify my review by saying I have an EXTREMELY difficult time reading about abuse to children or animals (particularly dogs) and this story has many specific details of the dog Ra's abuse--too many for my taste. 
 The plot is predictable--you know how it's going to end by the close of the first chapter. That doesn't necessarily mean a book won't be good; the way a character gets to the ending is the engaging part of the story. In this case there are no surprises, no twists on the way to the ending. I was hoping the "ghost dog" aspect would provide that extra oomph in a tired plotline but, unfortunately, the ghost dog isn't present in the story enough to make any real difference. 
 Another reader who enjoys dog stories may enjoy Ghost Dog Secrets but for me (and my family) this one missed the mark by a mile. I would recommend One Dog and His Boy by Eva Ibbotson as a much superior story of boy rescuing dog.

a not so scary story that is more about a boy who saves an abused dog than it is about a ghost, although the ghost adds an element of suspense that younger readers would enjoy. Authentic characters and a well-paced plot that might surprise some readers. The action picks up quite a bit halfway through and stays compelling through the end. A good recommendation for Upper elementary boys (and girls) and could also work as a low-level high-interest read.

Flotsam was the first David Wiesner book I read and so far it remains my favorite. I have enjoyed most of his books and this one was excellent. It's an unusual Wiesner in that there's significant text, but the illustrations are amazing and on their own are able to tell the bulk of this story. 
 I love vegetables and I've never seen them in a story in such a creative and fantastic way, fantastic with every meaning of that word. I really enjoyed the humor; there's probably more that I found funny here than in any other Wiesner book I've read thus far. This is my fifth Wiesner book and, despite those initially disconcerting words, I think it's my second favorite of this author's, which is very high praise. I'm happy to see other Wiesner books I've yet to read, and I assume and hope that he continues to illustrate/write these wonderful books.

Neil Gaiman understands the basic underpinnings of most well-crafted fairy tales: there's an element of terror and danger, especially when an unhuman creature makes its appearance. Think of "Beauty and the Beast", "The Three Little Pigs" or "The Enchanted Pig". Animals who can talk human speech bear their own perils and a feeling of threat may be waiting in the wings or boldly present center stage. 
 In this bewitching, simple-seeming story about a talking tiger, a Rajah and Rani come to terms with their daughter's strangeness, that it's not a matter they can fix (especially with impractical gifts) and that a ferocious man-eating beast must be handled very carefully indeed. 
 The story resonates with quiet strength, beauty and a touch of humor. The illustrations are like cutouts, colorful and eye-popping. While the ending of the story hints of danger to the little princess, we can hope that she and her tiger found happiness together.

Igraine is a spunky type of heroine, stubborn to be sure but willing to listen to good advice. Her character is the sort that young girls will want to read as her tale deals with very real issues of kindly parents who are not all there (literally true as hers become enchanted pigs), an annoying superior older sibling and threats to the family home. While her problems are clothed in fairy tale trappings, with an evil sorcerer at the gates, annoyed dragons and a magic moat surrounding her decrepit castle, Igraine comes across as a fun, slightly rebellious, tender-but-tough, hoyden, one with a genuine interest in swordplay even as she finally concedes that magic has an important role to play as well. 
 Filled with charming black-and-white ink drawings throughout (including the Singing Books that are the objects of contention), "Igraine the Brave" is a delight for young readers as well as slightly older fans of Ms. Funke's darker novels.

Un libro infantil de lo mas bonito y que ensena muchas cosas. 
 Las historias de los pequenos monstruos son de los mas tiernas y entretenidas, aunque si es cierto que algunas son mas lindas que otras. 
 La historia de Argo muestra la importancia de perseverar. 5/5 
 La historia de Gigi muestra el valor de las segundas oportunidades. 3/5 
 La historia de Sunny ensena que siempre podemos aprovechar nuestros talentos para ayudar a los demas. 3/5 
 La historia de Halloween y sus amigos demuestra que la union logra cosas buenas. 3/5 
 La historia de Fluff-Puff demuestra que hasta lo que mas tememos puede terminar de nuestro lado. 4/5 
 En definitiva, este es un librito entretenido para pasar el rato, y los jueguitos del final son un plus.

This is a lovely book. I read it on a recommendation from a friend and am glad I did. When I first read it it made me sad. I felt bad for Miss Rumphius because she never had kids and I always feel a bit sad for people who don't have kids. Irrational, I know, but that's how feelings are. 
 The first time I checked it out from the library I wasn't terribly impressed. The illustrations are beautiful but the story didn't really speak to me and after reading it regularly and renewing it once I brought it back. That night DS5 asked me to read it. I told him I returned it to the library and his face fell. If you'd ever seen my kid's pathetic and adorable sad face you'd know why I went back and rechecked it out. He regularly requests it ad DS7 never fails to cuddle up while it is being read. 
 My kids have spent considerable time figuring out what they can do to make the world a better place. It's a deep conversation that I haven't seized the opportunity to have yet. My failing, not the book's. They want this one at bedtime and most nights I don't feel like an hour long conversation explaining abstract ideas to my literal children. 
 Some complaints, because I wouldn't be me if I didn't have some. I'm concerned about the way she chose to make the world more beautiful. I don't know anything about lupines, but the way they spread makes me concerned that they might perhaps be considered weeds by some. I have visions of giant fields of flowers attacking small children and tearing down houses, crowding out gardens and taking over the world. This eventually will lead to a conversation about being careful about what you plant, where you plant it, and why planting things all across the countryside might not be as wonderful as it sounds.
Has a rather Dr. Seuss-ish feel.

Baca waktu nginep di Penthouse Radal 
 Roos nyampulin buku, aku baca Jack hehe

I think my students will really enjoy this book! It held my interest and I found it exciting even though I was pretty sure how things would turn out. I would have liked to hear more from Gerald Jr. and what was going on in his world.

This is mostly a cute collection of little poems about witches, monsters, etc. However... 
 MAJOR WARNING TO ANYONE READING THIS BOOK TO YOUNG CHILDREN: 
 Stuck in the middle of this otherwise innocuous book is a story called "I'm Coming Up the Stairs" by Maria Leach which creeped me out...and my husband. Here's an even creepier audio version of it (because I didn't read it nearly this creepily). 
 We've morphed the story into a new game, but still...I wouldn't have read that one if I'd actually previewed the book.
Love Nancy Drew, but some are better then others and this is not one of my favorites in the series. To be Nancy with her fun car and great boyfriend Ned.

Saya banyak berkerut heran dan bingung atas tindakan-tindakan tokohnya. Polly yang percaya begitu saya (h. 52), Jim yang katanya takut ketinggian tapi berhasil mengalahkan Tweedle (h. 64-69), Mr. Killjoy dan Miss Gasket yang mudah dialihkan (h. 101-103), dan penyederhanaan-penyederhanaan lainnya. Lalu, gambar Jack di dalam juga tidak menggambarkan deskripsinya (katanya mengenakan pakaian seperti setan, tapi kok pakai topi tinggi kayak tukang sirkus? :<) 
 Lalu, saya baru ingat bahwa ini buku anak-anak. Yang disasar adalah anak kecil. Yah, berarti tidak seharusnya saya bersikap terlalu keras pada buku ini, kan? 
 Secara keseluruhan, bacaan yang menyenangkan. :D 
 Ulasan lebih panjang ada di blog.

This book almost seemed to tie up the story begun in book 1 perfectly. I have no desire to read book 3. 
 Will Henry find his real family? - answered 
 Will Frank get home? - answered 
 Will Nimiane be defeated? - answered 
 Will Henrietta ever stop being a pain? - not answered, ha ha 
 It was fun to see some of the ideas from book 1 get developed, too. For instance, Endor went from being a witch prison to being the world of the undead crazy wizards. Very interesting. Darien was interesting, too. His self-loathing fascinated me. It was nice to have an antagonist who wasn't a megalomaniac for a change. 
 Anyway, great book. I might read book 3 down the line.

Story: 2.0 
 Pictures: 4.5 
 My almost 3-yr-old was captivated by the tiger pictures -pretty much all this book has going for it. The story is weak. Doesn't stand up to memorable titans like "O, the Places You'll Go!" and "How the Grinch Stole Christmas" ;or modern greats like "Floatsam" and "Journey" ;or even the beloved yet IMO meh, "Where the Wild Things Are." 
 I'm always on the lookout for a great children's picture book to share with my boy, and Gaiman has yet to produce one. But, as always, I will read anything and everything that man writes. He has earned that.

Rodney has a lot of energy! So much energy that he winds up getting in trouble at school sometimes. He loves the outdoors and exploring. However, he isn't thrilled about their class field trip to the park. Parks are dirty, decrepit spaces in his neighborhood. Rodney learns the true meaning of the word majestic when they visit a metro park. This book is a gentle reminder to get outside and enjoy our metro parks and quiet green spaces. The illustrations by Floyd Cooper are gorgeously expressive.
Loved,loved,loved,
loved it in the 4th grade!
anyone with a dog in their life needs to read this wonderful little book-especially fun to read out loud.
Some clever tricks and detecting done by the villains and the boys.
I enjoyed this mystery just as much as the first. I look forward to reading even more!
Such a fun read! The value of telling the truth through imagination and ninjas!

For anyone who played rock, paper, scissors in their life, they will enjoy this book. The value of friendship and in being proud of who you are. The best part is it gives you the rules for the new game: Cowboy, ninja, bear!

This perfectly pitched novel about a young black boy's musical journey out of grief after the death of his beloved Cool Papa is pure gold. Funny, smart and full of authentic middle school moments that made me nod in recognition on almost every page, it has the added personal bonus of being set in Queens and the neighborhood where I work in Manhattan. What a delightful, timely addition to RWG's already stupendous body of work.

This tale of a hirsute, half Sikh, half Methodist sixth grader torn between two friends and two religions is both timely and universal. Since her beloved Dadima died, Karma has felt unmoored. Mom is working all the time, Daddy is home too much and her older brother rarely leaves his room. Best friend Sara seems to be leaving Karma behind as she embarks on a friendship with new cool girl Lacy, and suddenly Karma has no one to talk to about seventeen dark hairs that have suddenly sprouted on her upper lip. What happens when Karma tries to fix both her karma and her mustache is middle grade gold. A deeply satisfying read that will resonate with young readers struggling wth puberty and friendship changes.

A charming slice of Mid-western middle school life, as translated by a lovable young man who is always one step behind the curve. His reactions to the death of his grandfather, the realization that a family member is gay and the acceptance of a differently abled classmate are sweet and realistic. I'm considering it for 5th grade read aloud.
Everything I wanted it to be and more. Better than Pax but perfect read-alike for fans.

Meh. Despite the hype, it didn't move me and I'm a KD fan. Some very nice sentences to be sure, but It seemed a little quirky for quirky's sake. The three main characters felt like adult archetypes wrought small. I kept thinking Raymie=Carrie, Beverly=Miranda, Louisiana=Charlotte.

"I remember thinking that my reading differences were like dragging a concrete block around every day and how I felt sorry for myself. Now I realize that everyone has their own blocks to drag around. And they all feel heavy." Wise words from a well rendered character who perseveres over bullies, tough circumstances at home, and her undiagnosed dyslexia with the help of a perceptive teacher. This title will be right at home on the shelf next to Wonder and Shug.

The hype is true. I was skeptical about half way through (a little too much Incredible Journey, one of my most hated childhood reads) then Vola explains "two not two" and I was IN IT. The ending is satisfying and cyclical. ALL THE LOVE.

A well written and timely tale of a transgender 4th grader trying to navigate her way towards telling everyone around her the truth about her identity. I applaud Alex Gino for not sugar coating how cruel kids can be behind adult backs, and think the tone is right on for grade level.

This magnificent story of an autistic girl and her beloved dog deserves all five of its starred reviews. Make no mistake, this is a first rate tearjerker and while I did indeed cry, Rose's painstakingly logical voice kept me from losing it too much. I haven't felt this way about a book since The One and Only Ivan and hope this one will find just as large of an audience. Keep the Kleenex and your dog close while reading.
At Reading Rants: http://www.readingrants.org/2013/07/1...

This story of a second grader's school year, related through his experiences with the key people on his life: Teacher, Father, Sister, Mother, is just right. Billy, his sister, friends and the caring adults that inhabit his small orbit are rendered darn near perfectly and provide a rich, warm portrait of a child's inner life. The short, meaty sentences are thoughtfully constructed, and it feels like not a word is wasted in this just over 200 page beginner novel for young fans of Ramona or Clementine. Or anyone who was ever 7.
Re-read after seeing it for sale on Kindle. Still just as good as when I was 11. Remember "One-Ball Reilly" ? How did Lois Lowry get away with THAT?
Super cute, and I loved the illustrations, but I wonder if the humor and vocab might be a twee bit advanced for the target audience.

This is a heart book. I love it deeply, probably because I relate far too much to Stella, who believes in the healing power of housekeeping and is a studious rule follower and because it is packed full of one of my favorite types of description: everyday domestic detail, especially as it pertains to cleaning and eating. Stella's voice is real and true and brought me to tears more than once. My new favorite for the Newbery, in a year already stuffed with juvenile literary goodness!

I liked this one even better than the first: tighter, grosser and a little less narrator. It's awesome to read aloud parts as a book tease. After reading just the intro to the first one aloud, my 5th graders have been lining up to read both Gidwitz titles with gruesome glee, totally delighting in the icky parts.

Rebecca Stead's books are like an onion--as the layers are peeled away and the characters reveal their secrets, the reader is left with a shiny nugget of essential truth. In this case, the truth is that pretending only keeps sadness at bay for so long. Seventh grader Georges is pretending that it's okay that his dad got laid off and his family had to sell their house and move to an apartment in Brooklyn. He's pretending that the school bullies that make fun of his name aren't really hurting his feelings. But most of all, he's pretending that he doesn't miss his mom (at least, not that much) who must work extra nursing shifts at the hospital to make up for his dad losing his job. But Georges is not the only one pretending. Safer, his new neighbor, is a homeschooled amateur spy who is also doing some heavy-duty pretending. The unusual friendship they forge, steeped in secrecy and sweetened by Safer's hilarious little sister Candy, will force both boys to stop pretending and face the truth about their hopes and fears. 
 Wild parrots, Scrabble tiles and Giant Swee-Tarts are just a few of the little details that season Stead's story and make this read so unique. As someone who feels like she had read the same 5 books over and over, this book is a treat in that it continued to surprise me as I peeled away the layers. Stead is also incredibly adept at showing the secret lives of children, which any twelve year old could tell you are completely separate from the lives of adults and come with their own set of complicated emotional vocabulary. Stead is like an accomplished spy in the House of Kids, spinning complex, quietly powerful stories from what she observes there. And I for one am very grateful for her powerful binoculars! An absolute must-read. Fantastic.

What a sweet little read. This story of a strip mall gorilla and the baby elephant he tries to save from a staid existence worse that death is both poignant and exhilarating. Just like certain humans, Ivan the gorilla, trapped in a poor man's mall zoo, refuses to feel his feelings and will only allow himself to express emotion through drawing with the finger paints or crayons provided by the night janitor's sensitive daughter. But when baby elephant Ruby moves in to the cage next to his, Ivan must come to terms with the life he lost and use his artistic skills to win freedom for both of them. Lessons of love, connection, memory and hope abound. I was terrified to read this book, because animal stories make me weep. This one was no different, but I'm glad I was able to overcome my crying phobia long enough to make it to the ultimately rewarding ending. If this isn't a 2013 Newbery contender, I'll eat my hat.

A strong first novel told in distinct voices. The unusual topic and intricate look at middle school politics forces middle grade readers to hold a mirror up to their character and see if they are part of the problem or part of the solution. A few parts are a bit treacly for this adult reader, especially the heart-warming speech by the school director at the end, but it will leave kids with something to chew on. As soon as I finished it, I promptly started reading it aloud to my 5th graders. And even if we don't finish, the short episodic chapters allow me to pick a good place to stop, and will ensure that this will probably be their first choice for summer reading!
Read for professional review.
Road tested on the 6th graders and the 7th graders in galley. They loved it, especially the interactive meowing.
Read for professional review.

Wonderful first 100 pages or so--fully realized 5th grade characters, realistic relationships and angst. Then, it all goes downhill after the tragic accident that changes the classroom and the all the kids in it. They begin to articulate platitudes and lessons learned that sound less like 5th grade kids and more like a well-meaning adult writing a childrens' book. Kids aren't dumb. They'll get the meaning, even if you spell it out for them. I was sad to see the story crash and burn after such a promising beginning.

A tongue-in-cheek retelling of some of the grimmer of Grimms' tales. I enjoyed the sarcastic voice-over of the unseen narrator, although it's hard to say whether kids will find it as amusing as adult readers. I also thought it was clever how the author used the characters of Hansel and Gretel as a narrative thread to tie all the stories together. Well executed.

** spoiler alert ** 
 A well-paced and solidly written supernatural thriller that makes an excellent read-alike to Coraline--readers will find parallels between the spooky houses, talking cats and smart tween heroines w/distant parents. There are some genuinely scary moments that may be too much for a 4th grader but that a 6th grader will shudder at and appreciate. 
 This title would have earned one more star from me had there not been a section where our intrepid girl Olive is given the entire backstory of the creepy house by one of the talking cats. One of my pet peeves--please, no lengthy explanation from other characters, I want the main character to discover the secrets on her own! Still, a great choice for middle school students looking for a "scary" book that isn't TOO scary.

Four 5th graders from very different backgrounds form a lasting friendship when they band together against the class mean girl. Lauren Myracle gets the middle school drama just right, sharply focusing in on all the little hurts and slights that seem so huge to the tween tribe. The varied group of characters ensures that any young female reader will be able to find someone to identify with. Camilla, she of the two moms who sparked the Scholastic book fair boycott last year, was my hands down favorite, as her worries about everything from boys to the sky falling ruefully reminded me of my own inability to tame my tangled mind. The short chapters, two-colored pages, IM format and sweet cover have made this an easy sell to my middle school girl students.
Read to prepare for author visit to school. Perfect tween fare, a delightful and engaging middle school mystery that would pair well with the Enola Holmes series or Shakespeare's Secret.

Assigned reading for the tween media literacy grad class I am co-teaching. What do I like best? The progressive school setting that is reminiscent of the school where I currently teach. What do I like least? The slow pacing. Gorgeous writing and great detail, but could have been cut down by 1/3.

First week's reading assignment in the "Tween Media Literacy" I am co-teaching. Pitch-perfect middle grade fare, with enough snarky laughs for adult readers as well. I snickered and snorted my way through this one. An absolute riot on the surface, with many absolute truths about the middle school mind-set expertly threaded through.
Read for professional review.
Read for professional review.
Read for professional review.

After experiencing the unthinkable, eleven year old Aubrey must put the pieces of her shattered life back together with the help of her loving grandma, best friend Bridget, and her blue Beta fish Sammy. A beautifully constructed first novel on the topic of mourning for tweensters. Really well done for the age group and a perfect recommendation for all middle school "crying girls" who love Kira Kira.

Kate DiCamillo's quiet new novel of hope, finding home and forgiveness is more along the lines of The Tiger Rising than Because of Winn Dixie, but her assured, wistful prose remains the same. In the wintery town of Baltese, a magician mistakenly conjures an elephant instead of a bunch of lilies, crushing one audience member's legs and getting himself thrown in prison for his efforts. A small boy named Peter is told by a fortune teller that the elephant holds the key to the mystery of his missing sister. The elephant herself just wants to go home but has no idea how to get there. The magician, boy and elephant are joined by a cast of other lost and broken characters, each looking in their own way to be healed. A tranquil, well-executed little fable about finding our missing pieces. Lovely. Coming September '09.
Read for professional review.
Mary Stolz sympathetically explained how bullies are made, not born.
Didn't everyone try to learn to see through things using the flame trick like Henry Sugar?
My favorite chapter is when Mitch finally realizes that reading can be fun. Clearly perfectly captures the everyday wonder of that moment for all of us.
My personal favorite RD book. I wanted to live in a cozy gypsy caravan like Danny.
The under appreciated red headed step sister of Harriet the Spy. Just as good, and in many ways, better.
Jimmy learns Braille and how to work with a seeing eye dog. I was transfixed.
Great examination of middle school politics and still walks off the shelf with my 5th graders.
What girl didn't want to join Katie John's Boy Hating Club of America in sixth grade?

I just introduced this stellar series to a fourth grade Little House reader and she came back with stars in her eyes. Ella, Henny, Charlotte, Sarah, Gertie and Charlie, the sweetest little family on the Lower East Side, you did it again.
One of the best books about the awkwardness of adolescence, hands down. Authentic teenage feelings, all the way from 1969. Geez.
Best Fat Camp Book Ever. I borrowed this one from my church library and just never returned it. Sorry, Mrs. Bergin.

Oh Marcy, could I love you more? This book helped me and a lot of other girls accept what we looked like and who we were. I especially like this cover (the one I own) as that is EXACTLY what I imagine Marcy to look like!

This delectable little treat took about half an hour to read and was absolutely charming. Young fans of Ratatouille will adore it (there is a cooking cat instead of rat) and the loose pencil drawings reminded me of Quentin Blake. It would make a fine readaloud for 4th/5th grade.
I read this with my daughter and she loved it. It's a charming chapter book with stunning illustrations. I recommend it for anyone wanting an unusual read. Igrane is a truly lovable protagonist.

I have read many reviews of this book offering high praise and thought it was about time I read it too. I'm glad I did. 
 dream 
 The Dream Snatcher tells the story of an orphaned gypsy girl called Moll who lives among other gypsies in a mysterious forest. Skull, an evil witchdoctor in the camp across the river, wants Moll dead. She embarks on a quest to find lost talismans that can help her defeat Skull's evil plans. 
 As the tale moves, Moll finds out more and more about her lost parents. The writing is enchanting and the relationships Moll has with her best friend, Siddy, the dubious Alfie and her wild cat, Griff are well rounded and engaging. The imagery in the book(dark forest, ancient riddles, voodoo, etc) together with the fiery, determined and endearing nature of Moll, make this a wonderful book for children. At it's heart it is a story about good against evil that children will love and understand. 
 It might be a little scary at times for younger ones. Skull does want Moll dead and the forest can be a dangerous place and Skull is a truly menacing antagonist. But kids love that sort of thing too and I don't think it's overdone. 
 The story has a fairy tale feel to it and an electric pace that just keeps the pages turning. I particularly liked the subliminal message that gypsies are the good guys. It's about time that commonly held prejudices against travellers are excised from our psyche. 
 Highly recommended.
This is a wonderful book that I have read and re-read to my children. It is about a lovely old lady who plants lupines all over.
Short and sweet inspiring story of making the world a better place :)

I downloaded The Land of Broken Time as a free book from Amazon. This cute children's story contains a few words young kids may not understand (i.e. pince-nez), but the illustrations are colorful and interesting, and the plot is easy to follow. It may be enjoyable to children who like adventure stories in the vein of Treasure Island and Peter Pan. This would make a good bedtime read for parents and children.

I received a copy of the Secret of the Sacred Scarab from the author. The gift did not determine the rating or my review. While I prefer adult complexity for my usual reading, this excellent light-hearted YA offering was a fun read with lots of fast-paced action that's sure to engage the young reader. I loved the travels thru Egypt and look forward to reading the next book of the series.

The ARC was given to me in exchange for an honest review. Oh my goodness! What a cute book. I loved the illustrations and the rhyming storyline. Kudos to the author for the two moms in the household! I thoroughly enjoyed this wonderful book!
One of my favorite books as a child and potentially my first role-model. I still go crazy every time I find a hillside full of lupines.

A princess who is blind also doesn't speak. Her parents, the Rajah and the Rani, offer a place in the palace and other rewards to anyone who can get Cinnamon to talk. Though the kingdom is remote, people journey there to try but no one was successful. The one day a talking tiger came to the palace and offered to help. Though everyone was frightened, Cinnamon's parents allowed the tiger to try. Using a series of experiences like pain, fear and love, the tiger proceeded to tell Cinnamon stories. The next morning, the princess was able to talk but things don't quite go according to plan. 
 Gaiman excels at writing books with a deep ambiguity and no pressure to have a moral or lesson at the end. This book has exactly that and it is why the book works to very well. He embraces the questions, allows the wonder to simply be there, and twists the story away from where traditional tales would end and towards a more shifting place that allows more dreaming. 
 The illustrations firmly place this book of a mythical India. Filled with rich colors, they have a distinct flatness to them that works well with a folktale subject like this. They are also filled with small details that adds a delicacy and luxuriance to the images. 
 Great illustrations bring this book previously only available on audio into the world of children and stories. Appropriate for ages 6-9.

Duck has lost his new blue socks. He searches in his box, but they aren't there. He asks his friend Fox who hasn't seen them either. Perhaps Ox knows where his socks are? Ox remembers seeing some socks down by the rocks. But those socks are purple, not blue socks, and they aren't new either. Finally, Duck asks a group of peacocks about his socks. And they do know where his socks are! It turns out they are in a most surprising place! 
 Bunting has written a picture book in rhyme that dances along to a jaunty beat. The rhymes are merrily done, done in a humorous way. She makes it all look so easy and effortless, but rhyming picture books are some of the most difficult to do well. Kudos to Bunting for maintaining the joy in simple rhymes. Her words read aloud well and are also simple enough for beginning readers to tackle. 
 Ruzzier's illustrations are the key to young readers spotting the blue socks which are slowly revealed as the book progresses. Expect eagle-eyed children to figure out the answer even before the adults. Ruzzier fills Duck's world with lots of clutter from starfish to soccer balls to underwear. Done in ink and watercolor, the colors are bright and add to the surreal nature of the story itself. 
 Socks lost and then found, rhymes and rhythms, and a delight of a read aloud to share, this book has it all! Appropriate for ages 3-5.

This is another joyous book by the master of YA, Daniel Pinkwater. While the cover has a unique style, it is actually the third installment of a series, the first being the Neddiad, followed by the Yggyssey. Here the main character is the Cat Whiskered girl, who goes off on an adventure in the human world. It's what you expect from Pinkwater. Lots of mystery and danger, and a fun adventure for all everyone involved.

A fairly well written SF book for the ya market. My daughter enjoyed it, which says something since she's not a big SF fan. Also, I think this book is unique because its 1st person narrative POV is a little alien named Chorkle. Putting yourself in the shoes, er, alien feet of the main character is fun. The ending is a major cliffhanger, which is okay but in some ways is too much of a tease. I would rather read the second book because the characters and story were totally engrossing, not because the ending leaves a major plot line unresolved. Anyway, I don't want to sound negative. If you have young kids 5-12 that like SF, it's a good book. Get a copy.

Like many Pinkwater books, it starts off weird and gets weirder as you read on. The story: Walter Galt and Winston Bongo, they're two regular boys (sort of) who sneak out of their homes to watch late night movies. What could go wrong? They soon meet a girl, Bently Saunders Harrison Mathews (nicknamed Rat), who's introduces them to her uncle Flipping Hades Terwilliger, after which things steadily go off course. 
 From my perspective, the characters are great. Full of surprises, just reading their names are a laugh. But the story draws you in soon enough. It involves a kidnapping, pro-wrestlers, and giant avocados. You get the idea. With the help of the world's greatest detective, the small gang is challenged to find out who's the kidnapper, and what they want with Rat's uncle. 
 The only negative thing I can comment on is content that "might" be considered politically incorrect by today's uptight standards. Nothing major. Some ethnic jokes and political jibes that may not appeal to everyone. Don't get me wrong, tough. I loved it.

An incredible compilation of books. Pinkwater proves, yet again, that he is a master storyteller for young adults. Each book enclosed is full of wacky characters and humor. No point going into detail here, I will comment on each individual book on this site. The only strange thing about this book is the YA novel tucked in at the end. It's clearly for an older audience, so I was unable to read it to my child. I suppose it's one way to publish a book. However, I believe parents would be better served if the age level of all books in this Omnibus were the same. I'm not complaining though. I will just have to come back to that book at a later time, when my child is a bit older. Something to look forward to.

Another Pinkwater classic! Rare is a book that tries to teach art appreciation, and this story pulls it off in a natural way that won't scare off kids. And like many of his other books, Pinkwater mixes mystery, learning and wacky fun into a delightful tale. Surely, all readers will get the urge to buy colored chalks and begin drawing on the nearest sidewalk. You have been warned.

This is a fine second installment of the series. I'm not sure I love the idea that Neddie is no longer the first person narrator, but that's no big deal. And while the Pinkwater wacky world generator is going full tilt, it seems very much like an Alice in Wonderland tale. This surely would make a nice movie one day, with all sorts of weird creatures and giant talking heads. I loved the imagery. 
 Highly recommended as good bedtime reading with kids.

This book starts out simple enough. A young boy named Victor from a semi-dysfunctional family, left at home without any supervision. So when musical lizards show up on TV after hours, a mystery begins to unfold. It involves a strange man with a chicken under his hat and late night horror films. Victor can't say what it all means, but he's gonna find out. 
 My daughter enjoyed reading this together with me before bed. It's a a wonderful Pinkwater tale. One where the story takes on dreamlike qualities and draws the reader into a magical world. At times, nothing makes sense, but that's okay because just like life, everything seems to work out somehow.
My daughter and I enjoyed this very much. Not only fun, it's full of historical facts that span all sorts of topics. A mystical wacky adventure story for all ages.

I read this book to my daughter and she liked it a great deal. It's full of Pinkwater zaniness and made us laugh out loud many times. It also contains some nice themes: Fear not what you don't understand; violence is not a solution; playing with mother nature is not dangerous; respect your parents. Overall, a great book for kids.

I've lived my life loving the animated Disney movie, so I was excited to read the story that inspired it all. My copy of this story is illustrated by Walter Crane, and it looks like an illuminated manuscript. Each page of text is framed by roses and leaves, and the periodic full-page illustrations are very detailed. 
 This version, while different from the Disney movie we all love, is still quite magical. Beauty's father has lost everything he has to pirates. One day he learns that one of his ships has been recovered and journeys to town to claim what's rightfully his. Before he leaves he asks each of his daughters what they would like him to bring back for them. All Beauty wants is a rose. So, father sets out on his journey only to find that his partners have divvied up all his possessions because they thought he was dead. He heads back home, depressed, defeated, and even more broke than he was before he left. He presses on through the cold, winter night and falls ill. He ends up in the beast's castle, where he is nursed back to health. As he leaves the castle for home, he picks a single rose for Beauty. This makes the beast very mad and he tells the old man that unless one of his daughters volunteers to live in the castle forever, the beast will kill him. When father returns home, of course Beauty volunteers because it was her silly request of a rose that got her father into trouble in the first place. Beauty lives with the beast and dreams of a handsome prince each night, who tells her to look past outside appearances and save him from his plight. Each day the beast proclaims his love for her and proposes marriage. For some reason, Beauty cannot make the connection and is convinced that a handsome prince is imprisoned somewhere in the castle. Oh, he is... He just might not be where she expects to find him. 
 Looking past outward appearances is a very common theme throughout this book, and I find it to be a timely message given today's expectations of what a person must look like in order to be worthwhile or successful or loved. However, it does bother me that there's a double standard. Beauty is noted as being beautiful-the most beautiful person in her family. The beast falls in love with her, but we are led to believe it's because she's beautiful. We're basically being told here that women should look past outward appearances and love unattractive men, but men can still require the highest of standards. Of course, this story was written in the 1750s. We've come a long way since then, but there is still this "women must look like this" stipulation today that I hope dies out with other things from the 1750's. Like Smallpox. And dying of pneumonia. 
 The writing is very antiquated and simplistic, but I loved reading the original story and comparing it to all the versions I've read and seen since then! I highly suggest you snag the free ebook and give this a read if you're a fan of today's Beauty and the Beast.

I didn't realize this was juvenile fiction when I downloaded it as an e-book from my library. I'm an adult and so it was a fast, uncomplicated but still interesting enough to hold my attention read. I liked the way the book was written to make kids think and challenge their thought process. I liked the way the grown-ups said or did the right thing (even though no one is quite that perfect) and the teachers and parents allowed the children to come to their own conclusions because I think it provided a good moral compass. I imagined lots of great classroom discussions if this book was a school assignment. 
 The story at first appears simple. A boy wants to rescue a dog he perceives as abused because it is chained up to a tree with no obvious shelter, food or water in the front yard of a house he passes by. He also sees a ghost dog no one else can see keeping company with the abused dog. The ghost dog visited the boy at night and in Lassie-like fashion tries to communicate an urgent message to the boy. The ghost dog part of the plot turned this into a good, fun ghost/campfire story and it was a great way to move the story forward. 
 There is a lot to learn about the world when you're young. The boy has to learn the proper way to report to animal control and substantiate the accusations. After he rescues the dog, he has to learn to care for the dog responsibly. He has other unexpected challenges at school and home to overcome and has to bravely face threats and his own fear. 
 Each day, sixth-grader Rusty feeds a dog that's left chained in the frigid weather with no shelter, food, or water. When he realizes the dog has been injured, he tries to have Animal Control help - but when that fails, Rusty and his friend Andrew unchain the dog and take it. With the dog in their hideout, the boys face multiple challenges, including Andrew's snoopy sister and the escalating threats of the dog's abusive owner. Even more challenging? The appearance of a ghost dog that appears in Rusty's room, and is trying to lead him to an even deeper secret. . . .
Let us be agreed that this is probably the best Nancy Drew book out there.

What a great little fantasy novel by one of the best storytellers in Sweden! I liked the beginning more than I liked the end. I had a hard time connecting the ending with the beginning, I'm not sure how to put the two together in one and the same story. And the narration techniques sadly faltered in the big resolution. However, it's still one of the best written Swedish fantasy novels for kids I've read so far. I love that Astrid doesn't compromise the writing style or the choice of words just because it's not a book primary for adults. Kids would do well with more great writing in their lives, there's no need to deny them that. I also value the difficult topics Astrid chose to talk about here. There's self-sacrifice for the greater good, bravery and excellent imagery on how negative thoughts can pollute everyone and everything around one as well. I mean, how many children's book have the spite to bring all this up? But who are we to say that kids won't understand that. Maybe, if the authors out there were half as good a writer as Astrid, they would. I think we ought to give the kids a chance at least.

Sv: Vilken komplex historia. Den lyckas med att vara bade vacker, kul och sorglig pa samma gang. Liksom skymningen tacker staden finns det en dimma av sorgsenhet over berattelsen. Tank dig att aldrig kunna ga ut sa att du maste forestalla dig varlden istallet for att uppleva varlden. Varlden ar en gava och att aldrig fa ta emot den gavan vore hemskt. Fran det perspektivet borjar jag tvivla pa att det har verkligen ar en glad historia. For mig liknar det snarare skrack. Ar det har en historia om formagan att kunna rymma genom fantasin? Ar det har en historia om att inte lata dina problem begransa dig eftersom de inte spelar nagon roll? Eller ar det helt enkelt en historia till for att hjalpa barnen att somna nar de motvilligt maste ga till sangs och pa sa vis kan kanna sig bundna? Jag ar inte saker. Men jag tror faktiskt att jag foredrar den verkliga varlden framfor Skymningslandet. 
 Eng: What a complex story. It manages to be both beautiful, fun and sad at the same time. Like the dusk are covering the city there is a mist of sadness over the story. Imagine never being able to go outside so that you have to imagine the world instead of experiencing the world. The world is a gift so to never receive it would be horrible. From that perspective, Im doubting this to be a very happy story at all. Somehow it sounds more like horror to me. Is this a story about the ability to escape through imagination? Is this a story about not letting your problems restrict you because they do not matter? Or is it simply a story to help children fall asleep when they reluctantly need to go to bed and in that way may feel tied up? I am not sure. But I do think I prefer the real world to the land of dusk.
