 Seeing Peg Kehret and hearing her talk make you adore this author and want to read more of her books. When I heard her speak at a local library recently, she was wearing a necklace with a charm from every state that has given her books a Young Reader award. She has at least 19 of them - probably more! Across the country, she is well-known and much-loved as a children's book author, not the least because many of her books feature cats or dogs. 
 This is book #52 from Peg Kehret - a record I can scarcely fathom. Hats off to you, Peg!

This is probably the best dystopian novel I have ever read. I skipped meals just so I could finish this book. There was not one time I felt bored of it. This is a great book for anyone who is planing on getting into dystopian novels.
It wasn't my favorite. I'm not a big realistic fiction fan. I find them not very interesting.

I remember checking this book out of the elementary school library perhaps twenty times. It tells the story of the history of the Earth as a play in several acts composed of scenes (eras and epochs). Needless to say, this book had a huge impact on the way I think about time and history, and it holds an honored place in my library. I recommend this book to kids, even if the folk art may turn them off at first. It is beautifully illustrated, and Burton obviously took great care to make sure the information was accurate (though be advised that much scientific knowledge has accrued since publication in the early 1960s).
Great Childhood book. So good that I laugh whenever the thought of it comes back up.

3.5 STARS, just average really, although I have to remember I'm a grown man reading a children's book so it obviously didn't cater to my audience in the first place, nevertheless a sweet story with a great message.
such a pointless end to the story sorry to say, some enjoyable parts but overall just crap for lack of a better word.
3.5 stars, pretty meh, but by no means awful.
terlalu banyak gambar...ceritanya memang khas anak-anak...tpi patut diteladani sikap tolong menolong dari karakter2 dalam buku tersebut..lumayan cemilan ringan :D

This is a sweet, and thought provoking story. The other reviews on Amazon are more about the comfort the story gave related to the loss of a loved one. I believe this story goes deeper. 
 So many times, we overlook the contributions of our children. We take it at face value, or as something that needs to be cleaned up without finding out why they colored on the wall or picked every flower in the garden. As a young, impatient mom I saw the annoying and the frustrating things more often than not. I blame it on a lack of sleep. I can appreciate their worth so much easier now that I am a grandmother. I can see what was meant to be a gift in what I once saw as frustrating. 
 It reminds me of a movie (that I can't remember the title of) about a tired, frustrated mom whose little girl drew crayon pictures on the wall. Her initial reaction was the frustrated one. Later, instead of washing the wall, she finds a couple of empty frames to put over the wall art. That taught her daughter that she and her artwork were valued. 
 You'll enjoy the ending. I think that Delilah Kain's mommy was the kind of mom who made Delilah scrub the walls when she colored on them. 
 The illustrations are adorable and full of details. 
 As reviewed on www.thestubbypencilslibrary.com

This is a charming children's book. It is simple enough for a third grader to read by themselves but still be interesting. It'll be fun to read more in this series. I think my 5 and 8-year-old grandkids would love it.

I had fun reading this book, I think kids would REALLY enjoy this one. It is journal entries written by ten year old twins, they have fun sharing their opinions and teasing each other. It is cute and clever the way it was done. I did have a hard time believing that it could be written by ten year olds though. I have a nine year old and an eleven year old and it just doesn't fit. Their sense of humors are too mature, and their ability to express themselves with clear, coherent, and entertaining ideas is also too developed. I really did enjoy it, and I think the idea of it is very fun. My only complaint was that it didn't seem realistic. But maybe that's why it would be best for kids.

In the second book Delilah and her business of traveling maids are invited to Transylvania to aid a certain Count Dracula in readying his castle for his annual Halloween Ball. This job is somewhat different than others, in that the castle is already spotless, and Delilah is put to the job of adding dust and cobwebs to the castle instead of removing them. 
 The lesson of the story is to embrace your unique gifts instead of conforming to what others want you to do or to be like. Your life is your own, and you will only be happiest when you are true to yourself. 
 I can't wait for the next book in this series. I would place these books at the same level as Amelia Bedelia. I used to love those books as a kid, and Delilah Dusticle would have been right there along with that series if it had been around at that time. I think these are extremely entertaining stories with plenty of adventure as well as a bit of silliness and fantasy. The lessons these stories teach just make them all the better. I would definitely recommend these books to any of my friends who are looking for something wonderful for their children to read.

These books were quite charming. I found them entertaining, but they also taught some very important lessons for young people. These books were meant for a much younger audience but I found them to be a good read as an adult as well. 
 The lesson related in this first book of the series: that a healthy self-image can affect more than we know, and kindness toward others can make a world of difference. We do not know what others are truly going through in their lives, but if we are simply kind to those around us, we can make a big difference. 
 I would place these books at the same level as Amelia Bedelia. I used to love those books as a kid, and Delilah Dusticle would have been right there along with that series if it had been around at that time. I think these are extremely entertaining stories with plenty of adventure as well as a bit of silliness and fantasy. The lessons these stories teach just make them all the better. I would definitely recommend these books to any of my friends who are looking for something wonderful for their children to read.

What did I like about this book? 
 The characters are well developed and I learned something from each of them. Toad and Melena are likeable kids who share a huge adventure for different reasons. The story is split between each of their points of view. 
 I enjoyed Izzie, Agatha and Joe. I think there is a lot more to learn from and about Izzie, if the author decides to write a sequel. I like the underlying theme of the book which is (for me, at least) that characters come into our lives at different times and seasons to teach us something and we shouldn't take them for granted--from a magical spider to an enchanted mug, to the kid who lives in a den of thieves. 
 The action and adventure are paced well from beginning to end with edge-of-your-seat suspense and rest periods where I could catch my breath and absorb new information. 
 The author did a good job with the world building. It reads like historical fiction. 
 There were some typos--probably just formatting issues, and a couple of scenes seemed a little contrived. It reminded me of a MG version of LOTR meets Harry Potter. I think my grandkids would really enjoy it. I know I did! Over all I'd give this book 4 stars****
Such a beautiful story!

Hugo is a cute character any child can relate to. 
 The illustrations are very colorful and bright attracting the attention of all children. 
 The writing is wonderful and to the point. 
 This is a great story to teach our kids that it is okay to be different and that they are just perfect just the way they are. 
 This timeless story teaches self-esteem and appreciation for yourself.

He was huge and fierce, a nightmare in black and orange, and he moved like a God through the world, which is how tigers move. 
 I loved the name better than I loved the book. Also, hot and ancient is a lovely way to describe my country. The illustrations are vibrant and stately. 
 The book itself is very unlike Neil Gaiman. It was like he was given a tiger, a princess, a Rajah and a Rani and he didn't know what to do. 
 I'm giving it a 3.5 because I really liked the tiger.

Recuerdo que lei este libro por primera vez a la edad de 12 o 13 anos y desde ese momento me impacto. Las travesuras de Zeze, la amabilidad de Portuga y el desenlace final me hizo llorar y aun hoy a mis 28 anos creo que lloraria nuevamente.
Love books that make children think about leaving a legacy worth carrying on

What a remarkable story of Hugo The Starfish, he explores the ocean, looking in the mirror, comparing himself to others, unsure of his own greatness and beauty. A lesson we at times even need to teach ourselves and not just our children. In this world we are our own tough critics.

There was a huge lilac bush outside my window and the scent of connected strongly with this story. I read both the Hardy Boys and Nancy Drew growing up. I grew up with these books and they contributed to my love of the story--especially mystery. I suspect they also contributed to my desire to write. I recommend the series as a whole for young readers. I have to admit to still having all my Nancy Drew's from the 60's.

A really enjoyable read. The Characters of Toad, Ratty, Badger and Mole return when the Ground is all frosty and crisp...Mole's Nephew comes visiting and Toad is up to his old tricks again, leading to one or two scrapes with the law, and the arm of Badger! 
 This had me smiling at every page.

Despite being aimed at children, this was a most enjoyable read! The Opening story was really funny (imagine dragons taking over your house :) ), and I enjoyed the other short tales held within. In particular a version of "The Carpet People" - STP's first book.

Great Book, follows on from the tale of Swallows and Amazons, but is a story in its own right. This story starts at Holly Howe and tells of the crew of the Swallows adventures on Wild Cat Island. A Brilliant read for any child big or small with a taste of adventure for the outdoors. I'll be returning to read this again and again (or after i've read Peter Duck :) the next book in the series)
I really love all the poems in this book and still read some of it upon occasion.

I have read this book more times than I can remember since I bought it long ago. It is an excellent read. It is very entertaining and engaging, the artwork is excellent (especially the parts when Hypolyta is going insane), and the writing is some of Gaiman's best.

Having read the first 5 Sandman collections multiple times, I decided to re-read the remaining again! The Sandman series is unique among comics, with myths and legends, stories about stories, dreams about stories and stories about dreams!! It's philosophical, spiritual, and multi-layered. There are some TPBs which are brutal in their depiction of what the characters go through. Reading The kindly ones is like watching the progression of an earthquake as it destroys everything on the surface of the earth, or watching a tsunami roll inland.. Neil Gaiman is a stunning writer.
This was an interesting chapter. I liked it, although I kept feeling like I was missing something or forgetting stuff that happened in earlier volumes...

Moonshot is a beautiful comics collection with stories that range from thought provoking to haunting to sad. All of these stories are Indigenous tales from the authors tribes and are told in a variety of ways, there's an odd balance of two or three space stories but most feel slightly disconnected from time. I would recommend this collection for anyone looking for an unusual and beautiful change from more narrative comics. Some of the stories feel more like the equivalent of a poem, while a few of the stories are in worlds, I would love to read more of. 
 These comics contain death and cannibalism. I would recommend them for a mature younger reader, who wants to understand better stories that aren't told enough.

A charming book about how movie ninjas and real life ones don't really match up. Vernon's illustrations are wonderful and help the story flow from believable to a touch of fantasy. Danny is a hilarious and wonderful protagonist and this book can stand on its own.

A beautiful and fascinating prelude to Sandman. The artwork is gorgeous and the story in a different part of the Sandman universe. I enjoyed reading it and found it provided background to the original comics. The deluxe edition has wonderful interviews and explanations of how the artists create in the back.

This is a wonderful graphic novel about growing up and being different. Cece loses her hearing at a young age and works to get comfortable. In El Deafo, she has troubles with friends who understand and don't. A charming and powerful read about friendship and being different with great art.

An amazing graphic novel about what it means to be a monster and a hero. I love how Stevenson combines fairy tale ideas alongside science. A great read and one I'd recommend for kids starting in middle school who are looking for a different take on heroes. I look forward to reading more of her work.

I found this graphic novel disappointing as I was expecting Shakespeare's characters to be aware and have stories that fit into who they were. Fables is one of my favorite comics' series and sets a high bar for taking characters out of their stories and putting them elsewhere. Sadly Kill Shakespeare mainly took the names of Shakespeare's characters and put them on rather generic fantasy tropes such as the woman outlaw, the sexy villainess and the confused hero. The story begins in the midst of Hamlet and its a version that has differences which are I believe meant to signify that this isn't the world we know but it felt light to me. 
 The way the pages were structured, it was hard to follow the action and I rarely knew why things were happening. Apparently Hamlet lands on an island and is a chosen one who will help to take down Shakespeare who is powerful yet its not explained why, or why the various Shakespearan villains led by Richard III band against him. If this had been simply a fantasy story without the names of Hamlet, Iago, Othello, Juliet thrown in, I would have enjoyed it more. Instead I felt like there were good ideas lost in all the action and that while starting in the midst of the action was good, I never really figured out what was happening. 
 I bought my copy at ALA 2013.

The War within These Walls is a slim but powerful graphic novel that tells about the lives of the Jews in Warsaw before and during World War II especially the experience within the Ghetto. The narrator of the story is a boy who grows into a man during the terrifying experiences and the author uses black pages in a haunting way and the simple illustrations capture some of the horror. As time goes on, the narrator keeps trying to survive and has points where he comes close to giving up and there are many deaths and horrors, but still hope. 
 Reading this I kept thinking about visiting the Holocaust Museum in Washington, DC where as a visitor you are plunged into the reality and horror of the Holocaust. I would recommend using this book in a high school course on World War II and would cautiously give it out to a mature middle school student. This isn't an easy book but it is a beautiful one that knows how to use the graphic novel format. 
 I picked up my ARC from the publishers at ALA 2013.

Divas, Dames and Daredevils looks at the heroines of the comics in the 1930s and 1940s. The book is divided into various sections starting with the war heroines and ending with the more magic ones. The bulk of the book is beautiful reprints of the original comics. Overall I enjoyed reading this book but my main complaint was that I wanted more. I wished that there was greater detail into the backgrounds of the various heroines, who created them, how popular were they as well as about what changed. There were points where the author would refer to great changes in the comic book world but not with complex explanations. 
 I think part of the problem might have been my expectations when I picked up the book as I thought it would be more of a historical and anthropological book. Instead it turned out to be focused on reprinting the comics themselves with minimal but interesting discussion of them. I would recommend this book to anyone curious about the history of comics and a reminder of how the history of comics isn't a straight line. 
 I picked up my ARC from the publisher's booth at ALA 2013.

I got this copy from the author and illustrator at ALA 2013 and they both signed it for me. Level Up is the story of Dennis who is trying to figure out his life when his choices seem to be medical school or playing video games. I enjoyed the art and story, but my main issue is that I wished this story was longer. It stands up as it is but there were points such as with the friendships at medical school or with a gamer friend at college that seemed as if they could have been deepened. 
 Its a book I would recommend to middle or high school students who are feeling a lot of pressure from their families. It captures some of the nuances of the various immigrant experience, which I appreciated, but to an adult, I would warn that its short. It felt more like a novella to me than a novel.

This is a thoughtfully put together graphic novel anthology though most of the retellings of the ballads aren't that groundbreaking instead they're beautifully done. A few of them truly shone and anyone who enjoys Charles Vess' art will find this worth a look. For those wanting unusual takes on these older ballads, this isn't the best book, I would recommend newer anthologies but it made me curious about some of the ballads.

This awkward retelling of Frankenstein moves the story forward into the modern world by using the device of Deucalion, who was supposedly Dr. Frankenstein's creature and has lived through time. The story begins when he's in an Eastern monastery and then a letter takes him to New Orleans where the story slips into the rather cliched realm of genetic manipulation and serial killers to portray what has happened to Dr. Frankenstein. Due to the violence that is shown in this story, it would only be appropriate for an older and more mature reader though reading the original Frankenstein would be a better experience. This retelling does not do justice to the source material since it dissolves quickly into various cliches of the supernatural murder mystery with a strong but sweet female cop who has to fight her way to the top, an over the top emotional monster who speaks in long speeches and a villain who wishes to remake the world.

An unusual graphic novel who's two main characters are Charles and Edwin, boys who have chosen not to die. They are almost caricatures of the boys from the classic English boys boarding school story yet this graphic novel takes place in a more modern world so a good amount of the humor comes from their slightly out of date ideas. Charles and Edwin run a detective agency and when a runaway finds them and asks for their help, things quickly become quite dark. The setting would be familiar to anyone who knows the Sandman novels since many of the characters appear within this but the story is not quite as dark as Sandman. In terms of who would enjoy this, it would probably be more appropriate for a high school student or mature middle school one due to the darkness of the subject manner in terms of death and violence. Also an avid reader who is aware of the classic tropes of Sherlock Holmes and the world of Tom Brown's Schooldays and their spinoffs will find more humor along with the original story.

A darkly cute collection of a comic series that follows Finney Bleak who's the most normal kid at a school full of monsters. The art style resembles some of the newly made cartoons from Cartoon Network and Nickolodeon with a mix of humor and knowing humor that would be recognizable to someone who enjoys Foster's Home for Imaginary Creatures. Though the presentation of the comics in a manga format from TokyoPop sends a slightly confusing message in terms of who would enjoy reading it because the art style is quite American as is the humor. 
 The publishers are doing their best to appeal to a number of audiences and the story has some cute elements as Finney finds a girl who seems perfect until he discovers she's a ghost just like most of his family. This is truly the greatest issue faced in this comic, which makes it a good read for any range from late elementary school to early high school due to the comic take on violence. Overall this is a nice addition to the world of goth and supernatural works for young readers but slightly confusing in terms of the style combined with how its published. If it was presented in a true comic book format instead of a fake manga one, it would be easier for it to reach its possible audience of guys.

The first volume of this compelling manga series introduces Yuki who is a member of the Disciplinary Committee at Cross Academy, where she and Zero and the headmaster are the only ones who know that the Night Class is made up of vampires. Yuki narrates this wonderful story that deals with the issues of can anyone truly be reformed and what makes someone dangerous, the blood of a vampire or their choices. Yuki truly stands between the Day Classes of mortal girls who adore the Night Class with their elegance and the two men in her life Kaname, the vampire who saved her when she was six and brought her to Cross Academy and Zero, her fellow Disciplinary Committee member who lost his family to vampires. One of the nice things about this series is that even though there are many erotic moments with the open collared shirts of the girls and the moments of blood sucking, none of the violence or suggestions would be too much for a middle school student. 
 Also Yuki is truly the main character and makes her own choices and decisions so a young woman could admire her while also enjoying the love triangle that she's in. Overall, this is a good manga to give a young female reader who wants to read about vampires and has some knowledge of manga since there is adventure and romance but the female lead holds her own amongst the men.

This fascinating and cleverly done graphic novel follows the story of Jane as after a bomb explodes in her city, her family moves to the suburb to be safer. Jane narrates the book through a series of letters that she writes to a John Doe who was knocked into a coma during the same explosion and that she feels she has a connection with. The John Doe had been an artist and so when Jane has trouble fitting in at her school, she connects to a group of girls also called Jane and they plan art attacks. 
 These simple acts of art end up transforming the town and how people think as Jane becomes more comfortable in her new home. In this work, the graphic novel style suits the story and the striking black and white illustrations move the story to a stronger place as we see transformations in people and places. 
 Due to the hard subject matter that is dealt with in terms of the violence and the struggles of high school, this book would work best for a high school reader and could be very effective as a way to open up a discussion about how disasters and moving can change and affect us. Though the violence is dealt with from a slightly indirect viewpoint as Jane works to a point of being able to deal with it herself which means that a younger but mature reader but also find a connection.

A powerful graphic novel that follows the story of four lions who escaped from the Baghdad zoo into the chaos of the 2003 invasion and died. The story begins in the zoo and ends on the bloody streets of Baghdad. Throughout the story, the lions discuss ideas of freedom and what it means to be caged and tamed as they work to survive. This is not an easy story and the illustrations don't stint on showing the violence of animals and of war. 
 A high school student who is interested in more mature themes and comfortable reading graphic novels and comics could gain a lot from this book. On the other hand, it is a difficult work and so would not be recommended for a squeamish reader.
A charming graphic novel that follows three Bones as they leave their homes and end up in the forest. I look forward to reading more and seeing how the story proceeds.

I can't even pretend that I got all of this. I'm not sure it's possible for anyone to get all of it in a single reading. Perhaps in the kind of intensive studying one associates with a doctoral thesis. But even then only maybe. 
 Fun coincidence: I was reading this and also reading Hades: Lord of the Dead, because every time I got up some kid would swipe one of my books, and I'd have to switch to the other. Two books starring the Kindly Ones at once. 
 I'm starting to view Greek mythology the same way I view the tarot. Not as inherently meaningful, but as suggestive patterns that permit our own consciousnesses to make up the stories they need at the moment. 
 Library copy. (Although when I win the lottery, one of the first things I will do is buy the The Absolute Sandman, Vol. 1 complete set. The second thing will be to build the library of my dreams in which they will reside)
Liked the artwork, the story was a little short and not as developed as I would have liked.
Reviewing for Booklist

Thanks to Yen Press for a free copy via Goodreads giveaway! :D 
 I very much enjoyed volume 1 and am looking forward to the next. I thought the translation was done well and I like how they translated the sound effects. Also, gorgeous formatting. 
 The genre and story are right up my ally so I liked all of that. The only thing I didn't enjoy was the thing with Jeanne and Vanitas in the last chapter so I'm a bit wary now of that and the fact that Noe is going to kill Vanitas apparently? Definitely will read further to find out what happens.

3.5 
 Was disappointied at the lack of development of the other couple, but despite that it was a really sweet, lightly angsty story.

Whew. it feels like a lot happened in this volume! There was a lot of suspense and moments that made my heart reach out for the characters. A lot of it takes place in school, but there are times where it takes place in another place that I found interesting and feel will be a bigger part of the plot soon. There is a lot of Ritsu POV. With each volume I am more and more impressed with ONE's storytelling!

I agree with pretty much everything Miguel said. I really like reading about people working together to survive, not to mention when people underestimate them. There are enough characters involved now that plots like this are viable, and that makes me happy. =) The only thing I didn't like was a bit of sexism one on page but I liked how the woman handled it.

A very intense installment in the series, it kept me on the edge of my seat and guessing every step of the way what choices the characters would make and what would happen as a result. Mostly in Ritsu's POV but Mob is involved as well as Teru and Dimple.

I don't know what I can say that Miguel's wonderful review didn't already, but. 
 It was really interesting to read about Mob's brother, and I'm curious where that will go. It's nice getting backstory even if it makes me sad. 
 This volume was, to me, a lot darker than the previous in a way because of the other psychic that was introduced, Teru. I love seeing other sides of protagonists and Mob reminds me of Yuuri's demon transformation in Kyou Kara Maou!. 
 I still laughed quite a bit. ONE is very good at handling the timing of the humor and the serious or action. 
 I can't believe it but I actually felt bad for a certain ghost all because of Mob's reaction/flashbacks. 
 Time to hurry on to the next volume!

This volume has some hilarious moments in it, I loved it! OPM never fails to make my day brighter. And it's actually really nice to read about other characters (Child Emperor and Metal-Bat are two), so long as it goes back to Saitama (and Genos) after. 
 Gotta say it's pretty interesting watching Garou go around looking for Heroes, it gives the reader a chance to see more characters for one, and more chances for Saitama to swat him down. =P 
 Very excited to read more (as always)!

I can't get over the mix of seriousness and comedy in this manga. It makes it so very entertaining to read. 
 I like seeing more characters interacting, like Genos and Sonic, and I also enjoyed getting to see Saitama hanging out with someone (besides Genos). <3 
 I'm excited yet nervous to see where things go from here. I could read about Saitama and Genos forever, but more and more characters are getting involved, and I'm hoping I will enjoy it just as much. I am already taking a liking towards King and Fubuki and already really liked Mumen Rider. 
 The thing I'm most curious about seeing where it's going is with Bang's disciple, Garou. And I hope that nothing permanent happens to Bang... He's one of the few who see Saitama's strangth for what it is and seems to care about him.

I started reading Mob Psycho 100 after reading the first ten volumes of One Punch Man. An artist I follow on Tumblr has been drawing fanart for this manga for a while and that got me a little curious before I even watched the OPM anime. 
 Despite knowing how fabulous the story and characters in OPM are, I went through the first chapter tentatively. After that, I suddenly found myself at the end of the volume and hooked. 
 Like another reviewer said, for a story where the main character is supposedly emotionless, I sure did laugh a lot. There's plenty of humor to be found (how could there not be with Reigen's character in it!) as well as suspense, intrigue and room for development. 
 As for the art... Well, when I first started reading One Piece, I thought the art was a bit strange, and now I love it so much, it fits the story very well. It helped me when I started reading Gash Bell later. For this manga, I think it fits the story. (Not that I wouldn't mind seeing it get the same treatment as OPM!)

Naruto and Sasuke are best friends. They go to the beach together but Naruto is struggling with his attraction towards Sasuke, and has a flashback to what started it. 
 Cute and heartwarming, although it seems like the sequel might be angsty!
Highly recommended for those studying Japanese, it's an easy and very entertaining read so you'll want to keep going even if you don't understand %100 of everything.
Now being officially translated here and updated every week here: http://www.webtoons.com/episodeList?t...

** spoiler alert ** 
 The beginning was really confusing, it condensed down the events that led to Takumi and Gui's relationship to deepen. Which means that we get instalove by page 6 without me falling with them. Too much telling + confusing glimpses versus playing it out and showing us that build-up. Maybe it's better in the novel. 
 One thing I noticed was that the sound effects and little texts weren't translated. :/ They really add something to a story for me. 
 I was REALLY conflicted by the scene were Gui 'cured Takumi's rape trauma by raping him'. Doesn't matter if Takumi got into it by the end. In fiction they can get by with that, but if a friend of mine ever told me that someone, lover or not, forced themselves on them to 'get them over' their trauma, I'd be so pissed. But whatever, the author created them, not me, and rape=healing love prevails. 
 Despite that, if I happened across the sequels, I might be curious enough to read them because the notes at the end mention two characters I'm curious about. 
 I actually really liked the chapter where Akaike spent the night at Gui's house, it was cute and funny. Their friendship is nice, and I liked Namiko's conversation with Gui.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I think I've gotten more sensitive from my time away from BL manga. I can't abide by Kiriya's attitude about cheating. 
 Kiriya is fine with cheating and breaking up relationships but doesn't want to continue to be with a minor (who he thought was 19 but turned out to be to 17). I just don't get it. 
 I think how jealous Yuuya would get is a problem. It's a common theme in BL manga and it's almost treated like it's a positive thing, a sign of the seme's love. I think that's so problematic - look what jealousy and greed has made people do. Does murder ring a bell? I think before any relationship goes too far, the jealousy should be addressed. I understand that Yuuya is young, but he's the one trying to be in a relationship with a 27-year-old so he needs to learn to deal with these feelings instead of letting them control him. 
 "I just want to run off with him." - Yuuya 
 If you had a secure job and friends, wouldn't that scare you if your lover started saying things like that, along with the jealousy issues? 
 I did think the piano part was interesting, it's not often a character has a permanent disability. I also thought it was unusual in a BL manga for a teacher/student relationship to get caught, so that was new. Yuuya didn't even apologize for making Kiriya lose his job though, one which he clearly enjoyed. He didn't care that his fellow students were getting a better education because of him and would now lose that. He just wanted Kiriya to himself. 
 I did find myself enjoying it a bit more after they were caught and had to find a way to see each other again. 
 I just hope that in time, they'll both grow as people more together and apart, and their relationship will strengthen.

I should have known after reading the mangaka's comment about "real men" that I wouldn't like it, but I was willing to give it a try. Buut it's just way too problematic and unhealthy of a relationship for me, although the art is very pretty.

It's been a while since I've read a story with Martial Arts in it! It was amusing how Tasuku used it on Ryouta. Definitely the tsundere type. And Ryouta was yandere at times when it came to Tasuku. XP 
 The first sex scene was hot (I wrote something like that some time ago myself). 
 So anyway, I quite enjoyed this story, probably enough to reread it sometime. Where it will travel after that, we shall see!

I enjoyed it well enough. I don't know if it's because I've been listening to a podcast that talks about honesty and communication in relationships a lot recently, but while reading this I often found myself thinking that a lot of heartache could be avoided if they just TALKED. But then it wouldn't be yaoi. Besides, they're young and new at love, and by the end they were on their way to learning. Once I considered that, it wasn't so bad. 
 I'll try and get the manga to read! I find that I prefer manga over novels anyway.

First read a long time ago and never got to finish it. I'm glad I got the chance to get this volume. 
 Kotori is so cute! I really like the character designs and story. The oneshots at the end surprised me a bit because the styles are so different, but they were alright. I'd love to read volumes 2 & 3!

This is a great start to the Dark Avengers series. I read this as separate comic issues, but decided that I would review it as the graphic novel. 
 When the government disbands the Avengers as a result of the Secret Invasion story arc, they place Norman Osborn as the big boss. I've been collecting the Avengers and so getting Dark Avengers was just a logical step. I really wanted to see what Bendis would do with this new line-up of villains (for the most part) running the US superhero defence. 
 The Dark Avengers consisted of team leader, Norman Osborn (aka Iron Patriot), which was a mix of Captain America and Iron Man; Moonstone (becoming Ms Marvel); Mac Gargan's Venom (becoming Spiderman); Bullseye (becoming Hawkeye) and Wolverine's evil son, Dakken (becoming Wolverine). Added to this list is Ares (as a stand in for Thor), Noh-Varr (as Captain Marvel) and The Sentry stayed with the new team. 
 Although I can't say that the storyline, which had the Dark Avengers helping Doctor Doom battle Morgan Le Fay was that great, I can say that Bendis' ability to develop the characters as a team was most enthralling. I enjoyed the witty banter between them and I was wondering how the team would be able to function with so many crazy, loners trying to work as a team.

At first I was a bit worried about what I would find when I opened up the pages of Marvel 1602, but to my surprise, I found myself getting lost in the story and enjoying the appearances of so many Marvel characters altered to some degree to suit the era, but not having lost all of their usual characteristics that we have come to know and love. Gaiman was able to reinvent the characters in a very interesting way that made me want to continue reading and, of course, enjoying this view of the dark underbelly of the Elizabethan Era. 
 Some highlights were Sir Nicholas Fury's appointment as the Queen's spy network. Although I have enjoyed watching Samuel L Jackson's version of the character, I haven't really enjoyed reading much about Fury; but this was one of the first portrayals of the agent that I had fun reading. I also liked the somewhat cheesy, but highly amusing, scene where a beloved, blind Matt Murdock is a bard singing about the loss of the ship Fantastik and its four heroes. 
 A well written and enjoyable graphic novel, which didn't disappoint me, as I assumed it might have.

And so it has come to this. Here we reach the long-coming conclusion of the Sandman saga, with all that remains being to clean up assorted loose ends and tie them neatly in a bow. Years ago, Lyta Hall spent a near-eternity in the Dreaming with her dead husband and unborn son. As a result, Morpheus has a claim on young Daniel at some point in the future. Thus, when Daniel goes missing, his mother understandably jumps to the conclusion that it was Dream who took him, and vows to unleash vengeance upon his head. Of course, perhaps the only beings who could actually hurt Morpheus are the legendary Furies, also known as The Kindly Ones for reasons. The Kindly Ones, however, are bound by the same ancient laws as the Endless. They can only avenge blood debts, and then only if the blood was spilled by a family member. So Morpheus should be safe, right? Oh. Oh, yeah. Crap. He just killed Orpheus, his own son. It was Orpheus' own request, tired of living for millenia as a disembodied head, but that won't matter to the Kindly Ones. They'll rip the Dreaming to shreds about Morpheus' ears, not stopping until he is dead. And in this situation, even Morpheus will be powerless to save himself....

6 stars!!! 
 Now, you are probably looking at the title of the ninth volume of Neil Gaiman's fantastic "Sandman" series, which is called "The Kindly Ones" and you are probably thinking to yourself about how this volume will be all sunshine and roses. Definitely not! Do not let the innocent title of this volume fool you! The ninth volume "The Kindly Ones" is probably the darkest volume out of all the "Sandman" series since "A Game of You" and yet this is probably the best volume out of the entire "Sandman" series ever created! 
 Lyta Hall (also known as Hippolyta Hall) was always on edge when it came to taking care of her baby son Daniel, who was born after her husband Hector had died. One night however, when Lyta Hall decided to leave her baby son Daniel in the care of a babysitter while she went for a job application, she finds out that her baby son had been kidnapped as soon as she got home and she desperately wanted to find him. Unfortunately, when Lyta believes that the worse has happened to Daniel after there were no clues tracing to him, Lyta goes into an emotional shock and a deep rage where she confronts the "Kindly Ones" in the dream world and wants them to help her seek vengeance on Dream, the Sandman for she believed that Dream was the one who harmed her baby. Can Dream protect his dream realm from the forces of darkness? 
 Now I just have to say that this was the 
 LONGEST 
 volume I have ever read from the "Sandman" series as it was well over two hundred pages worth of disturbing scenes and plot development, but it was worth the read! Neil Gaiman's writing is just as brilliant as ever in this volume as the story is exciting and creepy at the same time and it is like once you started reading this volume, you really cannot put this graphic novel down since there is so much excitement building up on each page regarding the mystery surrounding the "Kindly Ones." I also loved the fact that all of the characters that we were introduced to in the "Sandman" series all make an appearance in this volume, sort of giving this volume a finale feel as everything is set in place for the huge battle that awaits the Sandman. I really loved the way that Neil Gaiman focused so much of the story on the characters as I was really interested in hearing about Matthew the Raven's obsession about finding out what happened to the other ravens before him since I wanted to also find out about Matthew's origins and his connections with the ravens. But probably the part about the graphic novel I was most impressed with was how Neil Gaiman developed the character Lyta Hall and it was apparent from the previous "Sandman" books that Lyta harbored a deep hatred for Dream because she believes that he killed her husband Hector in the Dream world. It was definitely a frightening and intense experience seeing how Lyta's hatred for Dream could cause so much turmoil for everyone involved, even though it was based on her worst assumptions about what happened to her son Daniel. Marc Hempel, Richard Case, D' Israeli, Teddy Kristiansen, Glyn Dillon, Charles Vess, Dean Ormston, and Kevin Nowlan's artwork were brilliant creative in this novel and they all contributed well to the story at hand. I will admit that some of the artwork is a bit blocky and I would have expected epic illustrations to accompany this epic volume, but these illustrations do bring a sort of uniqueness to the story and I still really enjoyed the artwork being done in this volume. 
 Some of the problems I did had with this graphic novel is that some of the artwork looks a bit cartoony to me since some of the artwork made some of the characters have blocky heads, which made it hard for me to take the story seriously at times. Although, I will admit that the artwork did provide some creativity to the story. Also, there is so much disturbing content in this volume which involves a mother losing her son, which would be upsetting for any parent who has fears of losing their own children. There are also some gory images in this volume which involves birds pecking out people's eyes out, which would be extremely disturbing to anyone who is not a fan of gory imagery. 
 Overall, "The Sandman: The Kindly Ones" is easily one of the best volumes in the "Sandman" series as it clearly seems like the true finale for the "Sandman" series and is full of disturbing and intense moments that will go down in history as the greatest moments in comic book history! Now that I am interested in seeing what will become of Dream and his crew, I will now start reading the tenth volume, The Sandman, Vol. 10: The Wake to find out!

I chose not to count all seven of these slim volumes as books against my total for the year, so am reviewing the whole of the series so farwith a review of Saga, Vol. 1 and this, the last volume to be published so far. Because I would rather not recapitulate what I said in that previous review, you might want to go there to read what I thought at the time. 
 Not much has changed in my estimation of these clever novels. They are heartfelt and emphasize the value of love and loyalty. They are also very violent and sexual--not a complaint, of course; we are all adults here. Until the very end I was engaged in the twists and turns of plot and characters. 
 But...the end. There is a darkness to the ending of this volume that feels rather gratuitous. Not that I am asking for fairies and elves and deus ex machina. And, hey, I know that real life can be pretty grim. But stories are not life, and to be entertaining, even the darkest night must be led up to and elucidated rather than just thrown in our faces. We seem to be told here that we simply need to cope with it, suckers, and get on with your life. 
 I assume this will all be redeemed in further volumes. I had gotten the impression that this was the last of the series and the earlier version of this review was quite opprobrious because of that. But when it was pointed out to me that I was mistaken (thanks, Mitchell!), I changed my tune. I am glad to hear that we have not heard that last of these engaging characters. Much as my criticisms above still stand, I feel less negativity than I did when I first wrote the review. I guess we'll just have to wait and see.

Oh, what fun! I really enjoyed the beginning of this tale, which is now up to seven volumes of highly regarded and award-winning storytelling and art. I have read few graphic novels, I will admit, though at one time I devoured Watchmen, The Sandman, Vol. 1: Preludes and Nocturnes series, The Complete Maus, the excellent graphic memoir Fun Home: A Family Tragicomic, Jeff Smith's engaging Bone series and several others I can't recall the name of right now, but which have made a profound impression on me nonetheless. I quite enjoy the genre, but rarely place these books high on my list to read. 
 But I fully intend to read all seven of these jewels. The beginning contained in this volume is quite promising, with a pair of star-crossed lovers fleeing the forces seeking to bring them to a form of rough justice they don't deserve, merely for the crime of having the desire to be a peaceful family. It takes place on worlds at war, quite outside our solar system, in a time that could be any time. It is inhabited by the usual habitues of such imagined worlds, with multiple legs and arms, horns in their heads, and wings. 
 Something about modern graphic novels that has been niggling at me but that this book helped me to define is the question of why so many of these seem to similar one to another. There is, I find, a particular idiom to this genre, as well as a set of attitudes and modes of expression universally in use, that serve more to bind them together than set them apart. Almost every one of the main characters is capable of the wry grin, for instance. Everyone has a heart of gold behind a rough exterior (except those who don't, of course, and they are as clearly villainous as Snidely Whiplash). There is always a sort of snarky irony in the telling of these tales that makes them seem a bit more shallow than the genre is capable of being. This may be why I recall the Neil Gaiman-written Sandman series with such pleasure, because it avoided these cliches. 
 Don't get me wrong, though. Though it sticks to the form, Saga is a pleasure to read, and I look forward with joy to the time I can pick up the next one. Stay tuned. And watch out for that magic!

Really a quite wonderful and stunningly honest memoir of the decline and death of the author's parents, told mostly through graphic images, though there is some plain text and a few photographs. This is a phase of life most of us must face as we ourselves age, the inevitable passing of our parents and the gradual decline of their 80s and 90s. Those of us who are most fortunate get the gift of having our parents around that long, but I know from personal experience that one begins to grieve the loss of capabilities long before death approaches. Roz Chast faces the demons of these years with more honesty, humor, and courage than anyone I have encountered.

The Arrival is one of the closest things I have read recently that approaches a work of genius. This is a book without words, skillfully illustrating the immigrant experience with grace, humor, and compassion. Perhaps the most affecting thing about this book is the choice Tan made to set this tale in a world so very foreign to our eyes, with fanciful animals and oddly shaped and decorated buildings, so that our sense of dislocation might recapitulate in miniature what it must feel like to come to a world that is almost entirely unrecognizable as a place to live and thrive. His protagonist struggles with language, with wayfinding, with finding work and lodging--everything, one would imagine, any immigrant would face. 
 But this is not the half of the magic of The Arrival, for the drawings--lavish, lovingly-drawn, careful, kind, and evocative--are as breathtaking in their emotional content as in their sheer technical skill. Tan makes clear in an afterward that many, many years were spent studying the immigrant experience and interviewing many people, including members of his family, to derive a clear understanding of it. But to be able to translate those inferences to something as coherent and heartfelt as this feels a bit like a miracle. 
 If you have not yet, you really ought to give this beautiful book a look. But take your time. Study the lovely drawings and all their details. Repeated viewings pay richly.
From Neil Gaiman

Whenever someone starts a sentence with the phrase, "There are two kinds of people in the world..." my response is, "Yes, there are two kinds of people in the world: those who think there are two kinds of people in the world and those who don't." Be that as it may.... 
 It seems to me there are two kinds of people in the world: those who believe that the way to mental health is to root out the sources of our neuroses and thereby lay them to rest, and those who think this is malarkey, if only because the roots of such dysfunction lie buried so deeply that it is more than a life's work to dig that deep, not to mention that some of them are buried down there because their toxicity would poison us if we dredged them up. Besides, times-a-wastin'! There is life to live, the life right in front of us, not buried in the musty past. 
 I guess it's obvious into which of these two camps I fall. Alison Bechdel falls into the other. Which is not to say I don't deeply admire this work, in a slightly horrified way: Bechdel is nothing if not scathingly honest, revealing far more about her self than she does of her mother, the putative subject of this memoir in pictures and text. I'm just not at all convinced that the concerted navel-gazing in which she is indulging here and in her life is truly a healthy pursuit. 
 Odd, though, isn't it (and what does it say about my own pathology?) that I thought her previous memoir, this one of her father, Fun Home: A Family Tragicomic, was entirely necessary, even essential. In that case, though, the subject was not only dead but a likely suicide, leaving deep scars that had to be excised somehow, almost as if by killing himself he had incurred a debt that could only be repaid by revelation of his deeply held secrets. 
 Now, though, Bechdel is 52 and still struggling with therapy and the complex relationship with her mother. This book skillfully weaves her therapeutic insights, writings of passionate Victorian psychotherapists--in particular Donald Winnicott--and the autobiographical works of Virginia Wolff with the description of her relations, both past and present, with a distant, cold, loving, infuriating, intelligent mother. When is it time to move on? 
 I love Bechdel's simple pen-and-ink drawing style that can be so evocative and clear. Her use of the frame of the comic is telling and precise. She is a perfectionist (by her own description) and it shows in her meticulous choices. Every now and then I simply stepped back and marveled at the sheer gall of the task she had taken on, considering the fears she reveals of being imperfect and judged. How does one overcome such a burden to make such masterful invocations of a deeply tortured life? 
 Yet I kept coming back to the thought that perhaps a dose of forgiveness was all that was required, that one can make a choice to leave much of the grief of our imperfect childhoods behind. To dredge and dredge and dredge up the pain does not seem to have been very fruitful for her; when does she think she might require a different path to joy? Or has she abandoned any aspiration to true happiness? What a sad commentary that would be. Alison, I had the urge to say, over and over, get over it! Move on! Yes, your mother was imperfect, but isn't what Winnicott telling you is that they all are? That it is not only in the nature of motherhood for this to be so but that those imperfections are, in fact, essential to the individuation of the child? So, hey, Alison, indviduate, already! 
 I would not like for the last word I say to be anything other than admiration, though. It takes great courage to lay oneself bare, and all the more so in such an unflattering light. I cannot but praise her commitment to the truth, while wishing all the best for her and that her truth could be just a little less cruel. As one of her therapists tells her, she is deserving of all that is good in the world. She is, in fact, and in every way, adorable.

A fascinating graphic novel which adapts H.P. Lovecraft's hallucinogenic dream fantasies into the art of the unfathomable. There is more than just a hint of paranoid delusion here, tempered by the acknowledgement that in the world of dream there is no dependable reality and that therefore whatever comes next is what makes sense, even if in the world of the non-dreamer it might be over the edge of sanity. 
 Jason Bradley Thompson's art is admirable and evokes the Lovecraft's dreamscape with style and elan. He seems at home in this world (a frightening prospect) and gives to the words a substantiality of meaning they might otherwise have lacked. One caveat: though I understand that it was an aesthetic choice rather than a lack of skill (or any other lack), to make the main character utterly featureless and more or less a stick figure detracted from my enjoyment of the story. Yes, I understand that in the world of dream we ourselves might indeed be a mere representation of an entirely corporeal being, while those who inhabit this world full-time are likely to be more thoroughly fleshed out. We also don't want to go confusing the waking person with the dreamer. Still, my ability to identify with Carter was hampered by this choice and decreased my overall enjoyment of it, but not to any great degree. I still consider this work a major achievement and applaud the effort behind it. 
 I also think it's worth mentioning that the publication of this work was funded by Kickstarter. Though I had no dog in this particular fight, I have since looked into Kickstarter and made a few pledges. If you are not familiar with this unique way to fund worthwhile projects at the grassroots level, you should check it out.

This is a superb evocation of life in Iran under the last Shah through the first decade or so of the Islamic revolution. We in the West carry with us many assumptions about what Iran is, what it is like to live there, and who the Iranian people are. This book explodes most of those assumptions, and leads us to a better understanding of what it truly means to be Iranian. 
 Satrapi was born into the last days of the Shah and though we in the West may have the impression that, at the very least, the reign of the Shah was more benign than that of his fundamentalist successors, from Satrapi's perspective this was far from true. The Shah was, as we know, a puppet of the British and the United States, but he was also a cruel and despotic ruler who the Iranian people were just as glad to see the back of. What the defeat of the Shah ushered in, however, was not more democracy or freedom but more despotism, this time in the form of religious fundamentalism. 
 What is magical about this graphic memoir is that Satrapi was not only there, but was in the most formative stages of her life during these tumultuous events, and therefore the impressions they have made are deep and lasting; we then get the benefit of the clarity and strength of those impressions. Even when she spent some years out of the country, her thoughts were quite often with her parents and other loved ones in Iran. 
 Satrapi uses simple drawings to evoke the extremities and the normality of what she experiences; this form is particularly well-suited to the task because of the artist's ability to exaggerate or diminish for a particular effect of emotional expression or importance of an event or realization. 
 All in all, this is a wonderful (if occasionally harrowing) book and is highly recommended.

An excursion into graphic non-fiction, this is a memoir of the author's complex and conflicted relationship with her father and how it shaped her life. 
 Bechdel is the author of the comic strip Dykes To Watch Out For, though "comic" is something of a misnomer, as it is the sometimes humorous but often acerbic picture of a group of friends, many of them (as one might expect) lesbians, who go through all of the challenges, hatreds, make-ups, and sexual adventures inherent in any multifaceted life. Sometimes painfully close to real life, the comic can be overwhelming (and even boring) at times, but it is a truthful and well-composed slice of these fictional people's lives. 
 Given this description of her primary oeuvre, it should come as no surprise that in Fun Home, the description of her family life focuses on dysfunction, particularly that of her father's closeted homosexuality. His outlet for this frustrated desire seems to have taken the form of obsessive interior decoration, which she acknowledges would be absurdly stereotypic if it weren't in fact the case. Notwithstanding this essential truth, Bechdel does seem to engage in rather excessive typing of what behaviors may indicate one's incipient gayness; not merely interior decoration, but a love of flowers and nice clothing are attributed by her to this tendency in her father. This type of prejudgment is not particularly helpful in a measured conversation about sexuality. 
 It becomes clear that Bechdel was (is?) somewhat unhinged. No spoilers here, but her behaviors in childhood suggest a disturbance that cannot wholly be laid at her father's door. This makes the tension of the story that much more palpable and enticing, and induces in us a sympathy for this little girl struggling with forces she cannot even begin to comprehend. One further criticism, indeed, is that her portrait of her father and she herself are three-dimensional and fleshed out, but the rest of her family seem to be rather more like cardboard cut-outs than real people. Is this perhaps one of the failings of this form, wherein the labor-intensive and space-consuming drawings limit the ability of the author to expend excess words on clarity? If so, she has made a good choice in her focus, choosing to highlight this, the most salient and conflicted relationship in her life. 
 Overall, this is an affecting and engaging story. It is never much less than quite dark. Laughs are few and far between, but she did not set out to write a lighthearted romp; this is a true and harrowing tale of growing up with a form of emotional abuse most of us have never encountered. If you have the stomach and the heart for this kind of tale, I cannot recommend it too enthusiastically.

Justice Is blind. In Wayne of Gotham a story unfolds of what made justice blind in Gotham, why that was bad, and how bad that it got. Batman, Bruce's father, Thomas Wayne is at the center of the tale. Secrets are revealed such as why Thomas Wayne was killed and why Gotham is so ridden with strange costumed villains. 
 I attended Tracy Hickman's reading at Space City Houston earlier this year. He said that when discussing what book he might write next, his agent brought up the idea of a super hero. The author deiced if he were to write about any super hero it would be batman because he had no actual super powers. He told us about a fond memory form childhood when he and his brother saw the bat mobile at a car show. The author did an excellent job of describing the bat mobile and its technical features in the book. He did his research into the entire history of batman and kept to the traditional story so fans of the original comic will not be disappointed. 
 The book is action packed and intriguing. The character of batman, Bruce Wayne, is well flushed out as is that of his father, Thomas Wayne. This is an interesting, enjoyable read and I highly recommend it.

The clockwork girl is a story of star crossed lovers from two different houses. Sounds familiar? One of the two fantastic castles is built by the grafter as a monument to the science of nature and the other is built by the tinker as a tribute to the science of technology and machines. The tinker creates a clockwork girl named Tesla. You will even find two quotes of Nikola Tesla within the story. "I do not think there is any thrill that can go through the human heart like that felt by the inventor as he sees some creation of the brain unfolding to success . . . Such emotions make a man forget food, sleep, friends, love, everything."-and-"Let the future tell the truth, and evaluate each one according to his work and accomplishments. The present is theirs; the future, for which I have really worked, is mine. There are several images of the little clockwork girl and the monster boy that though different are reminiscent of scenes from Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. As the Clockwork Girl is an obvious nod to and inspired by William Shakespeare, Nikola Tesla, and Mary Shelley it has to be good, and it is. 
 I fell in love with the characters, Tesla, the clockwork girl and Huxley, the monster boy and I imagine everyone who reads this will do the same. It's a heartwarming story that is brilliant in its simplicity and it is actually suited not only for adults but children as young as grade school, say seven years old on up. 
 The dedication in the front of the book sums The Clockwork Girl up best, "To love and those who purse it relentlessly." It's a fun, fast, full filling read, I highly recommend.

In this dieselpunk/alternative history comic book, washed up, space heroes live in Ignition City, a rough and rowdy settlement cut off from civilization on Earth's last spaceport. Ignition City has a strong woman for the main character, Mary Raven, a space pilot and daughter of the famous spaceman, who stopped a Martian missile plot. She heads to the spaceport to discover how her father died and who killed him. It has colorful language and a Wild West tone. There are aliens, ray guns, and the marshal flies around in a rocketeer type outfit. It's a fun, action packed read.

The author and artist, BryanTablot, was inspired by a 19th century illustrator, who drew anthropomorphized characters in contemporary costumes of the period and used the pen name J J Grandville. The story takes place in an alternate world where the British lost the Napoleonic War and a British Inspector, a badger, investigates the murder of a British diplomat. The events of 911 and a conspiracy theory are woven in to the plot. The cast is made up of animals garbed in Victorian clothing, there are few humans now and then, maids and bell hops, who are called doughfaces, which I find hilarious. Grandville is smart, interesting, well plotted and the art is incredible. I highly recommend it.

A rugged, old west cowboy hero, Struck, robs banks, cheats at poker, lies to women with promises of marriage, and runs away at any hint of trouble. Yeah, this bad boy is a real charmer. Still when some old prospectors dig up robots, who in turn dig up a whole army of metal men, who go on a rampage to kill humans, he comes to the rescue of his woman and his town. Of course he has to, he's set for a hanging and the sheriff gives him no choice but to help or to hang. Our hero, Struck , has some help himself form an elderly Native American gentleman and Sasquash. Yes that's right, Big Foot himself. This comic book is a blast, so much fun. You've got to read Iron West, it'll make your day. Drew "Moriarty" McWeeny of Ain't It Cool News summed it up best with this tidbit from his review of it, "Iron West, a book that is as innocent and enjoyable as an afternoon spent as kids playing cowboys and 'injuns."

This is a fun steam-punk graphic novel and I especially think tween girls would really like it. I think 13 -15 year girls would find it cool, although I don't know if cool is the right word for their generation. But in my day this would have been really cool. It's black and white, great art work, but there's a full color short story in the back, The Electric Coffin, that's brilliant colors. The heroine is a young university student, a girl, of course I love that.Girl Genius Vol. 1 Agatha Heterodyne & the Beetleburg Clank

I really enjoyed this tan, black, and white graphic story. It DOES have a very strong message about the environment, and oversimplifies the ecological issues a bit, but it's appropriate for the grade 3+ audience to do so. Because of the comic format, concepts about the advantage of "buy local", for example, are easier to visualize. The main character, Luz, is a mall-shopping, sneaker-craving girl who doesn't understand why multiple car trips are a problem for her mom's pocketbook and the environment. Slowly she comes to understand the issue AND finds a way to have a positive impact on her own neighborhood. 
 Yes, it's preachy to the adult ear, but for kiddos I think it could really work. Will test it out on my daughters and update.

this was good. Really good. 
 It's not the lenght of a life that matters, just the depth of it. The chances we take. The paths we choose. How we go on after our hearts break. Hearts always break, and so we bend with our hearts, and we sway. But in the end, what matters is that we loved and lived. 
 Good story, good backstory, awesome characters and we do get to know a lot about black widow's past!
wtf was this story

after reading the newer versions of black widow, this one is a little more spy and a lot less human. Does it make sense? 
 And what's up with Daredevil and her? iwannaknooooooow 
 also she was married? whaaat?!

I liked this more than vol 1. 
 Winter Soldier appears and it gets really interesting.
big big meh

i really like the drawing style of this. I like the pace and the way the story is told. Makes me really want to know more about her, about her past. 
 She's trying to be good using the skills that made her bad in the first place. It's a really interesting theme. What's good, what's bad... 
 I don't have time for a full review, but I really enjoyed this. It's a easy and yet intriguing read that gives you a thirst for more. And it's black widow... like common... who doesn't like to read about powerful/badass woman ?
Rick tries to figure out what to do next
Two friends, the war in Iraq and its aftermath. The boredom and the fear of the war, written and illustrated by someone who was there. Everyone should read this graphic novel.
Warren Ellis can write Bond. A entertaining entry in the cannon.
A great story with wonderful artwork. Well worth reading.
Entertaining view of the history of dinosaurs. Perfect for a little older children interested in the subject. But adults will learn something as well.
Highly entertaining, fun for all ages. A good teaching tool for all. Maris Weeks is a true talent.
Marvelous.
A wonderful, illustrated look at your body, from bones to skin. Perfect for young and old.
Bleak story and art to match. Well worth reading.
Sam Glanzman is one of the great storytellers, as well as a great artist. This some of his best.
What's not to like, similar to Clan Apis. Very enjoyable, I look forward to the next volume.
Anything by Jason is wonderful.
Warren Ellis is amazing. Can't wait for part two.
A very noir adaptation. The art works with the tale.
Amazing story, well worth seeking out.

Autobiographical stories of one of the giants of the underground comix scene. Spain's work is amazing and somewhat stylized, but incredible in it's detail. A great illustrator, who deserves more acknowledgement.
Better than the usual. Trying to figure out our parents is often difficult, this is a good start. Look forward to seeing it move along.
Great art, good stories.
New Orleans, hard boiled private investigator, Jazz what is not to like. The artwork is gorgeous, this is noir at its best.
The future? With photo realistic art and a quirky story. It will make you want to read the next volume.
The good old days of Eerie are represented well. Lots of good art and an interesting tale.
Clever as all get out, typical Bourdain.
This will takeaway bit to digest.
You can never go wrong with Lewis Trondheim.
As cluttered as some of Thompson's later work. It is entertaining.

The only big city I ever lived in was Cleveland and this is a love note to that city, warts and all. Harvey has a wonderful eye and the ability to make the mundane shine. 
 I miss Cleveland and I miss Harvey, I undoubtedly passed by him on Conventry. I have a feeling I could have learn a lot from him had we met.
A very clever piece of fun. Hit all the right notes.
A twisted tale of espionage at the end of the Cold War.
How the Genie got out of the bottle.
The things in the corner that happen while your not looking, surreal and sad. Worth seeking out.
Reading Matt Kindt is like listening to Phillip Glass. A worthwhile challange.

Enjoyable trip through one persons edible life. Food memories and learning about good food. It also shows how parents can lead the way in making the entire food journey worth taking. Good for both young and old.
Deviously twisted, right up there with " Go The F#ck to Sleep. Recommend for all adult children.
Will keep you away from fast food joints forever.
The alphabet with Zombies, how can that not be fun!
Not a graphic novel, it is a Hellboy novel. Tom Piccirilli does a fine job of capturing the Hellboy mythology.
A collection of columns from the website Bleeding Cool. Short and to the point. Well worth seeking out.
Two short stories, with a lot of information on the origin of the character, lots of fun. Pat Mills writes very good illustrative prose.
Max Brooks strikes again, with more Zombie goodness. We see the beginnings of World War Z.
Just flat out wonderful. The stories and art go hand in hand, both are near perfect.
Learned more than I thought about the mess of Macedonia. Harvey teams with Heather Roberson to tell her tale of her trip and what she discovers.

A wonderful Gothic Horror novel. Mignola's illustrations add a certain creepiness to an already creepy novel. 
 My copy has a different cover and may have added content, like a collection of Mignola sketches and the original Steadfast Tin Solder tale. 
 Well worth seeking out.
Wonderful for all!
Laugh out loud fun.
I'm stunned! To tell you the truth, I never saw this coming. This is probably the most painful Sandman volume for me to read, and yet it was excellent in its depth and complexity of narrative.

Found this hidden little gem when I was at a (manga) library ( which was located at Ohayocon this year) . Just want to say that it was a really great read and something I highly reccommend this series. Going to give the whole series a 4.5 out of 5.

A man recalls his six year-old self, a summer that has stuck in his memory for years with hazy visions of his grandfather's failing amusement arcade. It was that year that the boy met Mr Punch, the puppet who entertains audiences by murdering his baby, wife, a policeman and then the judge. The boy doesn't find Punch's antics funny, in fact he's terrified, but when his grandfather allows a Punch show to open in his arcade as a last ditch effort to stay in business, the boy has no choice but to see more of Mr Punch. 
 I love Punch and Judy. They're creepy, and the photos used in this GN are collaged with drawings and produce some eerie results. There are some side stories about the various family members, so it's almost a short story. 4.5 stars

Britten is a depressed private detective who hates his life, mainly because he's known for delivering news that ends marriages, a fact that has earned him the nickname of "The Heartbreaker". Brulightly is his partner, a lecherous tea bag that sometimes has a good idea. The latest case involves a wealthy young woman who hires Britten to prove her fiance didn't commit suicide, as she believes he was murdered by the same someone who was blackmailing her father. The detectives quickly find that everyone the woman knows has something to hide. 
 A graphic novel, noir style. The mystery holds til the very end, where there are not one, but two twists. The artwork is mostly shades of gray, with Britten himself being a raccoon-eyed fellow who dresses like Gomez Adams.

As the unique citizens of Bon Temps gather one night at Merlotte's Bar, one of the customers reveals himself to be a Trickster from Native American mythology. Someone in the bar has enraged him, but everyone will take part in the creature's feeding by telling the most shameful secret of their life. 
 I'm not a real "True Blood" watcher, though my sister is nuts over the show. I don't read many graphic novels either, but this is a good one.

I hereby declare Sandman a part of me; so whoever loves Sandman loves me. 
 Wasn't it really inevitable, that the story of Dream had to end this way? I knew what was coming at every step I took towards the end of the story, and yet I read on. 
 And Gaiman didn't disappoint. It was not some grand battle, it was like how a fire dies, little by little till you cannot remember where. 
 Still, I loved the little moments of artistry, where the writing touches your heart and kills you at the same time. It was like being granted love and having it taken away - it's hard on you but, you would go through it all over again.
Most stressful and exciting IMO

Well I must say that this was better adapted than the manga version of Pride and Prejudice put out by this publisher thanks to no additional made up scenes and a closer adherence to the original characters. 
 My biggest complaint though is that manga will just never be a good medium for this type of story. Manga typically requires its characters to over express, and so much of Jane Austen's stories are a result of subtlety and nuances. Emma's reactions in this telling were often over the top and over exaggerated which often gave a different meaning to the scenes than in the original novel. 
 Many thanks to Netgalley and the publisher for a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

Loryn Brantz is another comic artist I have been following via Instagram for a long time now! I love her works mostly because I just totally relate to them all the time!! 
 This book in particular was funny, but I felt like I had seen a number of the comics before online already via Instagram or maybe Buzzfeed. I was expecting all the works to be new, so that was a surprise. She also used some of the same comics more than once and simply changed the captions. 
 Overall though still funny, relatable, witty, and cute! 
 Thanks to Netgalley and the publisher for a copy of this book for an honest review.

I have been following The Awkward Yeti on Instagram for a year...years...I don't know but its been a long time and I love his Heart and Brain comics. They are witty, ridiculously adorable, and funny! Sometimes even laugh out loud, crying funny! 
 This book seemed to revolve a lot around health, exercise, and anxiety, and I loved that Gallbladder made an appearance!! <3 
 Definitely one of my fave comic artists! 
 Thanks to Netgalley and the publisher for the book in exchange for an honest review.

This graphic novel had lovely art, but the story was a bit too disjointed for me. True the character is pretty much suffering from fever dreams, so thats a bit to be expected, but still hard to follow along.

This was just lovely! I am never not amazed by how kids see the world and interact with it, and treat one another. If you love manga you should totally read this sweet, surprising, and wonderful story to see how strong kids can be!

The combination of two things that I love - Austen and manga - should have resulted in perfection. Sadly that was not the case here. Frankly even finishing it was a chore. 
 This work was disappointing on many levels. First and foremost the story! This adaptation was almost painful to read at times with newly invented scenes and the changing of characterizations. Example: Elizabeth Bennet cries over Wickham after accidentally coming across him and Miss King walking together only to go running off into a storm where she looses her bonnet, becomes soaked, and needs Wickham to find her and save her bonnet. Ug...excuse me while I go vomit. 
 Also these additional scenes with terrible dialogue made for very choppy reading as the text went back and forth from new created text and Austen's original text. One minute Elizabeth is very articulately turning down Darcy's proposal using Austen's original text, but then when Mrs. Gardiner tells her they will be visiting Pemberly during their tour she replies: 
 Lizzy: "Oh no, I can't go there! I mean we can't! We! All of us! We shouldn't go! 
 Mrs. G: "But why not? They are often open for visitors." 
 Mr. G: "And they have the finest woods in the country!" 
 Lizzy: "Bears!The woods are full of bears! And boars! And...bees!" 
 Mrs G: "You have such a sense of humor." 
 Bears. BEARS! REALLY?! And so many exclamation points!!! 
 Second, the rules of society that are absolutely integral to Austen's works are completely flaunted here with men entering the heroines bedrooms, calling them by their first name, and always running around with their hair down. Yes, I get these things won't mean much to the casual manga reader, but they are necessary to the story and the characters for anyone who reads Austen's works. 
 Finally, the artwork was lacking in many areas. Some comics and manga strive for the unfinished look with characters/scenes purposely distressed/unfinished, but that was not the case here. Mostly the mistakes could be seen in characters hands. Many times the characters had hastily added fingers because they were originally only drawn with 4, or their fingers looked painfully broken, or the details were completely lacking and they all looked like they had webbed fingers a la Mr. Penguin in Batman. 
 All in all just so disappointing as I had been looking forward to reading this. I also have Emma and Sense and Sensibility from this same series, but I don't think I will read them as I expect them to be just as frustrating as this was. 
 Copy provided by NetGalley for review.

Will that was interesting. The first 80% of the volume was just meh. Like 2 stars really. But the last 20% was awesome. Like 4.5 stars so I'm splitting the different here. 
 The whole story line revolving around Bigby's and Snows cubs was a bit weird and frankly Therese was just so freaking annoying I couldn't wait to finish that section. The part about Bigby's fate though was great but also gave away quite a bit which makes me interested to keep reading.
